question: A company is building a solution to provide customers with an API that accesses financial data. The API backend needs to compute tax data for each request. The company anticipates greater demand to access the data during the last 3 months of each year. A solutions architect needs to design a scalable solution that can meet the regular demand and the peak demand at the end of each year. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Demand swings with the season. Which option scales automatically in both directions without managing servers?
keywords: compute tax data for each request
regular demand and the peak demand

options.A: Host the API on an Amazon EC2 instance that runs third-party software. Configure the EC2 instance to perform tax computations.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Create an AWS Lambda function to perform tax computations. Integrate the Lambda function with the REST API.
options.C: Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of two Amazon EC2 instances. Configure the EC2 instances to perform tax computations.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Configure an Amazon EC2 instance to perform tax computations. Integrate the EC2 instance with the REST API.

explanation: A is wrong: a single EC2 instance cannot scale for the year-end peak and is a single point of failure.
B is correct: API Gateway and Lambda scale automatically with each request, handle the year-end peak, and cost nothing during quiet periods.
C is wrong: two fixed EC2 instances do not scale out for the peak.
D is wrong: API Gateway scales, but one EC2 instance behind it becomes the bottleneck.
tldr: Seasonal, request-driven APIs suit API Gateway + Lambda: they scale with each request and cost nothing when idle.

wrong_reasons.A: a single EC2 instance cannot scale for the year-end peak and is a single point of failure.
wrong_reasons.C: two fixed EC2 instances do not scale out for the peak.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway scales, but one EC2 instance behind it becomes the bottleneck.

question: A company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts a website both on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company's on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company hosts the website on AWS in the eu-central-1 Region. The company wants to optimize load times for the website as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which Route 53 routing policy sends each user to the location with the lowest latency, including non-AWS locations tied to a Region?
keywords: on premises and in the AWS Cloud

options.A: Create a DNS record with a failover routing policy that routes all primary traffic to eu-central-1. Configure the routing policy to use the on-premises data center as the secondary location.
options.B: Create a DNS record with an IP-based routing policy. Configure specific IP ranges to return the value for the eu-central-1 website. Configure all other IP ranges to return the value for the on-premises website.
options.C: Create a DNS record with a latency-based routing policy. Associate the record for the on-premises data center with us-west-1.
options.D: Create a DNS record with a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.

explanation: A is wrong: failover sends everyone to eu-central-1 unless it fails, so users near us-west-1 get slow loads.
B is wrong: IP-based routing needs you to maintain IP ranges by hand and does not measure latency.
C is correct: latency-based routing sends each user to the faster location, and associating the on-premises record with us-west-1 lets Route 53 estimate its latency.
D is wrong: weighted routing splits traffic regardless of where users are.
tldr: Latency-based routing sends users to the lowest-latency endpoint; associate an on-premises endpoint with its nearest Region.

wrong_reasons.A: failover sends everyone to eu-central-1 unless it fails, so users near us-west-1 get slow loads.
wrong_reasons.B: IP-based routing needs you to maintain IP ranges by hand and does not measure latency.
wrong_reasons.D: weighted routing splits traffic regardless of where users are.

question: A company is developing a content sharing platform that currently handles 500 GB of user-generated media files. The company expects the amount of content to grow significantly in the future. The company needs a storage solution that can automatically scale, provide high durability, and allow direct user uploads from web browsers. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Unlimited growth, very high durability and browser uploads (for example with presigned URLs).
keywords: direct user uploads from web browsers

options.A: Store the data in an Amazon EBS volume with Multi-Attach enabled.
options.B: Store the data in an Amazon EFS Standard file system.
options.C: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Standard bucket.
options.D: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Express One Zone bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: EBS volumes have a fixed size, live in one Availability Zone and cannot take uploads from browsers.
B is wrong: EFS costs far more per GB and has no browser upload path.
C is correct: S3 Standard scales without limit, stores data across multiple Availability Zones for 11 nines of durability, supports direct browser uploads, and costs the least per GB here.
D is wrong: S3 Express One Zone stores data in a single Availability Zone at a higher price; it is built for low-latency access, not cheap durable storage.
tldr: User media at scale: S3 Standard gives unlimited, highly durable storage with direct browser uploads through presigned URLs.

wrong_reasons.A: EBS volumes have a fixed size, live in one Availability Zone and cannot take uploads from browsers.
wrong_reasons.B: EFS costs far more per GB and has no browser upload path.
wrong_reasons.D: S3 Express One Zone stores data in a single Availability Zone at a higher price; it is built for low-latency access, not cheap durable storage.

question: A company has deployed infrastructure on AWS. A solutions architect wants to create an AWS Lambda function that will retrieve data from an Amazon Aurora database. The Amazon Aurora database is in a private subnet in company's VPC. The VPC is named VPC1. The data is relational in nature. The Lambda function needs to access the data securely. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Lambda must run inside the VPC, and the security group rules must let it reach the database port.

options.A: Create the Lambda function. Configure VPC1 access for the function. Attach a security group named SG1 to both the Lambda function and the database. Configure the security group inbound and outbound rules to allow TCP traffic on Port 3306.
options.B: Create and launch a Lambda function in a new public subnet that is in a new VPC named VPC2. Create a peering connection between VPC1 and VPC2.
options.C: Create the Lambda function. Configure VPC1 access for the function. Assign a security group named SG1 to the Lambda function. Assign a second security group named SG2 to the database. Add an inbound rule to SG1 to allow TCP traffic from Port 3306.
options.D: Export the data from the Aurora database to Amazon S3. Create and launch a Lambda function in VPC1. Configure the Lambda function query the data from Amazon S3.

explanation: A is correct: attaching the function to VPC1 and giving both the function and the database a security group that allows TCP 3306 between its members lets the function reach the database privately.
B is wrong: a public subnet in a new VPC with peering is more complex and less secure than attaching the function to VPC1.
C is wrong: the inbound rule is on the wrong group; the database's group must allow traffic from the function, not the other way round.
D is wrong: exporting relational data to S3 loses the live database and adds a pipeline to maintain.
tldr: VPC-attached Lambda reaches a private database through security group rules: one shared group, or the database group allowing the function's group.

wrong_reasons.B: a public subnet in a new VPC with peering is more complex and less secure than attaching the function to VPC1.
wrong_reasons.C: the inbound rule is on the wrong group; the database's group must allow traffic from the function, not the other way round.
wrong_reasons.D: exporting relational data to S3 loses the live database and adds a pipeline to maintain.

question: A media streaming company needs to deploy its video processing application across multiple Availability Zones for high availability. The application consists of containerized microservices that process video files. The microservices must automatically recover from failures. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Containers across Availability Zones with automatic recovery, and no servers to manage.

options.A: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type.
options.B: Deploy the containers to Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes.
options.C: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type.
options.D: Deploy the containers to Amazon EC2 instances.

explanation: A is wrong: the EC2 launch type means managing and patching the container instances.
B is wrong: EKS with self-managed nodes is the most operational work of the container options.
C is correct: Fargate runs tasks across Availability Zones without servers, and the ECS service replaces failed tasks automatically.
D is wrong: plain EC2 instances have no container orchestration or automatic recovery.
tldr: ECS on Fargate runs containers across AZs and replaces failed tasks automatically, with no instances to manage.

wrong_reasons.A: the EC2 launch type means managing and patching the container instances.
wrong_reasons.B: EKS with self-managed nodes is the most operational work of the container options.
wrong_reasons.D: plain EC2 instances have no container orchestration or automatic recovery.

question: A solutions architect is designing a three-tier web application. The architecture consists of an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a web tier that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application tier with the business logic runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. The database tier consists of Microsoft SQL Server that runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. Security is a high priority for the company. Which combination of security group configurations should the solutions architect use? (Select THREE.)
hint: Chain the tiers: each tier accepts traffic only from the tier in front of it, referenced by security group.

options.A: Configure the security group for the web tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the ALB.
options.B: Configure the security group for the web tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
options.C: Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound Microsoft SQL Server traffic from the security group for the application tier.
options.D: Configure the security group for the database tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.
options.E: Configure the security group for the application tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the web tier.
options.F: Configure the security group for the application tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.

explanation: A is correct: the web tier should accept HTTPS only from the ALB's security group.
B is wrong: opening all outbound HTTPS to the internet is not needed to serve the application and weakens security.
C is correct: the database should accept SQL Server traffic only from the application tier's security group.
D is wrong: the database never starts connections to the web tier, and the web tier should not talk to the database at all.
E is correct: the application tier should accept HTTPS only from the web tier's security group.
F is wrong: the application tier sends SQL traffic to the database, not to the web tier.
tldr: Tiered security groups: web allows the ALB group, app allows the web group, database allows the app group.

wrong_reasons.B: opening all outbound HTTPS to the internet is not needed to serve the application and weakens security.
wrong_reasons.D: the database never starts connections to the web tier, and the web tier should not talk to the database at all.
wrong_reasons.F: the application tier sends SQL traffic to the database, not to the web tier.

question: A company uses AWS Cost Explorer to monitor its AWS costs. The company notices that Amazon EBS storage and snapshot costs increase every month. However, the company does not purchase additional EBS storage every month. The company wants to optimize monthly costs for its current storage usage. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Snapshots are piling up. What removes the unneeded ones and keeps new ones under a retention policy automatically?
keywords: does not purchase additional EBS storage

options.A: Use logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor the storage utilization of Amazon EBS. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
options.B: Use a custom script to monitor space usage. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
options.C: Delete all expired and unused snapshots to reduce snapshot costs.
options.D: Delete all nonessential snapshots. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create and manage the snapshots according to the company's snapshot policy requirements.

explanation: A is wrong: the storage is not growing, so shrinking volumes does not address snapshot growth, and EBS volumes cannot be made smaller in place.
B is wrong: a custom script adds work, and EBS volumes cannot be shrunk with Elastic Volumes.
C is wrong: a one-time cleanup helps, but snapshots will pile up again without a retention policy.
D is correct: deleting nonessential snapshots cuts today's cost, and Data Lifecycle Manager creates and expires snapshots by policy so the cost stops growing.
tldr: Growing EBS snapshot costs: delete the unneeded snapshots, then let Data Lifecycle Manager create and expire them by policy.

wrong_reasons.A: the storage is not growing, so shrinking volumes does not address snapshot growth, and EBS volumes cannot be made smaller in place.
wrong_reasons.B: a custom script adds work, and EBS volumes cannot be shrunk with Elastic Volumes.
wrong_reasons.C: a one-time cleanup helps, but snapshots will pile up again without a retention policy.

question: A company wants to optimize costs for an Amazon EC2 instance that has an attached Amazon EBS volume. The EC2 instance provides compute resources for an application that is often unused for scheduled periods of up to 30 days. The application requires the EC2 instance to retain its private IPv4 address. Additionally, the contents of the instance's RAM must be retained. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Keeping RAM contents across a stop is exactly one EC2 feature.
keywords: unused for scheduled periods of up to 30 days
contents of the instance's RAM must be retained

options.A: Create a daily Amazon Machine Image (AMI) snapshot backup of the EC2 instance. Terminate the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. Create a new EC2 instance from the most recent AMI backup when needed.
options.B: Ensure that hibernation mode is enabled on the EC2 instance. Transition the EC2 instance into hibernation mode during periods when the application is not required. Restart the EC2 instance when needed.
options.C: Create hourly backups of the EBS volume by using Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager. Terminate the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. When the application is required, create a new EC2 instance and restore the EBS volume from the most recent backup.
options.D: Ensure that stop protection is disabled on the EC2 instance. Stop the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. Restart the EC2 instance when needed.

explanation: A is wrong: a new instance from an AMI gets a new private IP address and loses the RAM contents.
B is correct: hibernation writes RAM to the EBS root volume, keeps the private IP address, and stops compute charges while the instance sleeps.
C is wrong: a new instance loses the private IP address and the RAM contents.
D is wrong: a normal stop keeps the private IP address, but the RAM contents are lost.
tldr: Hibernation saves RAM to the EBS root volume and keeps the private IP, while you pay nothing for the stopped instance's compute.

wrong_reasons.A: a new instance from an AMI gets a new private IP address and loses the RAM contents.
wrong_reasons.C: a new instance loses the private IP address and the RAM contents.
wrong_reasons.D: a normal stop keeps the private IP address, but the RAM contents are lost.

question: A company has a regional subscription-based streaming service that runs in a single AWS Region. The architecture consists of web servers and application servers on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in Auto Scaling groups behind Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancers. The architecture includes an Amazon Aurora global database cluster that extends across multiple Availability Zones. The company wants to expand globally and to ensure that its application has minimal downtime. Which solution will provide the MOST fault tolerance?
hint: Auto Scaling groups cannot span Regions. Which database feature replicates across Regions with fast promotion?

options.A: Extend the Auto Scaling groups for the web tier and the application tier to deploy instances in Availability Zones in a second Region. Use an Aurora global database to deploy the database in the primary Region and the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region.
options.B: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Add an Aurora PostgreSQL cross-Region Aurora Replica in the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region. Promote the secondary to primary as needed.
options.C: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Create an Aurora PostgreSQL database in the second Region. Use AWS DMS to replicate the primary database to the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region.
options.D: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Use an Amazon Aurora global database to deploy the database in the primary Region and the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region. Promote the secondary to primary as needed.

explanation: A is wrong: an Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions; each Region needs its own group.
B is wrong: a cross-Region replica works, but Aurora Global Database replicates faster and fails over more quickly.
C is wrong: replicating with DMS adds lag and a pipeline to run, compared with a built-in global database.
D is correct: a full stack in the second Region, Aurora Global Database with sub-second replication, and Route 53 failover give the most fault tolerance.
tldr: Multi-Region fault tolerance: a full stack in a second Region, Aurora Global Database, and Route 53 failover.

wrong_reasons.A: an Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions; each Region needs its own group.
wrong_reasons.B: a cross-Region replica works, but Aurora Global Database replicates faster and fails over more quickly.
wrong_reasons.C: replicating with DMS adds lag and a pipeline to run, compared with a built-in global database.

question: A company seeks a storage solution for its application. The solution must be highly available and scalable. The solution also must function as a file system, be mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises through native protocols, and have no minimum size requirements. The company has set up a Site-to-Site VPN for access from its on-premises network to its VPC. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
hint: Linux, NFS, elastic size, and reachable over VPN. For high availability, how many mount targets?
keywords: multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises

options.A: Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments.
options.B: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volumes.
options.C: Amazon EFS with multiple mount targets.
options.D: Amazon EFS with a single mount target and multiple access points.

explanation: A is wrong: FSx file systems are provisioned with a minimum storage size.
B is wrong: EBS Multi-Attach works only within one Availability Zone for specific instance types, and cannot be mounted from on premises.
C is correct: EFS is an elastic NFS file system with no minimum size, and a mount target in each Availability Zone keeps it highly available to instances in AWS and on premises.
D is wrong: a single mount target makes access depend on one Availability Zone.
tldr: EFS is elastic NFS for Linux with no minimum size; a mount target in each AZ keeps it highly available.

wrong_reasons.A: FSx file systems are provisioned with a minimum storage size.
wrong_reasons.B: EBS Multi-Attach works only within one Availability Zone for specific instance types, and cannot be mounted from on premises.
wrong_reasons.D: a single mount target makes access depend on one Availability Zone.

question: A company runs several AWS Lambda functions in the same AWS Region. The company notices that some calls to the Lambda functions are throttling. A business-critical function named Function A runs 100 times each second, for an average of 7 seconds. Other Lambda functions that run in the same AWS account exceed the default quota. The quota is 1,000 concurrent invocations across all functions in the same Region. A solutions architect needs to resolve the throttling issue for Function A within the account. The solutions architect must ensure that Function A meets its demands without impacting the other functions. Which combination of configurations will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
hint: Function A needs 100 x 7 = 700 concurrent executions. Reserving that leaves only 300 for everything else, so what else must change?

options.A: Set the reserved concurrency for Function A to 700.
options.B: Migrate Function A to another AWS account.
options.C: Set the provisioned concurrency for Function A to 700.
options.D: Increase the account's Lambda concurrency quota.
options.E: Migrate Lambda functions other than Function A to another AWS account.

explanation: A is correct: reserved concurrency of 700 (100 per second x 7 seconds) guarantees Function A the capacity it needs.
B is wrong: moving Function A to another account is far more work than configuration changes.
C is wrong: provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but does not guarantee capacity from the shared pool the way reserved concurrency does, and it costs more.
D is correct: reserving 700 leaves only 300 for the other functions, which already exceed the quota, so the account quota must be raised.
E is wrong: moving the other functions is a large migration, not a configuration change.
tldr: Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for a critical function; raise the account quota so other functions are not starved.

wrong_reasons.B: moving Function A to another account is far more work than configuration changes.
wrong_reasons.C: provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but does not guarantee capacity from the shared pool the way reserved concurrency does, and it costs more.
wrong_reasons.E: moving the other functions is a large migration, not a configuration change.

question: A company has a single AWS account. The company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple VPCs in one AWS Region. The company also runs workloads in an on-premises data center that connects to the company's AWS account by using AWS Direct Connect. The company needs all EC2 instances in the VPCs to resolve DNS queries for the internal example.com domain to the authoritative DNS server that is located in the on-premises data center. The solution must use private communication between the VPCs and the on-premises network. All route tables, network ACLs, and security groups are configured correctly between AWS and the on-premises data center. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
hint: Queries leave AWS through an outbound endpoint, a forwarding rule chooses which domain to send, and the rule must apply to every VPC.
keywords: authoritative DNS server that is located in the on-premises data center

options.A: Create an Amazon Route 53 inbound endpoint in all the workload VPCs.
options.B: Create an Amazon Route 53 outbound endpoint in one of the workload VPCS.
options.C: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the Forward type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.D: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the System type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.E: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with all the workload VPCs.
options.F: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the workload VPC with the new Route 53 endpoint.

explanation: A is wrong: inbound endpoints let on-premises servers query AWS DNS, which is the opposite direction.
B is correct: one outbound endpoint sends queries from AWS to the on-premises DNS server over Direct Connect.
C is correct: a Forward rule sends queries for the internal domain to the on-premises DNS server.
D is wrong: a System rule makes Resolver answer the queries itself instead of forwarding them.
E is correct: associating the rule with every workload VPC makes all instances use it, while the queries still leave through the one endpoint.
F is wrong: associating the rule only with the endpoint's VPC leaves the other VPCs unable to resolve the domain.
tldr: To resolve an on-premises domain from VPCs: Resolver outbound endpoint + Forward rule, then share or associate the rule with every VPC.

wrong_reasons.A: inbound endpoints let on-premises servers query AWS DNS, which is the opposite direction.
wrong_reasons.D: a System rule makes Resolver answer the queries itself instead of forwarding them.
wrong_reasons.F: associating the rule only with the endpoint's VPC leaves the other VPCs unable to resolve the domain.

question: A company runs production workloads in its AWS account. Multiple teams create and maintain the workloads. The company needs to be able to detect changes in resource configurations. The company needs to capture changes as configuration items without changing or modifying the existing resources. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Configuration items is AWS Config vocabulary.
keywords: without changing or modifying the existing resources

options.A: Use AWS Config. Start the configuration recorder for AWS resources to detect changes in resource configurations.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation. Initiate drift detection to capture changes in resource configurations.
options.C: Use Amazon Detective to detect, analyze, and investigate changes in resource configurations.
options.D: Use AWS Audit Manager to capture management events and global service events for resource configurations.

explanation: A is correct: the AWS Config recorder captures every configuration change as a configuration item without touching the resources.
B is wrong: drift detection only covers stacks created by CloudFormation, not resources made by hand.
C is wrong: Detective investigates security findings; it does not record configuration items.
D is wrong: Audit Manager collects evidence for audits; management events come from CloudTrail.
tldr: AWS Config records configuration items and change history for resources without modifying them.

wrong_reasons.B: drift detection only covers stacks created by CloudFormation, not resources made by hand.
wrong_reasons.C: Detective investigates security findings; it does not record configuration items.
wrong_reasons.D: Audit Manager collects evidence for audits; management events come from CloudTrail.

question: A company has several Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. These EC2 instances host applications that read and write large amounts of data to and from Amazon S3. Subnet routing currently directs all the traffic destined for the internet through a NAT gateway. The company wants to reduce the data transfer costs associated with the Amazon S3 communication. The solution must not affect the ability of the applications to communicate with Amazon S3 or the outside internet. The EC2 instances must continue to reside in a private subnet. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: S3 traffic from private subnets is going through the NAT gateway. Which free endpoint bypasses it?
keywords: large amounts of data to and from Amazon S3

options.A: Create an additional NAT gateway. Update the route table to route to the additional NAT gateway. Update the network ACL to allow Amazon S3 traffic.
options.B: Create an internet gateway. Update the route table to route traffic to the internet gateway. Update the network ACL to allow Amazon S3 traffic.
options.C: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Specify the route table to direct traffic to the gateway VPC endpoint. Attach an endpoint policy to the gateway VPC endpoint.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function outside the VPC to handle Amazon S3 requests. Attach an IAM policy to the EC2 instances that allows the EC2 instances to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation: A is wrong: another NAT gateway adds hourly and per-GB costs.
B is wrong: instances in a subnet routed to an internet gateway are no longer private, and they would need public IP addresses.
C is correct: a gateway endpoint sends S3 traffic privately at no charge, avoiding NAT processing fees, while other internet traffic still uses the NAT gateway.
D is wrong: sending S3 traffic through Lambda adds cost and complexity and does not remove data charges.
tldr: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 removes NAT gateway processing charges for S3 traffic from private subnets.

wrong_reasons.A: another NAT gateway adds hourly and per-GB costs.
wrong_reasons.B: instances in a subnet routed to an internet gateway are no longer private, and they would need public IP addresses.
wrong_reasons.D: sending S3 traffic through Lambda adds cost and complexity and does not remove data charges.

question: A company has an application that generates a large number of files. The file sizes vary between 1 KB and 10 MB. The company wants to build a store and forward solution that keeps the files in a temporary Amazon S3 location. The solution must then pre-process the files and archive the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select THREE.)
hint: Short-lived objects, many of them tiny. Watch minimum storage durations and per-object overhead in Glacier.

options.A: Configure the temporary S3 location to use the S3 Standard storage class.
options.B: Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new file is moved into the temporary S3 location.
options.C: Use event source mappings to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new file is moved into the temporary S3 location.
options.D: For files sized 128 KB or smaller, use an AWS Lambda function to add the files to a ZIP file. Offload the ZIP file to S3 Glacier when the ZIP file size reaches 1 MB.
options.E: For files sized 128 KB or smaller, use an AWS Lambda function to change the files' storage class to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).
options.F: Configure the temporary S3 location to use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class.

explanation: A is correct: files are stored only briefly, and S3 Standard has no minimum storage duration or minimum object size charges.
B is correct: S3 Event Notifications invoke Lambda directly when a file arrives, with no extra service.
C is wrong: event source mappings are for polling sources such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not for S3.
D is correct: Glacier adds about 40 KB of overhead per object, so zipping small files into larger archives before archiving cuts cost.
E is wrong: One Zone-IA bills objects under 128 KB as 128 KB and has a 30-day minimum, which is wasteful for temporary files.
F is wrong: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum and a 128 KB minimum billable size, which are expensive for short-lived small files.
tldr: Temporary data belongs in S3 Standard (no minimum duration); bundle tiny files before archiving to cut Glacier per-object overhead.

wrong_reasons.C: event source mappings are for polling sources such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not for S3.
wrong_reasons.E: One Zone-IA bills objects under 128 KB as 128 KB and has a 30-day minimum, which is wasteful for temporary files.
wrong_reasons.F: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum and a 128 KB minimum billable size, which are expensive for short-lived small files.

question: A company is using a loosely coupled serverless architecture on AWS. The architecture consists of multiple web applications and APIs distributed across multiple teams. The company uses AWS Control Tower to provision AWS accounts. The company's development teams use AWS CloudFormation. The company wants to improve trace monitoring and gain insight into how individual services in application stacks are performing. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Tracing across services is X-Ray. Where is tracing turned on for each Lambda function and API?

options.A: Enable AWS CloudTrail across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.B: Enable AWS X-Ray across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.C: Enable Amazon CloudWatch in the CloudFormation templates.
options.D: Enable AWS X-Ray in the CloudFormation templates.

explanation: A is wrong: CloudTrail records API calls, not request traces through services.
B is wrong: X-Ray is not something Control Tower turns on for accounts; tracing is enabled on each resource.
C is wrong: CloudWatch provides metrics and logs, not end-to-end traces.
D is correct: turning on X-Ray tracing for each function and API in the CloudFormation templates traces requests through every service in the stacks.
tldr: Enable X-Ray tracing on each resource (Lambda, API Gateway) through the teams' CloudFormation templates.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudTrail records API calls, not request traces through services.
wrong_reasons.B: X-Ray is not something Control Tower turns on for accounts; tracing is enabled on each resource.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudWatch provides metrics and logs, not end-to-end traces.

question: An application uses an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance. The RDS database is becoming low on disk space. A solutions architect wants to increase the disk space without downtime. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of effort?
hint: Which RDS setting grows storage by itself when free space runs low?

options.A: Enable storage autoscaling in RDS.
options.B: Increase the RDS database instance size.
options.C: Change the RDS database instance storage type to Provisioned IOPS.
options.D: Back up the RDS database, increase the storage capacity, restore the database, and stop the previous instance.

explanation: A is correct: storage autoscaling adds storage automatically, with no downtime, whenever free space runs low.
B is wrong: a larger instance class adds CPU and memory, not disk space.
C is wrong: changing the storage type changes performance, not capacity.
D is wrong: a backup and restore is manual work and causes downtime.
tldr: RDS storage autoscaling grows storage automatically without downtime when free space runs low.

wrong_reasons.B: a larger instance class adds CPU and memory, not disk space.
wrong_reasons.C: changing the storage type changes performance, not capacity.
wrong_reasons.D: a backup and restore is manual work and causes downtime.

question: A company has multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations with an organizational unit (OU) for the production account and another OU for the development account. Corporate policies state that developers must use only approved AWS services in the production account. What is the MOST operationally efficient solution to control the production account?
hint: Limit which services an entire account can use, in one place.
keywords: only approved AWS services in the production account

options.A: Create a customer managed policy in IAM. Apply the policy to all users within the production account.
options.B: Create a job function policy in IAM. Apply the policy to all users within the production OU.
options.C: Create a service control policy (SCP). Apply the SCP to the production OU.
options.D: Create an IAM policy. Apply the policy in Amazon API Gateway to restrict the production account.

explanation: A is wrong: IAM policies must be attached to every user and can be changed by account administrators.
B is wrong: IAM policies are not applied to OUs.
C is correct: an SCP on the production OU limits every principal in its accounts to the approved services, managed in one place.
D is wrong: API Gateway has nothing to do with restricting AWS service usage.
tldr: SCPs on an OU cap which services every principal in its accounts can use.

wrong_reasons.A: IAM policies must be attached to every user and can be changed by account administrators.
wrong_reasons.B: IAM policies are not applied to OUs.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway has nothing to do with restricting AWS service usage.

question: A company runs an application that uses Docker containers in an on-premises data center. The application runs on a container host that stores persistent data files in a local volume. Container instances use the stored persistent data. The company wants to migrate the application to fully managed AWS services. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Fully managed containers plus shared persistent file storage without code changes.
keywords: persistent data files in a local volume

options.A: Use Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes. Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance. Mount the EBS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.B: Use Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon EFS volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.C: Use Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure the application to use the DynamoDB table for persistent storage.
options.D: Use Amazon ECS with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Create an Amazon EFS volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.

explanation: A is wrong: self-managed nodes are not fully managed, and an EBS volume is tied to one instance.
B is correct: Fargate is fully managed, and EFS gives the containers persistent file storage without code changes.
C is wrong: switching to DynamoDB means rewriting the application's file access.
D is wrong: the EC2 launch type still requires managing instances.
tldr: Managed containers with persistent files: ECS on Fargate with an EFS volume mounted into the tasks.

wrong_reasons.A: self-managed nodes are not fully managed, and an EBS volume is tied to one instance.
wrong_reasons.C: switching to DynamoDB means rewriting the application's file access.
wrong_reasons.D: the EC2 launch type still requires managing instances.

question: A company wants to experiment with individual AWS accounts for its engineer team. The company wants to be notified as soon as the Amazon EC2 instance usage for a given month exceeds a specific threshold for each account. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Which service tracks spending against a threshold and alerts you?
keywords: exceeds a specific threshold for each account

options.A: Use Cost Explorer to create a daily report of costs by service. Filter the report by EC2 instances. Configure Cost Explorer to send an Amazon SES notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.B: Use Cost Explorer to create a monthly report of costs by service. Filter the report by EC2 instances. Configure Cost Explorer to send an Amazon SES notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.C: Use AWS Budgets to create a cost budget for each account. Set the period to monthly. Set the scope to EC2 instances. Set an alert threshold for the budget. Configure an Amazon SNS topic to receive a notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.D: Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report with hourly granularity. Integrate the report data with Amazon Athena. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule an Athena query. Configure an Amazon SNS topic to receive a notification when a threshold is exceeded.

explanation: A is wrong: Cost Explorer reports do not send threshold alerts through SES.
B is wrong: a monthly report arrives too late and cannot trigger threshold alerts.
C is correct: a monthly cost budget scoped to EC2 in each account alerts through SNS as soon as the threshold is crossed.
D is wrong: building a CUR, Athena and EventBridge pipeline is far more cost and work than a budget.
tldr: AWS Budgets tracks spending against thresholds per account or service and sends alerts through SNS or email.

wrong_reasons.A: Cost Explorer reports do not send threshold alerts through SES.
wrong_reasons.B: a monthly report arrives too late and cannot trigger threshold alerts.
wrong_reasons.D: building a CUR, Athena and EventBridge pipeline is far more cost and work than a budget.

question: A company is developing a latency-sensitive application. Part of the application includes several AWS Lambda functions that need to initialize as quickly as possible. The Lambda functions are written in Java and contain initialization code outside the handlers to load libraries, initialize classes, and generate unique IDs. Which solution will meet the startup performance requirement MOST cost-effectively?
hint: SnapStart snapshots the initialized function for free on Java, but anything in the snapshot, such as generated IDs, is reused by every environment.

options.A: Move all the initialization code to the handlers for each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for each Lambda function. Configure SnapStart to reference the $LATEST version of each Lambda function.
options.B: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Create an alias for each Lambda function. Configure each alias to point to its corresponding version. Set up a provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding alias.
options.C: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Set up a provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding version. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.
options.D: Update the Lambda functions to add a pre-snapshot hook. Move the code that generates unique IDs into the handlers. Publish a version of each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.

explanation: A is wrong: moving initialization into the handler defeats SnapStart, and SnapStart cannot be used with $LATEST.
B is wrong: provisioned concurrency works but is billed continuously, so it costs more than SnapStart.
C is wrong: SnapStart cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency, and paying for both is not cost-effective.
D is correct: SnapStart on published versions restores an initialized snapshot at no extra cost, and generating IDs in the handler (with a hook for snapshot preparation) keeps each ID unique.
tldr: Lambda SnapStart speeds up Java cold starts for free; keep uniqueness-dependent code out of the snapshot and enable it on published versions.

wrong_reasons.A: moving initialization into the handler defeats SnapStart, and SnapStart cannot be used with $LATEST.
wrong_reasons.B: provisioned concurrency works but is billed continuously, so it costs more than SnapStart.
wrong_reasons.C: SnapStart cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency, and paying for both is not cost-effective.

question: A media publishing company is building an application on AWS to give users the ability to print their own books. The application frontend runs on a Docker container. The amount of incoming orders varies significantly. The incoming orders can temporarily exceed the throughput of the company's book printing machines. Order-processing payloads are up to 4 MB in size. The company needs to develop a solution that can scale to handle incoming orders. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Orders must wait somewhere durable when the printers fall behind. Lambda@Edge is not a queue consumer.

options.A: Use Amazon SQS to queue incoming orders. Create an AWS Lambda@Edge function to process orders. Deploy the frontend application on Amazon EKS.
options.B: Use Amazon SNS to queue incoming orders. Create an AWS Lambda function to process orders. Deploy the frontend application on AWS Fargate.
options.C: Use Amazon SQS to queue incoming orders. Create an AWS Lambda function to process orders. Deploy the frontend application on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type.
options.D: Use Amazon SNS to queue incoming orders. Create an AWS Lambda@Edge function to process orders. Deploy the frontend application on Amazon EC2 instances.

explanation: A is wrong: Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations and cannot consume an SQS queue, and EKS adds operational work.
B is wrong: SNS pushes messages and does not queue them for later processing.

C is correct: SQS buffers orders until the printers catch up, Lambda processes them, and Fargate runs the frontend container without servers; payloads larger than the SQS message limit go in S3 with a pointer in the message.
D is wrong: SNS does not queue, and Lambda@Edge is not an order processor.
tldr: Buffer bursts in SQS for Lambda to consume; payloads above the SQS size limit go in S3 with a pointer in the message.

wrong_reasons.A: Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations and cannot consume an SQS queue, and EKS adds operational work.
wrong_reasons.B: SNS pushes messages and does not queue them for later processing.
wrong_reasons.D: SNS does not queue, and Lambda@Edge is not an order processor.

question: A company wants to implement a backup strategy for Amazon EC2 data and multiple Amazon S3 buckets. Because of regulatory requirements, the company must retain backup files for a specific time period. The company must not alter the files for the duration of the retention period. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Backups must be immutable for everyone during retention. Which vault lock mode cannot be removed?
keywords: must not alter the files for the duration of the retention period

options.A: Use AWS Backup to create a backup vault that has a vault lock in governance mode. Create the required backup plan.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create the required automated snapshot policy.
options.C: Use Amazon S3 File Gateway to create the backup. Configure the appropriate S3 Lifecycle management.
options.D: Use AWS Backup to create a backup vault that has a vault lock in compliance mode. Create the required backup plan.

explanation: A is wrong: governance mode can be removed by users with enough permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability.
B is wrong: Data Lifecycle Manager handles EBS snapshots only and does not lock them.
C is wrong: S3 File Gateway is for on-premises file access, not immutable backups.
D is correct: compliance mode vault lock stops anyone, including administrators, from changing or deleting backups during retention.
tldr: AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode makes backups immutable for the retention period; nobody can change or delete them.

wrong_reasons.A: governance mode can be removed by users with enough permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability.
wrong_reasons.B: Data Lifecycle Manager handles EBS snapshots only and does not lock them.
wrong_reasons.C: S3 File Gateway is for on-premises file access, not immutable backups.

question: A company runs a serverless architecture that supports multiple projects and resources in the company's AWS account. The company wants to use resource tags to monitor and analyze costs contributed by individual projects to the company's AWS bill. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Once activated as cost allocation tags, which tool groups and filters historical costs by tag?

options.A: Use AWS Budgets to set budgets for each project based on the tags assigned to resources.
options.B: Use AWS Billing Conductor to configure reports for each project based on the tags assigned to resources.
options.C: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to model cost reports for each project based on the tags assigned to resources.
options.D: Use AWS Cost Explorer to create custom cost allocation reports based on the tags assigned to resources.

explanation: A is wrong: Budgets alert on thresholds; they are not for analyzing past costs.
B is wrong: Billing Conductor is for custom billing rates across account groups, not tag-based analysis.
C is wrong: the Pricing Calculator estimates future costs; it has no real spending data.
D is correct: with cost allocation tags activated, Cost Explorer groups and filters actual costs by project tag.
tldr: Activate cost allocation tags, then analyze spending by tag in Cost Explorer.

wrong_reasons.A: Budgets alert on thresholds; they are not for analyzing past costs.
wrong_reasons.B: Billing Conductor is for custom billing rates across account groups, not tag-based analysis.
wrong_reasons.C: the Pricing Calculator estimates future costs; it has no real spending data.

question: A company is moving a legacy data processing application to the AWS Cloud. The application needs to run on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application must handle incoming traffic spikes and continue to work in the event of an application fault in one Availability Zone. The company requires that a Web Application Firewall (WAF) must be attached to the ALB. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Survive an AZ problem, scale for spikes, and attach WAF, which works with ALBs.
keywords: application fault in one Availability Zone

options.A: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that is in a single Availability Zone. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic across the EC2 instances. Use AWS WAF to associate a web ACL with the ALB.
options.B: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic across the EC2 instances. Use AWS WAF to associate a web ACL with the ALB.
options.C: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups across multiple AWS Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to distribute traffic across the Auto Scaling groups. Use AWS WAF to associate a web ACL with the Route 53 routing configuration.
options.D: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to distribute traffic across the EC2 instances. Use AWS WAF to associate a web ACL with the NLB.

explanation: A is wrong: a single Availability Zone does not survive a fault in that zone.
B is correct: an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones behind an ALB absorbs spikes and zone faults, and a WAF web ACL attaches directly to the ALB.
C is wrong: multiple Regions go beyond the requirement, and WAF cannot attach to Route 53.
D is wrong: WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer.
tldr: Multi-AZ Auto Scaling behind an ALB handles spikes and AZ faults; attach an AWS WAF web ACL to the ALB.

wrong_reasons.A: a single Availability Zone does not survive a fault in that zone.
wrong_reasons.C: multiple Regions go beyond the requirement, and WAF cannot attach to Route 53.
wrong_reasons.D: WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer.

question: A company runs a non-production application. The application uses an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server database. The application uses SSD storage. The database needs low-latency access to block-level storage. The company wants to move the application and the database to the AWS Cloud. The company does not want to make any changes to the application and database architecture. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LOWEST storage latency?
hint: Keep SQL Server self-managed on EC2 to avoid changes, then pick the lowest-latency block storage.
keywords: does not want to make any changes

options.A: Install SQL Server on an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system with SSD storage.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon RDS for SQL Server instance. Use an Amazon EFS file system.
options.C: Install SQL Server on an Amazon EC2 instance. Use an Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Block Express volume.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon RDS for SQL Server instance. Use an Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume.

explanation: A is wrong: FSx for Windows is file storage over SMB, which adds latency compared with block storage.
B is wrong: RDS cannot use EFS, and moving to RDS changes the architecture.
C is correct: SQL Server on EC2 keeps the architecture unchanged, and io2 Block Express gives sub-millisecond, highest-performance block storage.
D is wrong: moving to RDS changes the architecture, and gp3 has higher latency than io2 Block Express.
tldr: Lowest-latency block storage for a self-managed database: EBS io2 Block Express.

wrong_reasons.A: FSx for Windows is file storage over SMB, which adds latency compared with block storage.
wrong_reasons.B: RDS cannot use EFS, and moving to RDS changes the architecture.
wrong_reasons.D: moving to RDS changes the architecture, and gp3 has higher latency than io2 Block Express.

question: A company needs to deploy a Microsoft SQL Server database on AWS. The database must handle real-time transactions. The database must be highly available within an AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Managed SQL Server with automatic failover across Availability Zones.
keywords: highly available within an AWS Region

options.A: Install SQL Server on two Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Ensure data synchronization through custom scripts.
options.B: Use Amazon Aurora to host the database. Enable Aurora replicas in different Availability Zones.
options.C: Create an Amazon RDS for SQL Server instance. Configure automated snapshots.
options.D: Create an Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ deployment.

explanation: A is wrong: self-managed replication with scripts is fragile and a lot of work.
B is wrong: Aurora does not run SQL Server.
C is wrong: snapshots are backups; restoring one is not high availability.
D is correct: a Multi-AZ deployment keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically, fully managed.
tldr: RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ gives managed, synchronous standby and automatic failover within a Region.

wrong_reasons.A: self-managed replication with scripts is fragile and a lot of work.
wrong_reasons.B: Aurora does not run SQL Server.
wrong_reasons.C: snapshots are backups; restoring one is not high availability.

question: A solutions architect has designed an application that gives users the ability to access images that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The application uses an Amazon EC2 instance hosted in a private VPC that has a VPC ID of vpc-11aabb22. The solutions architect enabled the block public access feature on the S3 bucket. The bucket is hosted in the us-west-2 Region of account 123456789012. The solutions architect needs to ensure that only resources within the VPC that hosts the EC2 instance can access the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Allow statements add access; to restrict access to one VPC, deny every request that does not come from it.

options.A: Create an S3 bucket policy statement that has a Deny effect and a Condition that includes "StringNotEquals": {"aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-11aabb22"}.
options.B: Create an S3 bucket policy statement that has an Allow effect and a Resource of "arn:aws:ec2:us-west-2:123456789012:vpc/vpc-11aabb22".
options.C: Create an S3 bucket policy statement that has an Allow effect and a Condition that includes "StringNotEquals": {"aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-11aabb22"}.
options.D: Create an S3 bucket policy statement that has a Deny effect and a Condition that includes "StringNotEquals": {"aws:PrincipalAccount": "123456789012"}.

explanation: A is correct: denying every request whose aws:SourceVpc is not vpc-11aabb22 ensures only traffic from that VPC, through its endpoint, reaches the bucket.
B is wrong: a VPC ARN is not a valid principal or resource in a bucket policy.
C is wrong: an Allow with StringNotEquals would allow access from everywhere except the VPC.
D is wrong: restricting to the account allows any principal in the account from any network.
tldr: Restrict an S3 bucket to one VPC with a Deny statement using StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpc (traffic via a VPC endpoint).

wrong_reasons.B: a VPC ARN is not a valid principal or resource in a bucket policy.
wrong_reasons.C: an Allow with StringNotEquals would allow access from everywhere except the VPC.
wrong_reasons.D: restricting to the account allows any principal in the account from any network.

question: A company is planning to deploy a managed MySQL database solution for its nonproduction applications. The company plans to run the system for several years on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: A managed database that runs steadily for years: what gives the biggest discount?

options.A: Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. Purchase a Reserved Instance.
options.B: Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. Use the instance on an on-demand basis.
options.C: Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with writer and reader nodes. Use the cluster on an on-demand basis.
options.D: Create an Amazon EC2 instance. Manually install and configure MySQL Server on the instance.

explanation: A is correct: RDS is managed, and a Reserved Instance for a database that runs for years costs much less than On-Demand.
B is wrong: On-Demand pricing costs more for a database that runs continuously for years.
C is wrong: an Aurora cluster with writer and reader nodes costs more than a non-production workload needs.
D is wrong: self-managed MySQL on EC2 is not a managed database and adds operational work.
tldr: A managed database running steadily for years is cheapest on RDS with a Reserved Instance.

wrong_reasons.B: On-Demand pricing costs more for a database that runs continuously for years.
wrong_reasons.C: an Aurora cluster with writer and reader nodes costs more than a non-production workload needs.
wrong_reasons.D: self-managed MySQL on EC2 is not a managed database and adds operational work.

question: An adventure company has launched a new feature on its mobile app. Users can use the feature to upload their hiking and rafting photos and videos anytime. The photos and videos are stored in Amazon S3 Standard storage in an S3 bucket and are served through Amazon CloudFront. The company needs to optimize the cost of the storage. A solutions architect discovers that most of the uploaded photos and videos are accessed infrequently after 30 days. However, some of the uploaded photos and videos are accessed frequently after 30 days. The solutions architect needs to implement a solution that maintains millisecond retrieval availability of the photos and videos at the lowest possible cost. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Access patterns differ per object and are not predictable. Which storage class moves each object by itself, with no retrieval fees?
keywords: some of the uploaded photos and videos are accessed frequently

options.A: Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the S3 bucket.
options.B: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition image objects and video objects from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
options.C: Replace Amazon S3 with an Amazon EFS file system that is mounted on Amazon EC2 instances.
options.D: Add a Cache-Control: max-age header to the S3 image objects and S3 video objects. Set the header to 30 days.

explanation: A is correct: Intelligent-Tiering moves each object to cheaper tiers when it goes unused and back when it is accessed, keeping millisecond access with no retrieval fees.
B is wrong: Deep Archive retrievals take hours, not milliseconds.
C is wrong: EFS costs more than S3 and needs EC2 instances to serve the files.
D is wrong: Cache-Control headers affect caching in CloudFront and browsers, not S3 storage cost.
tldr: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between access tiers automatically, keeps millisecond access and has no retrieval fees.

wrong_reasons.B: Deep Archive retrievals take hours, not milliseconds.
wrong_reasons.C: EFS costs more than S3 and needs EC2 instances to serve the files.
wrong_reasons.D: Cache-Control headers affect caching in CloudFront and browsers, not S3 storage cost.

question: A solutions architect needs to configure automatic rotation for Amazon RDS database credentials. The credentials must rotate every 30 days. The solution must integrate with Amazon RDS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Which service has built-in, managed rotation for RDS credentials?
keywords: automatic rotation for Amazon RDS database credentials

options.A: Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a secure string. Configure automatic rotation with a rotation interval of 30 days.
options.B: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure automatic rotation with a rotation interval of 30 days.
options.C: Store the credentials in a file in an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy an AWS Lambda function to automatically rotate the credentials every 30 days.
options.D: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Deploy an AWS Lambda function to automatically rotate the credentials every 30 days.

explanation: A is wrong: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation.
B is correct: Secrets Manager integrates with RDS and rotates the credentials on a 30-day schedule using managed rotation.
C is wrong: credentials in an S3 file with a custom Lambda rotator is insecure and custom work.
D is wrong: writing your own rotation Lambda is unnecessary, because Secrets Manager provides managed rotation for RDS.
tldr: Secrets Manager has managed, built-in rotation for RDS credentials; set the schedule and it handles the rest.

wrong_reasons.A: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation.
wrong_reasons.C: credentials in an S3 file with a custom Lambda rotator is insecure and custom work.
wrong_reasons.D: writing your own rotation Lambda is unnecessary, because Secrets Manager provides managed rotation for RDS.

question: A large company runs unique workloads in different Amazon VPCs. Each VPC uses a common set of VPC interface endpoints. The company will add new workloads to new VPCs as the company grows. The company wants to centralize the endpoints and the DNS management of the endpoints. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Interface endpoints can be centralized; gateway endpoints cannot. Route 53 profiles are shared with AWS RAM, and a transit gateway scales better than peering.
keywords: common set of VPC interface endpoints
centralize the endpoints and the DNS management

options.A: Create a shared services VPC that contains the interface endpoints. Create an Amazon Route 53 profile. Associate the profile with the VPC and endpoints. Share the profile by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) Connect the shared services VPC to the workload VPCs by using peering connections.
options.B: Create a shared services VPC that contains gateway endpoints. Create an Amazon Route 53 profile. Associate the profile with the VPC and endpoints. Share the profile by using Amazon VPC Lattice. Connect the shared services VPC to the workload VPCs by using a transit gateway.
options.C: Create a shared services VPC that contains the interface endpoints. Create an Amazon Route 53 profile. Associate the profile with the VPC and endpoints. Share the profile by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Connect the shared services VPC to the workload VPCs by using a transit gateway.
options.D: Create a shared services VPC that contains gateway endpoints. Create an Amazon Route 53 profile. Associate the profile with the VPC and endpoints. Share the profile by using Amazon VPC Lattice. Connect the shared services VPC to the workload VPCs by using peering connections.

explanation: A is wrong: peering every workload VPC to the shared VPC becomes hard to manage as VPCs are added.
B is wrong: gateway endpoints cannot be reached from other VPCs, and Route 53 profiles are shared with AWS RAM, not VPC Lattice.
C is correct: interface endpoints in a shared services VPC, DNS shared through a Route 53 profile with AWS RAM, and a transit gateway to reach new VPCs is the scalable, centralized design.
D is wrong: gateway endpoints cannot be centralized, VPC Lattice does not share Route 53 profiles, and peering does not scale well.
tldr: Centralize interface endpoints in a shared services VPC, share DNS with a Route 53 profile through AWS RAM, and connect VPCs with a transit gateway.

wrong_reasons.A: peering every workload VPC to the shared VPC becomes hard to manage as VPCs are added.
wrong_reasons.B: gateway endpoints cannot be reached from other VPCs, and Route 53 profiles are shared with AWS RAM, not VPC Lattice.
wrong_reasons.D: gateway endpoints cannot be centralized, VPC Lattice does not share Route 53 profiles, and peering does not scale well.

question: A company wants to migrate an on-premises, traditional three-tier web application to AWS. The migrated solution must have high availability because of the large number of transactions that the web application processes. The company plans to use Amazon EC2 instances for the processing tier. The company needs a solution that provides fault tolerance and scalability for the database and load distribution tiers. The web application serves HTTPS traffic and uses URL path-based routing. Which combination of options will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: One option is a highly available relational database; the other is the load balancer that routes by URL path.
keywords: fault tolerance and scalability for the database and load distribution tiers

options.A: Use Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment for the database tier.
options.B: Use Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) with Cluster Mode enabled for the database tier.
options.C: Use Amazon Route 53 to load balance the web application.
options.D: Use an Application Load Balancer to route traffic to the web application.
options.E: Use a Network Load Balancer to route traffic to the web application.

explanation: A is correct: RDS Multi-AZ gives the database tier automatic failover to a standby in another Availability Zone.
B is wrong: ElastiCache is a cache, not the system of record for a transactional database.
C is wrong: Route 53 resolves names; it does not do path-based routing or load distribution of HTTPS requests.
D is correct: an ALB terminates HTTPS, routes by URL path and spreads load across instances in several Availability Zones.
E is wrong: a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route by URL path.
tldr: Path-based HTTPS routing needs an ALB; a highly available relational tier is RDS Multi-AZ.

wrong_reasons.B: ElastiCache is a cache, not the system of record for a transactional database.
wrong_reasons.C: Route 53 resolves names; it does not do path-based routing or load distribution of HTTPS requests.
wrong_reasons.E: a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route by URL path.

question: A company uses an organization in AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts. Multiple business units use the AWS accounts. The company has multiple offices around the world. The company needs to update security group rules to allow new CIDR ranges or to remove unused CIDR ranges across the organization. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Keep the CIDR list in one object that many security groups can reference, and share it across accounts.
keywords: allow new CIDR ranges or to remove unused CIDR ranges across the organization

options.A: Create VPC security groups in the organization's management account. Associate the security groups with VPCs in the management account. Update the security group rules when a CIDR range update is necessary across the organization.
options.B: Create a customer-managed prefix list for the VPC. Include the desired CIDR ranges in the prefix list. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the prefix list across the organization. Use the prefix list in the security groups across the organization.
options.C: Create an AWS managed prefix list for the VPC. Reference the prefix list in security groups across the organization. Use an AWS Lambda function to update the prefix list automatically when the CIDR ranges change.
options.D: Create security groups in a central AWS account. Create an AWS Firewall Manager common security group policy for the organization. Select the security groups as primary groups in the policy.

explanation: A is wrong: security groups in the management account cannot be used by VPCs in other accounts.
B is correct: one customer-managed prefix list shared through AWS RAM is referenced by every security group, so a single update applies everywhere at no extra cost.
C is wrong: AWS managed prefix lists are maintained by AWS for AWS services; you cannot create or edit them.
D is wrong: Firewall Manager works but has an ongoing cost, which is more than a shared prefix list needs.
tldr: A customer-managed prefix list shared with AWS RAM lets security groups across the organization reference one CIDR list you update in one place.

wrong_reasons.A: security groups in the management account cannot be used by VPCs in other accounts.
wrong_reasons.C: AWS managed prefix lists are maintained by AWS for AWS services; you cannot create or edit them.
wrong_reasons.D: Firewall Manager works but has an ongoing cost, which is more than a shared prefix list needs.

question: A company uses an existing AWS account that is dedicated to management. The company needs to create separate accounts for multiple developer teams. Then, the developer accounts can host resources outside of the management account. A security team requires a centralized capability to audit user activity and to identify the resources that the teams create. Additionally, the company must apply a standard set of controls to any new accounts upon creation. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Standard controls applied to every new account at creation is what a landing zone and Account Factory provide.
keywords: standard set of controls to any new accounts upon creation

options.A: Enable AWS Organizations. Create a new security account. Configure AWS Config as an aggregator. Create new developer accounts by using Organizations. Configure AWS Config with developer accounts as aggregator sources.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket in the management account. Create new developer accounts by using AWS Organizations. Configure AWS CloudTrail in each new account. Use the S3 bucket in the management account as the target.
options.C: Enable AWS Organizations. Configure an AWS Control Tower landing zone. Set up an AWS CloudTrail organizational trail in the management account. Create new developer accounts by using Account Factory.
options.D: Enable AWS Organizations. Set up an AWS CloudTrail organizational trail in the management account. Create new developer accounts by using AWS Organizations.

explanation: A is wrong: Config aggregation shows resources but does not apply standard controls to new accounts.
B is wrong: setting up CloudTrail by hand in each account is manual and applies no controls.
C is correct: a Control Tower landing zone applies standard controls to every account created with Account Factory, and the organization trail audits user activity centrally.
D is wrong: an organization trail audits activity, but Organizations alone does not apply standard controls at account creation.
tldr: Control Tower sets up a governed landing zone: an organization trail for auditing and Account Factory to create accounts with standard controls.

wrong_reasons.A: Config aggregation shows resources but does not apply standard controls to new accounts.
wrong_reasons.B: setting up CloudTrail by hand in each account is manual and applies no controls.
wrong_reasons.D: an organization trail audits activity, but Organizations alone does not apply standard controls at account creation.

question: A company uses an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster to store structured sensitive data about its customers. To meet compliance requirements, the company introduced a policy that all the customer-related data must be encrypted at rest. Which solution will ensure that the company is compliant with the policy with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing Aurora cluster. Which path creates an encrypted copy with the least work?

options.A: Modify the existing Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster to enable encryption at rest by using an AWS KMS key. Use the encrypted cluster to store the customer data.
options.B: Create a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. Enable encryption by using an AWS KMS key during database creation. Manually migrate the data from the old database to the new database.
options.C: Create a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. Enable encryption by using server-side encryption (SSE) during database creation. Migrate the data from the old database to the new database.
options.D: Create a snapshot of the existing Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. Enable encryption by using an AWS KMS key. Restore the snapshot to a new Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.

explanation: A is wrong: encryption cannot be enabled on an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster.
B is wrong: migrating the data by hand is much more work than restoring a snapshot.
C is wrong: Aurora encryption uses KMS keys, and a manual migration is extra work.
D is correct: restoring a snapshot of the cluster to a new cluster with a KMS key produces an encrypted copy of all the data with little effort.
tldr: To encrypt an unencrypted Aurora cluster, snapshot it and restore to a new cluster with a KMS key.

wrong_reasons.A: encryption cannot be enabled on an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster.
wrong_reasons.B: migrating the data by hand is much more work than restoring a snapshot.
wrong_reasons.C: Aurora encryption uses KMS keys, and a manual migration is extra work.

question: A company receives data from several sources and stores the data in an Amazon S3 data lake. The company transforms the data and ingests it into multiple downstream data stores, including databases and data warehouses. A solutions architect wants to design an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline to orchestrate a process to prepare and load the data for analytics activities. The processed data must also be available for stakeholders through dashboards and visualizations. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
hint: Managed ETL, managed orchestration and a managed BI service.

options.A: Use Amazon EMR and a custom Scala script to create ETL pipelines. Use an AWS Lambda function to orchestrate the workflow. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to generate dashboards and visualizations.
options.B: Use AWS Glue to create ETL pipelines. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Use Amazon QuickSight to generate dashboards and visualizations.
options.C: Use an AWS Lambda function to create ETL pipelines. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Use Amazon QuickSight to generate dashboards and visualizations.
options.D: Use custom scripts that run on Amazon EC2 instances to create ETL pipelines. Use AWS Glue to orchestrate the workflow. Use AWS Glue DataBrew to generate dashboards and visualizations.

explanation: A is wrong: EMR with custom Scala and Lambda orchestration is the most development work.
B is correct: Glue provides managed ETL, Step Functions orchestrates the steps, and QuickSight builds dashboards, with little code.
C is wrong: writing ETL logic in Lambda is more development and hits Lambda limits on large data.
D is wrong: custom scripts on EC2 are more work, and DataBrew prepares data; it does not build dashboards.
tldr: Serverless analytics stack: Glue for ETL, Step Functions for orchestration, QuickSight for dashboards.

wrong_reasons.A: EMR with custom Scala and Lambda orchestration is the most development work.
wrong_reasons.C: writing ETL logic in Lambda is more development and hits Lambda limits on large data.
wrong_reasons.D: custom scripts on EC2 are more work, and DataBrew prepares data; it does not build dashboards.

question: A company is moving data from an on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud. The company must store all its data in an Amazon S3 bucket. To comply with regulations, the company must also ensure that the data will be protected against overwriting indefinitely. Which solution will ensure that the data in the S3 bucket cannot be overwritten?
hint: Object Lock needs versioning. Which Object Lock setting has no end date?

options.A: Enable versioning for the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) to protect the data.
options.B: Disable versioning for the S3 bucket. Configure S3 Object Lock for the S3 bucket with a retention period of 1 year.
options.C: Enable versioning for the S3 bucket. Configure S3 Object Lock for the S3 bucket with a legal hold.
options.D: Configure S3 Storage Lens for the S3 bucket. Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) to protect the data.

explanation: A is wrong: versioning keeps old versions but does not stop objects from being overwritten or deleted.
B is wrong: Object Lock requires versioning, and a 1-year retention period is not indefinite.
C is correct: Object Lock on a versioned bucket with a legal hold protects the data indefinitely, until the hold is removed.
D is wrong: Storage Lens is analytics, and encryption does not prevent overwrites.
tldr: An S3 Object Lock legal hold protects object versions indefinitely until it is removed; Object Lock requires versioning.

wrong_reasons.A: versioning keeps old versions but does not stop objects from being overwritten or deleted.
wrong_reasons.B: Object Lock requires versioning, and a 1-year retention period is not indefinite.
wrong_reasons.D: Storage Lens is analytics, and encryption does not prevent overwrites.
