question: A company runs an application that uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The application receives traffic only on weekdays during business hours. The company wants to optimize costs and reduce operational overhead based on this usage. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Stop paying for the database outside business hours without writing code.
keywords: only on weekdays during business hours
optimize costs and reduce operational overhead

options.A: Use the Instance Scheduler on AWS to configure start and stop schedules.
options.B: Turn off automatic backups. Create weekly manual snapshots of the database.
options.C: Create a custom AWS Lambda function to start and stop the database based on minimum CPU utilization.
options.D: Purchase All Upfront reserved DB instances.

explanation: A is correct: Instance Scheduler on AWS stops the database outside business hours on a schedule, cutting cost with no custom code.
B is wrong: turning off automatic backups weakens recovery and barely affects cost.
C is wrong: a custom Lambda function based on CPU is code to maintain and may stop the database at the wrong time.
D is wrong: reserved instances pay for 24/7 capacity that sits idle most of the week.
tldr: Instance Scheduler on AWS starts and stops RDS and EC2 on a schedule with no custom code.

wrong_reasons.B: turning off automatic backups weakens recovery and barely affects cost.
wrong_reasons.C: a custom Lambda function based on CPU is code to maintain and may stop the database at the wrong time.
wrong_reasons.D: reserved instances pay for 24/7 capacity that sits idle most of the week.

question: A company has set up hybrid connectivity between an on-premises data center and AWS by using AWS Site-to-Site VPN. The company is migrating a workload to AWS. The company sets up a VPC that has two public subnets and two private subnets. The company wants to monitor the total packet loss and round-trip-time (RTT) between the data center and AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Is there a managed CloudWatch feature that probes hybrid network paths?

options.A: Use Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor to set up Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) probe monitoring from each subnet to the on-premises destination.
options.B: Create an Amazon EC2 instance in each subnet. Create a scheduled job to send Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) packets to the on-premises destination.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function in each subnet. Write a script to perform Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) connectivity checks.
options.D: Create an AWS Batch job in each subnet. Write a script to perform Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) connectivity checks.

explanation: A is correct: CloudWatch Network Monitor runs managed ICMP or TCP probes from the subnets and reports packet loss and RTT with no infrastructure.
B is wrong: EC2 instances running scheduled jobs are infrastructure and scripts to maintain.
C is wrong: custom Lambda scripts are code to maintain, and Lambda is not suited to continuous network probing.
D is wrong: Batch jobs are built for batch computing, not continuous network monitoring.
tldr: CloudWatch Network Monitor measures packet loss and latency to on-premises destinations with managed probes.

wrong_reasons.B: EC2 instances running scheduled jobs are infrastructure and scripts to maintain.
wrong_reasons.C: custom Lambda scripts are code to maintain, and Lambda is not suited to continuous network probing.
wrong_reasons.D: Batch jobs are built for batch computing, not continuous network monitoring.

question: A company is building a serverless application that processes large volumes of data from a mobile app. The application uses an AWS Lambda function to process the data and store the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company needs to ensure that the application can recover from failures and continue processing data without losing any records. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Failed records need a durable place to wait so they can be retried.

options.A: Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for the Lambda function. Redrive failed records from the dead-letter queue back to the function for reprocessing, and use retries with an exponential backoff algorithm.
options.B: Configure the Lambda function to read records from Amazon Data Firehose. Replay the Firehose records in case of any failures.
options.C: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to store failed records. Configure AWS Lambda to retry failed records from OpenSearch Service. Use Amazon EventBridge to orchestrate the retry logic.
options.D: Use Amazon SNS to store the failed records. Configure Lambda to retry failed records from the SNS topic. Use Amazon API Gateway to orchestrate the retry calls.

explanation: A is correct: failed records land in an SQS dead-letter queue instead of being lost, and redriving them back to the function, with retries that use exponential backoff, lets processing recover without losing data.
B is wrong: Firehose delivers data to destinations; it is not a source Lambda reads from, and it cannot replay records.
C is wrong: OpenSearch is a search engine, not a retry queue.
D is wrong: SNS does not store messages, so failed records would be lost.
tldr: Send failed Lambda events to an SQS dead-letter queue, then redrive them for reprocessing with exponential backoff so no records are lost; Lambda does not read its own DLQ.

wrong_reasons.B: Firehose delivers data to destinations; it is not a source Lambda reads from, and it cannot replay records.
wrong_reasons.C: OpenSearch is a search engine, not a retry queue.
wrong_reasons.D: SNS does not store messages, so failed records would be lost.

question: A company has a web application that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are configured to stream logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The company needs to receive an Amazon SNS notification when the number of application error messages exceeds a defined threshold within a 5-minute period. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Turn matching log lines into a metric, then alarm on the metric.
keywords: stream logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs
exceeds a defined threshold within a 5-minute period

options.A: Rewrite the application code to stream application logs to Amazon SNS. Configure an SNS topic to send a notification when the number of errors exceeds the defined threshold within a 5-minute period.
options.B: Configure a subscription filter on the CloudWatch Logs log group. Configure the filter to send an SNS notification when the number of errors exceeds the defined threshold within a 5-minute period.
options.C: Install and configure the Amazon Inspector agent on the EC2 instances to monitor for errors. Configure Amazon Inspector to send an SNS notification when the number of errors exceeds the defined threshold within a 5-minute period.
options.D: Create a CloudWatch metric filter to match the application error pattern in the log data. Set up a CloudWatch alarm based on the new custom metric. Configure the alarm to send an SNS notification when the number of errors exceeds the defined threshold within a 5-minute period.

explanation: A is wrong: rewriting the application is unnecessary, and SNS cannot count errors over a time period.
B is wrong: subscription filters stream log events to a destination; they cannot count or apply thresholds.
C is wrong: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not application errors.
D is correct: a metric filter counts error lines, and an alarm on that metric over 5 minutes sends the SNS notification.
tldr: CloudWatch Logs metric filter turns error lines into a metric; a CloudWatch alarm on it notifies SNS.

wrong_reasons.A: rewriting the application is unnecessary, and SNS cannot count errors over a time period.
wrong_reasons.B: subscription filters stream log events to a destination; they cannot count or apply thresholds.
wrong_reasons.C: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not application errors.

question: A solutions architect launches an Amazon EC2 instance inside a new VPC. The solutions architect configures network ACL rules and security group rules that allow the appropriate traffic to flow to and from the instance. An Elastic IP address is associated with the instance. The solutions architect needs to be able to access the instance from the internet. Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to accomplish this goal? (Select TWO.)
hint: An internet gateway attaches to one thing, and a route sends traffic toward it.
keywords: access the instance from the internet

options.A: Create an internet gateway. Attach the internet gateway to the VPC.
options.B: Create an internet gateway. Attach the internet gateway to the instance's subnet.
options.C: Create an internet gateway. Attach the internet gateway to the instance.
options.D: Add a route to the route table of the instance's subnet. Route traffic from the instance's subnet to the internet gateway.
options.E: Add a route to the route table of the instance's subnet. Route traffic from the internet gateway to the instance's subnet.

explanation: A is correct: an internet gateway is attached to the VPC.
B is wrong: internet gateways attach to VPCs, not subnets.
C is wrong: internet gateways attach to VPCs, not instances.
D is correct: a route from the subnet to the internet gateway (0.0.0.0/0) makes it a public subnet.
E is wrong: routes point from the subnet to the gateway; this describes the direction backwards.
tldr: Internet access needs an internet gateway attached to the VPC and a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the subnet's route table.

wrong_reasons.B: internet gateways attach to VPCs, not subnets.
wrong_reasons.C: internet gateways attach to VPCs, not instances.
wrong_reasons.E: routes point from the subnet to the gateway; this describes the direction backwards.

question: A company runs a Microsoft Windows SMB file share on premises to support an application. The company wants to migrate the application to AWS. The company wants to share storage across multiple Amazon EC2 instances. Which solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
hint: Which managed FSx file systems serve SMB?

options.A: Create an Amazon EFS file system with elastic throughput.
options.B: Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system.
options.C: Use Amazon EBS to create a self-managed Windows file share on the instances.
options.D: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system.
options.E: Create an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system.

explanation: A is wrong: EFS supports NFS only, not SMB.
B is correct: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is managed and serves SMB shares to Windows clients.
C is wrong: a self-managed file server on EBS means running and patching it yourself.
D is correct: FSx for Windows File Server is a managed, native SMB file system.
E is wrong: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS, not SMB.
tldr: Managed SMB shares on AWS: FSx for Windows File Server or FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

wrong_reasons.A: EFS supports NFS only, not SMB.
wrong_reasons.C: a self-managed file server on EBS means running and patching it yourself.
wrong_reasons.E: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS, not SMB.

question: A company is building a news aggregation platform. The platform ingests news articles that need to be cleaned and categorized. The processed articles must be stored durably for one year. The platform must handle up to thousands of incoming articles each minute during peaks. The platform must also provide independent, scalable processing for each article. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Decouple ingestion from processing with a queue, then store results somewhere durable.
keywords: thousands of incoming articles each minute
independent, scalable processing for each article

options.A: Create a custom application to ingest articles and perform in-memory processing. Run the application on one large Amazon EC2 instance. Configure the application to store processed articles in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function to ingest articles. Send one message for each article to an Amazon SQS queue. Create a second Lambda function to consume the SQS queue. Configure the second Lambda function to process the articles and store the articles in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function to ingest articles. Store the output in a shared Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster. Deploy a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Configure the instances to retrieve the article data from the ElastiCache cluster, process the data, and write the data back to the ElastiCache cluster.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function to ingest articles. Send one message for each article to an Amazon SQS queue. Create a second Lambda function to consume the SQS queue. Configure the second Lambda function to process the articles and store the articles in a second SQS queue.

explanation: A is wrong: one large instance is a single point of failure and does not scale per article.
B is correct: one SQS message per article lets Lambda scale and process each one independently, and S3 stores the results durably for a year.
C is wrong: Memcached is not durable storage, and the EC2 fleet adds work.
D is wrong: SQS keeps messages for at most 14 days, so it cannot store articles for a year.
tldr: Queue each item in SQS for independently scaling Lambda processing, and store the results durably in S3.

wrong_reasons.A: one large instance is a single point of failure and does not scale per article.
wrong_reasons.C: Memcached is not durable storage, and the EC2 fleet adds work.
wrong_reasons.D: SQS keeps messages for at most 14 days, so it cannot store articles for a year.

question: A company uses AWS Direct Connect to connect its on-premises network to multiple VPCs. All VPCs are located in the same AWS account in one AWS Region. Each VPC uses its own private virtual interface (VIF) and virtual local area network (VLAN) on the Direct Connect connection. The company is growing and needs to add more VPCs and private VIFs. The existing connections cannot support the additional VPCs and private VIFs. The company's new VPCs must have connectivity to the on-premises network. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST scalable way?
hint: Stop needing one VIF per VPC. What connects many VPCs through a single virtual interface?

options.A: Provision a new Direct Connect connection to handle the additional VPCs and VIFs.
options.B: Create a virtual private gateway for each VPC that is over the connection service quota. Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect the virtual private gateways to the on-premises network.
options.C: Create a Direct Connect gateway and add virtual private gateway associations to all of the VPCs. Configure a private VIF for each new VPC to connect each new VPC to the on-premises network.
options.D: Connect a transit gateway to all the VPCs. Associate a Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway. Create a transit VIF for the Direct Connect gateway.

explanation: A is wrong: another connection keeps the one-VIF-per-VPC pattern and adds cost.
B is wrong: VPN connections per VPC are a workaround that is hard to manage and slower than Direct Connect.
C is wrong: this still creates a private VIF for each new VPC, which is exactly the limit the company is hitting.
D is correct: a transit gateway connects all VPCs, and one transit VIF through a Direct Connect gateway reaches on premises, so new VPCs only need an attachment.
tldr: Transit gateway + Direct Connect gateway + one transit VIF connects many VPCs to on premises without a VIF per VPC.

wrong_reasons.A: another connection keeps the one-VIF-per-VPC pattern and adds cost.
wrong_reasons.B: VPN connections per VPC are a workaround that is hard to manage and slower than Direct Connect.
wrong_reasons.C: this still creates a private VIF for each new VPC, which is exactly the limit the company is hitting.

question: A company has multiple consumers that consume data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The company wants to share throughput across all consumers. The company must prevent any one consumer from monopolizing the stream's throughput. Each consumer must have its own read throughput and must not compete with other consumers. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which Kinesis feature gives each consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard?
keywords: must not compete with other consumers

options.A: Configure enhanced fan-out to allow each consumer to receive its own dedicated throughput.
options.B: Increase the number of shards in the stream.
options.C: Configure lease management within the consumers.
options.D: Send the data to an Amazon SQS queue before distributing data to the consumers.

explanation: A is correct: enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard, so they do not compete.
B is wrong: more shards raise total throughput, but consumers still share it.
C is wrong: lease management coordinates workers within one application, not between separate consumers.
D is wrong: putting SQS in front adds a hop, and each message would be consumed by only one consumer.
tldr: Kinesis enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer dedicated read throughput per shard.

wrong_reasons.B: more shards raise total throughput, but consumers still share it.
wrong_reasons.C: lease management coordinates workers within one application, not between separate consumers.
wrong_reasons.D: putting SQS in front adds a hop, and each message would be consumed by only one consumer.

question: A company has a two-tier web application that uses Amazon EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. Application users have recently reported that the application performance degrades when users attempt to produce unique reports. The company needs to fix the poor performance without making significant changes to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Reports are read-heavy. Where can they run without slowing the main database?
keywords: without making significant changes to the application

options.A: Migrate the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance to a new DB instance that has a higher I/O capacity.
options.B: Reconfigure the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance from a Single-AZ DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance.
options.C: Create a read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance.
options.D: Create a snapshot of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Provision a new copy by using PostgreSQL.

explanation: A is wrong: more I/O on the same instance still makes reports compete with the application.
B is wrong: the Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, so it does not help performance.
C is correct: a read replica takes the report queries, so they no longer slow the primary; only the reports' connection string changes.
D is wrong: a copy from a snapshot is out of date and must be managed separately.
tldr: Send reporting queries to an RDS read replica to take read load off the primary.

wrong_reasons.A: more I/O on the same instance still makes reports compete with the application.
wrong_reasons.B: the Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, so it does not help performance.
wrong_reasons.D: a copy from a snapshot is out of date and must be managed separately.

question: A company runs an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system on Amazon EC2 instances in a single AWS Region. Users connect to the ERP system by using a public API that is hosted on the EC2 instances. International users report slow API response times from their data centers. A solutions architect needs to improve API response times for the international users. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Get international users onto the AWS network near them without building anything in other Regions.

options.A: Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection that has a public virtual interface (VIF) to connect each user's data center to the EC2 instances. Create a Direct Connect gateway for the ERP system API to route user API requests.
options.B: Deploy Amazon API Gateway endpoints in multiple Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to route requests to the nearest endpoint. Configure a VPC peering connection between the Regions to connect to the ERP system.
options.C: Set up AWS Global Accelerator. Configure listeners for the necessary ports. Configure endpoint groups for the appropriate Regions to distribute traffic. Create an endpoint in each group for the API.
options.D: Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish dedicated VPN tunnels between multiple Regions and user networks. Route traffic to the API through the VPN connections.

explanation: A is wrong: Direct Connect to every user's data center is expensive and slow to set up.
B is wrong: API Gateway in several Regions with peering adds complexity and cost when the backend is in one Region.
C is correct: Global Accelerator routes users through the nearest edge location over the AWS network to the API, improving response times without new Regions.
D is wrong: VPN tunnels run over the internet and are hard to manage for many users.
tldr: Global Accelerator brings distant users onto the AWS backbone at a nearby edge, speeding up a single-Region API.

wrong_reasons.A: Direct Connect to every user's data center is expensive and slow to set up.
wrong_reasons.B: API Gateway in several Regions with peering adds complexity and cost when the backend is in one Region.
wrong_reasons.D: VPN tunnels run over the internet and are hard to manage for many users.

question: A digital image processing company wants to migrate its on-premises monolithic application to the AWS Cloud. The company processes thousands of images and generates large files as part of the processing workflow. The company needs a solution to manage the growing number of image processing jobs. The solution must also reduce the manual tasks in the image processing workflow. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure of the solution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Managed batch processing, managed orchestration, and storage for large files.
keywords: does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure

options.A: Use Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Configure Amazon SQS to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon EFS.
options.B: Use AWS Batch jobs to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.C: Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Store the processed files in Amazon FSx.
options.D: Deploy a group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in an Amazon EBS volume.

explanation: A is wrong: ECS on EC2 Spot means managing instances, and SQS queues work rather than orchestrating a workflow.
B is correct: AWS Batch runs and scales the jobs on managed compute, Step Functions automates the workflow, and S3 stores large files cheaply.
C is wrong: mixing Lambda and Spot Instances means managing EC2, and Lambda has limits for large image jobs.
D is wrong: a group of EC2 instances is infrastructure to manage, and an EBS volume is tied to one instance.
tldr: Managed batch image processing: AWS Batch for jobs, Step Functions for the workflow, S3 for large output files.

wrong_reasons.A: ECS on EC2 Spot means managing instances, and SQS queues work rather than orchestrating a workflow.
wrong_reasons.C: mixing Lambda and Spot Instances means managing EC2, and Lambda has limits for large image jobs.
wrong_reasons.D: a group of EC2 instances is infrastructure to manage, and an EBS volume is tied to one instance.

question: A company needs to process data from multiple users. The company stores the data in a relational database. A solutions architect needs to extract the data, use business rules to transform the data, and store the data in Amazon S3. The solutions architect must ensure that the data is encrypted during processing. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
hint: Which managed ETL service can transform data with encryption built in?
keywords: business rules to transform the data

options.A: Use AWS Glue ETL jobs that use AWS KMS to provide built-in encryption. Configure an AWS Glue job to transform the data. Store the transformed data in a separate S3 bucket for each user. Encrypt each bucket with a KMS key that is specific to each user.
options.B: Use Amazon EMR clusters with encryption settings. Create one cluster for each user. Use AWS KMS keys to encrypt the data at rest and in transit.
options.C: Use AWS DMS with encryption enabled. Configure one replication task for each user to extract and load data into a separate S3 bucket for each user. Encrypt each bucket with a KMS key that is specific to each user.
options.D: Use AWS Lambda functions that run in response to database changes. Process data in memory, with encryption enabled. Write the processed data to Amazon S3. Use server-side encryption (SSE)

explanation: A is correct: Glue ETL jobs transform the data with built-in KMS encryption, and per-user buckets with per-user keys keep each user's data separate.
B is wrong: one EMR cluster per user is a lot of infrastructure to run.
C is wrong: DMS migrates data; it is not meant for applying business-rule transformations.
D is wrong: Lambda functions triggered by database changes are custom work, and Lambda has time and memory limits.
tldr: AWS Glue ETL jobs extract and transform data with built-in KMS encryption and no servers to manage.

wrong_reasons.B: one EMR cluster per user is a lot of infrastructure to run.
wrong_reasons.C: DMS migrates data; it is not meant for applying business-rule transformations.
wrong_reasons.D: Lambda functions triggered by database changes are custom work, and Lambda has time and memory limits.

question: A solutions architect manages a web application for a company. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group configuration includes a minimum of 3 instances and a maximum of 300 instances. The maximum helps handle unpredictable, short-lived traffic surges. The application must scale to meet demand. However, to help manage cost, the number of running instances should not exceed 180 for longer than 1 continuous hour. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: You need to react to a condition that lasts an hour. Which option watches group size over time and acts?
keywords: minimum of 3 instances and a maximum of 300
should not exceed 180 for longer than 1 continuous hour

options.A: Use a scheduled scaling policy. Set the maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to 180 during peak hours. Set the maximum capacity to 300 during non-peak hours.
options.B: Configure a target tracking scaling policy that scales based on average CPU utilization. Add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to terminate instances after 1 hour when capacity exceeds 180.
options.C: Set the maximum instance lifetime of the Auto Scaling group to 1 hour to force the replacement of instances when capacity exceeds 180.
options.D: Add a step scaling policy that uses an Amazon CloudWatch alarm. Trigger the alarm when the Auto Scaling group includes more than 180 instances for longer than 1 hour. Configure the alarm to set the maximum size of the group to 180 when triggered.

explanation: A is wrong: the surges are unpredictable, so a schedule cannot know when to cap capacity.
B is wrong: a CloudWatch alarm cannot terminate Auto Scaling instances directly, and terminated instances would be replaced.
C is wrong: maximum instance lifetime replaces old instances; it does not reduce the number running.

D is correct: an alarm on group size that has stayed above 180 for 1 hour can trigger a step scaling action; in practice that action sets the desired capacity to exactly 180 (neither an alarm nor a scaling policy can change the group's maximum size), which is the closest match to the requirement.
tldr: A CloudWatch alarm on group size over a 1-hour period can trigger a step scaling policy with an exact-capacity adjustment back to 180; scaling policies change desired capacity, not the maximum size.

wrong_reasons.A: the surges are unpredictable, so a schedule cannot know when to cap capacity.
wrong_reasons.B: a CloudWatch alarm cannot terminate Auto Scaling instances directly, and terminated instances would be replaced.
wrong_reasons.C: maximum instance lifetime replaces old instances; it does not reduce the number running.

question: A company runs all its business applications in the AWS Cloud. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts. A solutions architect needs to review all permissions that are granted to IAM users to determine which IAM users have more permissions than required. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
hint: Which IAM feature analyzes permissions and finds unused access?

options.A: Use Network Access Analyzer to review all access permissions in the company's AWS accounts.
options.B: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that activates when an IAM user creates or modifies resources in an AWS account.
options.C: Use AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer to review all the company's resources and accounts.
options.D: Use Amazon Inspector to find vulnerabilities in existing IAM policies.

explanation: A is wrong: Network Access Analyzer checks network paths, not IAM permissions.
B is wrong: an alarm on resource changes does not analyze permissions.
C is correct: IAM Access Analyzer reviews users' permissions and unused access across accounts in the organization.
D is wrong: Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities, not IAM policies.
tldr: IAM Access Analyzer finds unused access and over-broad permissions across the organization.

wrong_reasons.A: Network Access Analyzer checks network paths, not IAM permissions.
wrong_reasons.B: an alarm on resource changes does not analyze permissions.
wrong_reasons.D: Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities, not IAM policies.

question: A company manages millions of documents in hundreds of Amazon S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. The company must determine whether any of the S3 buckets contain personally identifiable information (PII). Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Which managed service discovers sensitive data in S3?

options.A: Use Amazon Detective to detect PII in the S3 buckets.
options.B: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to generate PII notifications.
options.C: Use Amazon Macie to detect PII in the S3 buckets.
options.D: Use AWS Lambda functions to review each file in the S3 buckets to identify PII.

explanation: A is wrong: Detective investigates security findings; it does not scan S3 content.
B is wrong: Trusted Advisor checks account best practices, not object contents.
C is correct: Macie scans S3 buckets across the account and Regions and reports objects that contain PII.
D is wrong: custom Lambda functions over millions of files are a lot of code and cost.
tldr: Amazon Macie discovers PII and other sensitive data in S3 buckets automatically.

wrong_reasons.A: Detective investigates security findings; it does not scan S3 content.
wrong_reasons.B: Trusted Advisor checks account best practices, not object contents.
wrong_reasons.D: custom Lambda functions over millions of files are a lot of code and cost.

question: A company hosts an application on AWS. The application has generated approximately 2.5 TB of data over the previous 12 years. The company currently stores the data on Amazon EBS volumes. The company wants a cost-effective backup solution for long-term storage. The company must be able to retrieve the data within minutes when required for audits. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Cheap archival storage, but restores within minutes. Which Glacier class offers minutes-level retrieval?

options.A: Create EBS snapshots to back up the data.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class to back up the data.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class to back up the data.
options.D: Create an Amazon EFS file system to back up the data.

explanation: A is wrong: EBS snapshots cost more per GB than Glacier for long-term storage.
B is wrong: Deep Archive retrievals take at least 12 hours, not minutes.
C is correct: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is low-cost archive storage, and expedited retrievals return data in 1-5 minutes.
D is wrong: EFS is far more expensive for archival storage.
tldr: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheap archive storage with expedited retrievals in 1-5 minutes; Deep Archive takes hours.

wrong_reasons.A: EBS snapshots cost more per GB than Glacier for long-term storage.
wrong_reasons.B: Deep Archive retrievals take at least 12 hours, not minutes.
wrong_reasons.D: EFS is far more expensive for archival storage.

question: A streaming analytics application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances needs 8 TB of attached block storage. The application has a sequential and throughput-heavy workload. The application has moderate input/output operations per second (IOPS) and runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The company wants to minimize storage cost while meeting performance needs. Which Amazon EBS volume type will meet these requirements?
hint: Large, sequential, throughput-heavy and running all the time: which HDD type is built for that?

options.A: General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volume with default throughput.
options.B: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume provisioned with 20,000 IOPS.
options.C: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS volume.
options.D: Cold HDD (sc1) EBS volume.

explanation: A is wrong: gp3 costs more per GB, and its default throughput of 125 MiB/s is too low for a throughput-heavy workload.
B is wrong: io2 with 20,000 IOPS pays for random IOPS the workload does not need.
C is correct: st1 is built for large, sequential, throughput-heavy workloads and costs much less per GB than SSD.
D is wrong: sc1 is for cold, rarely accessed data and has too little throughput for a constant workload.
tldr: Big sequential, throughput-bound workloads that run constantly fit st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) at a low price per GB.

wrong_reasons.A: gp3 costs more per GB, and its default throughput of 125 MiB/s is too low for a throughput-heavy workload.
wrong_reasons.B: io2 with 20,000 IOPS pays for random IOPS the workload does not need.
wrong_reasons.D: sc1 is for cold, rarely accessed data and has too little throughput for a constant workload.

question: A company hosts crowdsourced research projects. The company wants to run a very complex and long-running application. The application has many steps. Each step has checkpoints that can be resumed if necessary. There is no deadline for the application to finish running. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: A containerized job that can resume from checkpoints: which service queues and runs it on managed compute?

options.A: Create a job container for the application. Add the container to an Amazon ECR registry. Use AWS Batch to pull a container image from the container registry and to run the application.
options.B: Use the Amazon EC2 CreateFleet API to create a Spot Instances request. Set a maximum price in the request. Use an Amazon EFS file system to store interim and final results of the application.
options.C: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances on an Amazon EC2 Dedicated Host. Use an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system to store interim and final results of the application.
options.D: Use the Amazon EC2 CreateFleet API to create a Spot Instances request. Set the request type to persistent. Use Amazon EBS volumes to store interim and final results of the application.

explanation: A is correct: AWS Batch pulls the container from ECR, runs the job on managed compute (which can use Spot) and resubmits it through its retry strategy if it fails; the application itself saves checkpoints, for example to S3, and resumes from the last one, so no work is lost and no instances need managing.
B is wrong: a one-time Spot request is not relaunched after an interruption, so the job stalls.
C is wrong: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive way to run EC2.
D is wrong: a persistent Spot request can relaunch the instance, but results on EBS are tied to instances you manage yourself.
tldr: AWS Batch runs containerized jobs on managed compute (including Spot) and resubmits failed jobs; the application must save and reload its own checkpoints.

wrong_reasons.B: a one-time Spot request is not relaunched after an interruption, so the job stalls.
wrong_reasons.C: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive way to run EC2.
wrong_reasons.D: a persistent Spot request can relaunch the instance, but results on EBS are tied to instances you manage yourself.

question: A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from a database in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB cluster. The company needs to make the application more secure with minimal programming effort. The company has created credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which service stores database credentials and can rotate them?

options.A: Store the credentials in AWS KMS. Create keys in AWS KMS. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation.
options.B: Store the credentials in encrypted local storage. Configure the application to load the database credentials from the local storage. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating a cron job.
options.C: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule by creating an AWS Lambda function for Secrets Manager.
options.D: Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule in the RDS for MySQL database by using Parameter Store.

explanation: A is wrong: KMS stores encryption keys, not credentials, and key rotation does not change the database password.
B is wrong: local storage with a cron job is custom work and still keeps secrets on the server.
C is correct: Secrets Manager stores the credentials securely, the application reads them with one SDK call, and a rotation function changes them on a schedule.
D is wrong: Parameter Store cannot rotate RDS credentials.
tldr: Move embedded database credentials to Secrets Manager and enable rotation.

wrong_reasons.A: KMS stores encryption keys, not credentials, and key rotation does not change the database password.
wrong_reasons.B: local storage with a cron job is custom work and still keeps secrets on the server.
wrong_reasons.D: Parameter Store cannot rotate RDS credentials.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts. Each department in the company has its own AWS account. A security team needs to implement centralized governance and control to enforce security best practices across all accounts. The team wants to have control over which AWS services each account can use. The team needs to restrict access to sensitive resources based on IP addresses or geographic regions. The root user must be protected with multi-factor authentication (MFA) across all accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Central multi-account governance plus service restrictions that apply to whole accounts.
keywords: which AWS services each account can use

options.A: Use IAM to manage IAM users and IAM roles in each account. Implement MFA for the root user in each account. Enforce service restrictions by using AWS managed prefix lists.
options.B: Use AWS Control Tower to establish a multi-account environment. Use service control policies (SCPs) to enforce service restrictions in AWS Organizations. Configure MFA for the root user across all accounts.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager to enforce service restrictions across multiple accounts. Use IAM policies to enforce MFA for the root user across all accounts.
options.D: Use AWS IAM Identity Center to manage user access and to enforce service restrictions by using permissions boundaries in each account.

explanation: A is wrong: managed prefix lists are CIDR lists; they cannot restrict which services an account uses.
B is correct: Control Tower sets up central governance, SCPs restrict services (and can deny by IP or Region), and root MFA is configured in every account.
C is wrong: Systems Manager cannot restrict which AWS services accounts can use.
D is wrong: permissions boundaries must be set per role and do not cover whole accounts or the root user.
tldr: Control Tower sets up governed accounts; SCPs restrict services, IP ranges or Regions for whole accounts.

wrong_reasons.A: managed prefix lists are CIDR lists; they cannot restrict which services an account uses.
wrong_reasons.C: Systems Manager cannot restrict which AWS services accounts can use.
wrong_reasons.D: permissions boundaries must be set per role and do not cover whole accounts or the root user.

question: A company runs a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster. The company runs nightly automated jobs. The nightly jobs are short-lived but are CPU-intensive and storage-intensive. The nightly jobs create large temporary tables. To keep the nightly jobs reliable, the company uses a large cluster size. However, the company experiences increased cost. Daytime jobs are moderate. The company wants to reduce costs while continuing to meet the short, spiky nightly demand. The company wants to avoid paying for unused capacity when idle. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which Redshift option scales compute automatically and charges only while queries run?
keywords: short-lived but are CPU-intensive and storage-intensive
avoid paying for unused capacity when idle

options.A: Schedule an elastic resize operation to scale up the node count before the nightly jobs and scale down afterward.
options.B: Migrate to Amazon Redshift Serverless to handle both daytime and nightly jobs.
options.C: Enable concurrency scaling to add transient capacity during the nightly jobs without changing the cluster size.
options.D: Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to offload the temporary tables to Amazon S3 to reduce the existing cluster size.

explanation: A is wrong: scheduled resizes take time, can fail, and the cluster still costs money when idle.
B is correct: Redshift Serverless scales up for the heavy nightly jobs and charges only while queries run, so idle time costs nothing.
C is wrong: concurrency scaling adds capacity for many concurrent queries, not for heavy individual jobs, and the large base cluster stays.
D is wrong: Spectrum queries data in S3; temporary tables still live on the cluster.
tldr: Redshift Serverless scales capacity automatically and bills only for compute used, suiting spiky workloads.

wrong_reasons.A: scheduled resizes take time, can fail, and the cluster still costs money when idle.
wrong_reasons.C: concurrency scaling adds capacity for many concurrent queries, not for heavy individual jobs, and the large base cluster stays.
wrong_reasons.D: Spectrum queries data in S3; temporary tables still live on the cluster.

question: A media company has a multi-account AWS environment in the us-east-1 Region. The company has an Amazon SNS topic in a production account that publishes performance metrics. The company has an AWS Lambda function in an administrator account to process and analyze log data. The Lambda function that is in the administrator account must be invoked by messages from the SNS topic that is in the production account when significant metrics are reported. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Cross-account SNS to Lambda needs permission on both sides: one resource policy on the function, one on the topic.
keywords: SNS topic in a production account
Lambda function in an administrator account

options.A: Create an IAM resource policy for the Lambda function that allows Amazon SNS to invoke the function.
options.B: Implement an Amazon SQS queue in the administrator account to buffer messages from the SNS topic that is in the production account. Configure the SQS queue to invoke the Lambda function.
options.C: Create an IAM policy for the SNS topic that allows the Lambda function to subscribe to the topic.
options.D: Use an Amazon EventBridge rule in the production account to capture the SNS topic notifications. Configure the EventBridge rule to forward notifications to the Lambda function that is in the administrator account.
options.E: Store performance metrics in an Amazon S3 bucket in the production account. Use Amazon Athena to analyze the metrics from the administrator account.

explanation: A is correct: a resource-based policy on the function lets the production account's SNS topic invoke it.
B is wrong: an SQS buffer is not required; SNS can invoke the function directly once both policies are in place.
C is correct: the topic's access policy must allow the administrator account to subscribe its Lambda function.
D is wrong: EventBridge does not capture SNS notifications this way, and it adds a service you do not need.
E is wrong: storing metrics in S3 for Athena does not invoke the function on each message.
tldr: Cross-account SNS to Lambda: a Lambda resource policy lets SNS invoke the function, and the topic policy lets the other account subscribe.

wrong_reasons.B: an SQS buffer is not required; SNS can invoke the function directly once both policies are in place.
wrong_reasons.D: EventBridge does not capture SNS notifications this way, and it adds a service you do not need.
wrong_reasons.E: storing metrics in S3 for Athena does not invoke the function on each message.

question: A company is building a static website on AWS in a single VPC. The VPC has public subnets and private subnets in two Availability Zones. The company stores the website content in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company has deployed a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances as web servers in a private subnet. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The EC2 instances serve network traffic and pull content from the S3 bucket to render the webpages. The company is using an AWS Direct Connect connection with a public virtual interface (VIF) to provide on-premises connectivity to the S3 bucket. Network traffic between the EC2 instances and the S3 bucket travels through a NAT gateway. A solutions architect must reconfigure network connectivity to optimize the cost of NAT gateway traffic between the EC2 instances and the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which S3 endpoint type is free and works through the route table?
keywords: optimize the cost of NAT gateway traffic

options.A: Create a Direct Connect private VIF. Migrate the traffic from the public VIF to the private VIF.
options.B: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel over the existing public VIF.
options.C: Implement interface VPC endpoints for the S3 bucket. Update the VPC route table.
options.D: Implement gateway VPC endpoints for the S3 bucket. Update the VPC route table.

explanation: A is wrong: a private VIF connects on premises to the VPC; it does not change the EC2 to S3 path.
B is wrong: a VPN over the public VIF does not affect traffic from EC2 to S3.
C is wrong: interface endpoints work, but they have hourly and per-GB charges, and they use DNS rather than route tables.
D is correct: a gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic through the route table at no charge, removing the NAT gateway fees.
tldr: Use an S3 gateway endpoint to take S3 traffic off the NAT gateway at no cost.

wrong_reasons.A: a private VIF connects on premises to the VPC; it does not change the EC2 to S3 path.
wrong_reasons.B: a VPN over the public VIF does not affect traffic from EC2 to S3.
wrong_reasons.C: interface endpoints work, but they have hourly and per-GB charges, and they use DNS rather than route tables.

question: A company wants to migrate an on-premises Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) to a data lake in Amazon S3. The company needs an encrypted network connection to transfer the data. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
hint: Which transfer service reads from HDFS directly and encrypts data in transit?

options.A: Use AWS Application Migration Service with an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to migrate the data.
options.B: Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data.
options.C: Use AWS Application Migration Service and an AWS Direct Connect connection with SiteLink to migrate the data.
options.D: Use AWS DataSync and AWS Global Accelerator to migrate the data.

explanation: A is wrong: Application Migration Service rehosts servers; it does not move HDFS data into S3.
B is correct: DataSync reads directly from HDFS, encrypts data in transit with TLS and writes to S3, charged per GB.
C is wrong: Application Migration Service is the wrong tool, and Direct Connect SiteLink connects on-premises sites to each other.
D is wrong: Global Accelerator adds cost and does not work with DataSync this way.
tldr: DataSync copies from HDFS to S3 with TLS encryption in transit and integrity checks.

wrong_reasons.A: Application Migration Service rehosts servers; it does not move HDFS data into S3.
wrong_reasons.C: Application Migration Service is the wrong tool, and Direct Connect SiteLink connects on-premises sites to each other.
wrong_reasons.D: Global Accelerator adds cost and does not work with DataSync this way.

question: A company has a social media application that receives large amounts of traffic. User posts and interactions are continuously updated in an Amazon RDS database. The data changes frequently, and the data types can be complex. The application must serve read requests with minimal latency. The application's current architecture struggles to deliver these rapid data updates efficiently. The company needs a solution to improve the application's performance. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which in-memory cache works in front of RDS, and which strategy keeps it current as data changes?
keywords: continuously updated in an Amazon RDS database

options.A: Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the RDS database to provide a caching layer for the high volume of rapidly changing data.
options.B: Set up Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the RDS database to enhance the speed of data transfer from the databases to the application.
options.C: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the RDS database to provide a caching layer for the high volume of rapidly changing data.
options.D: Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster. Update the application code to use a write-through caching strategy and read the data from Redis.

explanation: A is wrong: DAX only works with DynamoDB, not RDS.
B is wrong: Transfer Acceleration is an S3 feature and cannot be used with RDS.
C is wrong: CloudFront caches HTTP responses; it cannot sit in front of a database.
D is correct: Redis serves reads from memory, and write-through updates the cache on every write so the fast-changing data stays current.
tldr: ElastiCache (Redis) with write-through caching keeps rapidly changing data fresh in memory for fast reads in front of RDS.

wrong_reasons.A: DAX only works with DynamoDB, not RDS.
wrong_reasons.B: Transfer Acceleration is an S3 feature and cannot be used with RDS.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudFront caches HTTP responses; it cannot sit in front of a database.

question: A company has recently migrated to AWS. The company runs an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The EC2 instances span multiple Availability Zones. Users connect to the application through an Application Load Balancer (ALB) Amazon CloudWatch metrics report that the CPU usage for all the instances surges to 99% when users log in between 8 am and 9 am every workday. The usage surge causes performance issues and application errors. The company wants to ensure that the application is able to handle the peak usage without disruption to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: The surge happens at the same time every day. Scale before it arrives.
keywords: between 8 am and 9 am every workday

options.A: Configure an auto scaling policy based on the CPUUtilization metric to scale out at 99%.
options.B: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the ALB.
options.C: Configure a scheduled scaling policy to scale the EC2 instances based on peak usage times.
options.D: Configure Amazon ElastiCache to reduce the load on the EC2 instances.

explanation: A is wrong: scaling out at 99% CPU reacts too late; users already see errors while new instances start.
B is wrong: CloudFront caches content but does not reduce CPU spent on logins.
C is correct: a scheduled scaling action adds instances just before 8 am every workday, so capacity is ready when users log in.
D is wrong: caching does not remove the CPU work of the login surge.
tldr: For predictable daily peaks, scheduled scaling adds capacity before the load arrives.

wrong_reasons.A: scaling out at 99% CPU reacts too late; users already see errors while new instances start.
wrong_reasons.B: CloudFront caches content but does not reduce CPU spent on logins.
wrong_reasons.D: caching does not remove the CPU work of the login surge.

question: A company is migrating a PostgreSQL database to AWS. The database load is consistently high. The company has no plans to modify the CPU or memory requirements for next year. The company wants a solution that maximizes cost savings and reduces maintenance overhead. Which combination of options will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: A managed database with steady load: pick the engine option and the discount that actually applies to it.
keywords: maximizes cost savings and reduces maintenance overhead

options.A: Launch an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL serverless instance.
options.B: Purchase a 3-year No Upfront Compute Savings Plan.
options.C: Launch an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance.
options.D: Purchase a 1-year All Upfront EC2 Instance Savings Plan.
options.E: Purchase a 1-year All Upfront reserved DB instance.

explanation: A is wrong: Aurora Serverless suits variable load and costs more for consistently high usage.
B is wrong: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda, not RDS.
C is correct: RDS for PostgreSQL removes database maintenance work.
D is wrong: EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not apply to RDS instances.
E is correct: a 1-year All Upfront reserved DB instance gives the largest discount for steady RDS usage over the planned year.
tldr: Steady managed database load: RDS plus a reserved DB instance; EC2 and Compute Savings Plans do not cover RDS.

wrong_reasons.A: Aurora Serverless suits variable load and costs more for consistently high usage.
wrong_reasons.B: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda, not RDS.
wrong_reasons.D: EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not apply to RDS instances.

question: A company runs game applications on AWS. The company needs to collect, visualize, and analyze telemetry data from the company's game servers. The company wants to gain insights into the behavior, performance, and health of game servers in near real time. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Stream the data, process it continuously, then chart and alarm on the results.

options.A: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to collect telemetry data. Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink to process the data in near real time and publish custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create dashboards and alarms from the custom metrics.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Firehose to collect, process, and store telemetry data in near real time. Use AWS Glue to extract, transform, and load (ETL) data from Firehose into required formats for analysis. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize and analyze the data.
options.C: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to collect, process, and store telemetry data. Use Amazon EMR to process the data in near real time into required formats for analysis. Use Amazon Athena to analyze and visualize the data.
options.D: Use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to collect and store telemetry data. Configure DynamoDB Streams to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the data in near real time. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to visualize and analyze the data.

explanation: A is correct: Kinesis collects the stream, Flink processes it continuously and publishes metrics, and CloudWatch dashboards and alarms show server health in near real time.
B is wrong: Firehose plus batch Glue ETL adds delay and does not give real-time health monitoring.
C is wrong: EMR is heavier to run, and Athena queries are not live dashboards.
D is wrong: DynamoDB Streams captures changes to a table; it is not a telemetry ingestion service.
tldr: Near real-time telemetry: Kinesis Data Streams in, Managed Service for Apache Flink to process, CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms.

wrong_reasons.B: Firehose plus batch Glue ETL adds delay and does not give real-time health monitoring.
wrong_reasons.C: EMR is heavier to run, and Athena queries are not live dashboards.
wrong_reasons.D: DynamoDB Streams captures changes to a table; it is not a telemetry ingestion service.

question: A company wants to run a production database in the AWS Cloud. The database will collect billions of sensor readings from multiple locations across multiple AWS Regions. Data is written to the database at a sustained rate of 50,000 writes per second. The company will run reports once every 3 months against the database. The company will run simple queries to retrieve data based on unique location IDs to run the reports. The query results will vary in size. The company needs a solution that will optimize data storage costs. The solution must be highly durable and must not compromise database performance. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Very high write rate, simple key lookups, rare reads. Which DynamoDB table class lowers storage cost for rarely read data?

options.A: Use Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 in one Region. Specify the desired capacity range.
options.B: Use Amazon DynamoDB Standard tables, and enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
options.C: Deploy an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance, and create a read replica.
options.D: Use Amazon DynamoDB Standard-IA tables in multiple Regions. Configure DynamoDB to manage capacity.

explanation: A is wrong: a single-Region relational database is not ideal for 50,000 sustained writes per second from many Regions.
B is wrong: DAX caches reads, but reads are rare, so it adds cost without benefit.
C is wrong: a single PostgreSQL instance with a replica struggles with this write rate and does not lower storage cost.
D is correct: DynamoDB handles the write rate, the Standard-IA table class lowers storage cost for rarely read data, and multi-Region tables add durability.
tldr: DynamoDB Standard-IA table class cuts storage cost for large, rarely read tables; global tables span Regions.

wrong_reasons.A: a single-Region relational database is not ideal for 50,000 sustained writes per second from many Regions.
wrong_reasons.B: DAX caches reads, but reads are rare, so it adds cost without benefit.
wrong_reasons.C: a single PostgreSQL instance with a replica struggles with this write rate and does not lower storage cost.

question: A company is building a new web application that serves static and dynamic content from an API. The company wants to minimize latency for users who access the application from around the world. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: One CDN in front of both the static origin and the API origin.
keywords: users who access the application from around the world

options.A: Deploy the static content to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to serve the dynamic content. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket and the HTTP API as origins. Enable caching for static content.
options.B: Deploy the static content to an Amazon S3 bucket. Provide the bucket website endpoint to users. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with caching enabled to serve the dynamic content.
options.C: Deploy the static content to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use two Amazon EC2 instances as web servers. Deploy an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket to cache static content.
options.D: Deploy the static content to an Amazon S3 bucket. Provide the bucket website endpoint to users. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket to cache static content.

explanation: A is correct: one CloudFront distribution serves static files from S3 and routes API calls to an HTTP API over the AWS network, reducing latency for both.
B is wrong: the S3 website endpoint is not served from the edge, and API Gateway caching only works on REST APIs.
C is wrong: EC2 web servers behind an ALB add cost, and dynamic requests do not go through CloudFront.
D is wrong: this handles only static content; there is nothing for the dynamic API.
tldr: A single CloudFront distribution with S3 and API Gateway origins lowers latency for both static and dynamic content.

wrong_reasons.B: the S3 website endpoint is not served from the edge, and API Gateway caching only works on REST APIs.
wrong_reasons.C: EC2 web servers behind an ALB add cost, and dynamic requests do not go through CloudFront.
wrong_reasons.D: this handles only static content; there is nothing for the dynamic API.

question: A company has a prototype application that runs in a Linux container on Amazon ECS. The company needs to provide sensitive environment variables to the container before the application starts. What is the MOST secure way to load the environment variables to the running container?
hint: ECS can inject secrets from a secure store at startup, using the task execution role.

options.A: Add task definition parameters to the task definition. Check the parameters into a Git repository to track changes.
options.B: Add an environment variable file in bulk to the task definition. Store the file in an Amazon S3 bucket that has versioning enabled.
options.C: Add the environment variables into the container Docker file. Build and tag the container image, and upload the container image to Amazon ECR.
options.D: Add the environment variables to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Update the task execution role to include the ssm:GetParameters permission.

explanation: A is wrong: putting sensitive values in the task definition and Git exposes them to anyone who can read either.
B is wrong: an environment file in S3 is plain text and less controlled than a secrets store.
C is wrong: baking secrets into the image exposes them to anyone who can pull it.
D is correct: Parameter Store keeps the values encrypted, and ECS injects them at startup using the task execution role's ssm:GetParameters permission.
tldr: Store sensitive container settings in Parameter Store or Secrets Manager and reference them in the task definition; the execution role needs read access.

wrong_reasons.A: putting sensitive values in the task definition and Git exposes them to anyone who can read either.
wrong_reasons.B: an environment file in S3 is plain text and less controlled than a secrets store.
wrong_reasons.C: baking secrets into the image exposes them to anyone who can pull it.

question: A company is building an application on AWS. The application uses multiple AWS Lambda functions to retrieve sensitive data from a single Amazon S3 bucket for processing. The company must ensure that only authorized Lambda functions can access the data. The solution must comply with the principle of least privilege. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Each function gets its own identity with only the access it needs.

options.A: Grant full S3 bucket access to all Lambda functions through a shared IAM role.
options.B: Configure the Lambda functions to run within a VPC. Configure a bucket policy to grant access based on the Lambda functions' VPC endpoint IP addresses.
options.C: Create individual IAM roles for each Lambda function. Grant the IAM roles access to the S3 bucket. Assign each IAM role as the Lambda execution role for its corresponding Lambda function.
options.D: Configure a bucket policy granting access to the Lambda functions based on their function ARNs.

explanation: A is wrong: one shared role with full access breaks least privilege.
B is wrong: VPC endpoint IP addresses are not a reliable way to identify individual functions.
C is correct: a separate execution role for each function, each granted only its bucket access, follows least privilege.
D is wrong: bucket policies identify callers by the IAM role, not the function ARN.
tldr: Give each Lambda function its own execution role with only the S3 permissions it needs.

wrong_reasons.A: one shared role with full access breaks least privilege.
wrong_reasons.B: VPC endpoint IP addresses are not a reliable way to identify individual functions.
wrong_reasons.D: bucket policies identify callers by the IAM role, not the function ARN.

question: A company hosts a public web application on AWS. The website has a three-tier architecture. The frontend web tier is comprised of Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application tier is a second Auto Scaling group. The database tier is an Amazon RDS database. The company has configured the Auto Scaling groups to handle the application's normal level of demand. During an unexpected spike in demand, the company notices a long delay in the startup time when the frontend and application layers scale out. The company needs to improve the scaling performance of the application without negatively affecting the user experience. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Instances take too long to become ready. What keeps pre-initialized instances waiting without paying full price?
keywords: long delay in the startup time

options.A: Decrease the minimum number of EC2 instances for both Auto Scaling groups. Increase the desired number of instances to meet the peak demand requirement.
options.B: Configure the maximum number of instances for both Auto Scaling groups to be the number required to meet the peak demand. Create a warm pool.
options.C: Increase the maximum number of EC2 instances for both Auto Scaling groups to meet the normal demand requirement. Create a warm pool.
options.D: Reconfigure both Auto Scaling groups to use a scheduled scaling policy. Increase the size of the EC2 instance types and the RDS instance types.

explanation: A is wrong: raising the desired count keeps peak capacity running all the time, which is expensive.
B is correct: a maximum sized for peak lets the groups grow enough, and a warm pool of pre-initialized instances cuts startup time without running them all the time.
C is wrong: a maximum sized only for normal demand cannot handle the spike.
D is wrong: a schedule cannot predict an unexpected spike, and larger instances raise cost.
tldr: Auto Scaling warm pools keep pre-initialized (often stopped) instances ready, cutting scale-out time cheaply.

wrong_reasons.A: raising the desired count keeps peak capacity running all the time, which is expensive.
wrong_reasons.C: a maximum sized only for normal demand cannot handle the spike.
wrong_reasons.D: a schedule cannot predict an unexpected spike, and larger instances raise cost.

question: A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances and uses an Amazon Aurora database. The EC2 instances connect to the Aurora database by using user names and passwords that the company stores locally in a file. The company changes the user names and passwords every month. The company wants to minimize the operational overhead of credential management. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which service stores credentials and rotates them on a schedule?
keywords: changes the user names and passwords every month

options.A: Store the credentials as a secret within AWS Secrets Manager. Assign IAM permissions to the secret. Reconfigure the application to call the secret. Enable rotation on the secret and configure rotation to occur on a monthly schedule.
options.B: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to create a new parameter for the credentials. Use IAM policies to restrict access to the parameter. Reconfigure the application to access the parameter.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store objects. Use an AWS KMS key to encrypt the objects. Migrate the credentials file to the S3 bucket. Update the application to retrieve the credentials file from the S3 bucket.
options.D: Create an encrypted Amazon EBS volume for each EC2 instance. Attach the encrypted EBS volumes to the EC2 instances. Migrate the credentials file to the new EBS volumes. Point the application to the encrypted EBS volumes.

explanation: A is correct: Secrets Manager stores the credentials, IAM controls access, and monthly rotation runs automatically.
B is wrong: Parameter Store has no automatic rotation, so monthly changes stay manual.
C is wrong: a file in S3 still has to be rotated by hand.
D is wrong: encrypted volumes protect the file at rest but do nothing about rotation.
tldr: Secrets Manager with scheduled rotation replaces manually rotated credential files.

wrong_reasons.B: Parameter Store has no automatic rotation, so monthly changes stay manual.
wrong_reasons.C: a file in S3 still has to be rotated by hand.
wrong_reasons.D: encrypted volumes protect the file at rest but do nothing about rotation.

question: A company is designing a tightly coupled high performance computing (HPC) environment in the AWS Cloud. The company needs to include features that will optimize the HPC environment for networking and storage. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: One adapter for low-latency node-to-node networking, one parallel file system for HPC storage.

options.A: Create an accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Configure custom routing for the accelerator.
options.B: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Configure the file system with scratch storage.
options.C: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the viewer protocol policy to be HTTP and HTTPS.
options.D: Launch Amazon EC2 instances. Attach an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) to the instances.
options.E: Create an AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment to manage the environment.

explanation: A is wrong: Global Accelerator speeds up internet users' traffic, not HPC node communication.
B is correct: FSx for Lustre scratch file systems give high-throughput, low-latency storage for HPC jobs.
C is wrong: CloudFront delivers content to viewers and has nothing to do with HPC.
D is correct: an Elastic Fabric Adapter gives the low-latency, high-bandwidth networking that tightly coupled HPC needs.
E is wrong: Elastic Beanstalk deploys web applications, not HPC clusters.
tldr: Tightly coupled HPC: EFA for low-latency networking between instances, FSx for Lustre for parallel storage.

wrong_reasons.A: Global Accelerator speeds up internet users' traffic, not HPC node communication.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudFront delivers content to viewers and has nothing to do with HPC.
wrong_reasons.E: Elastic Beanstalk deploys web applications, not HPC clusters.

question: A manufacturing company runs an order processing application in its VPC. The company wants to securely send messages from the application to an external Salesforce system that uses Open Authorization (OAuth). A solutions architect needs to integrate the company's order processing application with the external Salesforce system. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which service sends events to external HTTP APIs and handles OAuth for you?

options.A: Create an Amazon SNS topic in a fanout configuration that pushes data to an HTTPS endpoint. Configure the order processing application to publish messages to the SNS topic.
options.B: Create an Amazon SNS topic in a fanout configuration that pushes data to an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream that has a HTTP destination. Configure the order processing application to publish messages to the SNS topic.
options.C: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule and configure an Amazon EventBridge API destination partner. Configure the order processing application to publish messages to Amazon EventBridge.
options.D: Create an Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) topic that has an outbound MSK Connect connector. Configure the order processing application to publish messages to the MSK topic.

explanation: A is wrong: SNS HTTPS subscriptions do not handle OAuth token flows.
B is wrong: Firehose HTTP destinations do not handle Salesforce OAuth, and adding SNS does not help.
C is correct: EventBridge API destinations call external HTTP endpoints with OAuth authorization managed by a connection, and Salesforce is a supported partner.
D is wrong: running MSK and a custom connector is far more work than a managed integration.
tldr: EventBridge API destinations deliver events to external HTTP APIs such as Salesforce, with built-in OAuth handling.

wrong_reasons.A: SNS HTTPS subscriptions do not handle OAuth token flows.
wrong_reasons.B: Firehose HTTP destinations do not handle Salesforce OAuth, and adding SNS does not help.
wrong_reasons.D: running MSK and a custom connector is far more work than a managed integration.

question: An e-commerce company is redesigning a web application to run on the AWS Cloud. The application needs to store static website content and must use a Microsoft SQL Server database to store customer data. The company needs to deploy the application in a resilient way across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Static content goes in S3. For SQL Server, which managed option spans Availability Zones?
keywords: resilient way across multiple Availability Zones

options.A: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.B: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Create an Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ deployment for the database.
options.C: Create an Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.D: Create an Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy SQL Server on two Amazon EC2 instances in separate Availability Zones.

explanation: A is wrong: RDS Custom is for workloads that need OS access; it does not by itself make the database span Availability Zones.
B is correct: S3 stores static content across Availability Zones, and RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ fails over automatically.
C is wrong: EBS Multi-Attach works within one Availability Zone, and a single RDS instance is not Multi-AZ.
D is wrong: EBS Multi-Attach is single-AZ, and self-managed SQL Server on EC2 adds work.
tldr: Resilient web app with SQL Server: S3 for static content, RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ for the database.

wrong_reasons.A: RDS Custom is for workloads that need OS access; it does not by itself make the database span Availability Zones.
wrong_reasons.C: EBS Multi-Attach works within one Availability Zone, and a single RDS instance is not Multi-AZ.
wrong_reasons.D: EBS Multi-Attach is single-AZ, and self-managed SQL Server on EC2 adds work.

question: A company hosts a static website in an Amazon S3 bucket. The S3 bucket is the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The company has users in the United States, Canada, and Europe. The company wants to optimize distribution costs for the website. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: CloudFront bills differently by edge location. Which setting limits the locations used?

options.A: Configure CloudFront to send a Cache-Control response header. Set the maximum TTL to a low value.
options.B: Use CloudFront events to invoke Lambda@Edge functions to perform data processing for the website.
options.C: Modify the CloudFront price class to include only the countries that the company serves.
options.D: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to provision a public SSL/TLS certificate for the CloudFront distribution.

explanation: A is wrong: a low maximum TTL means more origin fetches, which raises cost.
B is wrong: Lambda@Edge adds cost and does nothing to lower distribution cost.
C is correct: a price class that uses only North American and European edge locations serves these users at lower rates.
D is wrong: an ACM certificate enables HTTPS but does not lower cost.
tldr: A cheaper CloudFront price class (for example North America and Europe only) lowers costs when users are in those regions.

wrong_reasons.A: a low maximum TTL means more origin fetches, which raises cost.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda@Edge adds cost and does nothing to lower distribution cost.
wrong_reasons.D: an ACM certificate enables HTTPS but does not lower cost.

question: A company's cloud operations team uses the AWS Management Console to administer AWS resources from remote locations, including employee home offices. The cloud operations team logs in by using individual IAM user accounts. IAM users belong to an IAM user group that has the PowerUserAccess AWS managed policy attached. A solutions architect needs to recommend a solution to improve security for the cloud operations team AWS account. The solution must not increase operational overhead for the cloud operation team. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Central sign-in with enforced MFA, without changing how the team works.

options.A: Enable AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure IAM Identity Center to always require users to use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to log in.
options.B: Disable console access. Require users to use the AWS CLI and AWS CloudFormation templates to manage cloud resources.
options.C: Disable the root user in the cloud operations account. Replace the PowerUserAccess AWS managed policy with a custom policy that is based on the principle of least privilege.
options.D: Configure a service control policy (SCP) that ensures only approved IP address can log in to the console.

explanation: A is correct: IAM Identity Center gives central sign-in and requires MFA on every login, improving security without changing the team's daily work.
B is wrong: removing console access forces a new way of working and adds overhead.
C is wrong: the root user cannot be disabled, and writing least-privilege policies is ongoing work.
D is wrong: SCPs cannot restrict console sign-in by IP address this way, and remote workers' IPs change.
tldr: IAM Identity Center centralizes workforce sign-in and can require MFA for every user.

wrong_reasons.B: removing console access forces a new way of working and adds overhead.
