wrong_reasons.C: the root user cannot be disabled, and writing least-privilege policies is ongoing work.
wrong_reasons.D: SCPs cannot restrict console sign-in by IP address this way, and remote workers' IPs change.

question: A company is using an Amazon EKS cluster. The company must ensure that Kubernetes service accounts in the EKS cluster have secure and granular access to specific AWS resources by using IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA). Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: IRSA uses an OIDC provider for trust and an annotation on the service account that points to the role.

options.A: Create an IAM policy that defines the required permissions. Attach the policy directly to the IAM role of the EKS nodes.
options.B: Implement network policies within the EKS cluster to prevent Kubernetes service accounts from accessing specific AWS services.
options.C: Modify the EKS cluster's IAM role to include permissions for each Kubernetes service account. Ensure a one-to-one mapping between IAM roles and Kubernetes roles.
options.D: Define an IAM role that includes the necessary permissions. Annotate the Kubernetes service accounts with the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the IAM role.
options.E: Set up a trust relationship between the IAM roles for the service accounts and an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider.

explanation: A is wrong: permissions on the node role are shared by every pod on the node, which is not granular.
B is wrong: Kubernetes network policies control pod traffic, not IAM permissions.
C is wrong: the cluster role is for the EKS control plane, not for workloads.
D is correct: annotating each service account with its IAM role ARN gives pods that use it only that role's permissions.
E is correct: the IAM role must trust the cluster's OIDC identity provider so service accounts can assume it.
tldr: IRSA: the IAM role trusts the cluster's OIDC provider, and the Kubernetes service account is annotated with the role ARN.

wrong_reasons.A: permissions on the node role are shared by every pod on the node, which is not granular.
wrong_reasons.B: Kubernetes network policies control pod traffic, not IAM permissions.
wrong_reasons.C: the cluster role is for the EKS control plane, not for workloads.

question: A company has hired an external vendor to work in the company's AWS account. The vendor uses an automated tool that the vendor hosts in its own AWS account. The vendor does not have IAM access to the company's AWS account. A solutions architect needs to grant access to the vendor. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST securely?
hint: Cross-account access without sharing long-term credentials.

options.A: Create an IAM role in the company's account to delegate access to the vendor's IAM role. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new IAM role to grant the permissions that the vendor requires.
options.B: Create an IAM user in the company's account that has a password that meets the company's password complexity requirements. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new IAM user to grant the permissions that the vendor requires.
options.C: Create an IAM group in the company's account. Add the IAM user for the vendor's automated tool from the vendor account to the IAM group. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the group to grant the permissions that the vendor requires.
options.D: Create a new identity provider (IdP) that has a provider type of AWS account. Supply the vendor's AWS account ID and username. Attach the appropriate IAM policies to the new IdP to grant the permissions that the vendor requires.

explanation: A is correct: a role in the company's account that trusts the vendor's role gives temporary, scoped credentials with no shared passwords or keys.
B is wrong: an IAM user gives the vendor long-term credentials.
C is wrong: users from another account cannot be added to an IAM group.
D is wrong: an identity provider is for SAML or OIDC federation; "AWS account" is not a provider type.
tldr: Grant a third party access with a cross-account IAM role that their role assumes (optionally with an external ID).

wrong_reasons.B: an IAM user gives the vendor long-term credentials.
wrong_reasons.C: users from another account cannot be added to an IAM group.
wrong_reasons.D: an identity provider is for SAML or OIDC federation; "AWS account" is not a provider type.

question: A company has a three-tier web application. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is in front of Amazon EC2 instances that are in the ALB target group. An Amazon S3 bucket stores documents. The company requires the application to meet a recovery time objective (RTO) of 60 seconds. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: A 60-second RTO leaves no time to start or build anything. What must already be running?

options.A: Replicate S3 objects to a second AWS Region. Create a second ALB and a minimum set of EC2 instances in the second Region. Ensure that the EC2 instances are shut down until they are needed. Configure Amazon Route 53 to fail over to the second Region by using an IP-based routing policy.
options.B: Use AWS Backup to take hourly backups of the EC2 instances. Back up the S3 data to a second AWS Region. Use AWS CloudFormation to deploy the entire infrastructure in the second Region when needed.
options.C: Create daily snapshots of the EC2 instances in a second AWS Region. Use the snapshots to recreate the instances in the second Region. Back up the S3 data to the second Region. Perform a failover by modifying the application DNS record when needed.
options.D: Replicate S3 objects to a second AWS Region. Create a second ALB and a minimum set of EC2 instances in the second Region. Ensure that the EC2 instances in the second Region are running. Configure Amazon Route 53 to fail over to the secondary Region based on health checks.

explanation: A is wrong: stopped instances take longer than 60 seconds to start, and IP-based routing is not a failover mechanism.
B is wrong: redeploying the infrastructure with CloudFormation takes far longer than 60 seconds.
C is wrong: recreating instances from snapshots and changing DNS by hand is far too slow.
D is correct: running instances in the second Region behind an ALB, replicated S3 data and Route 53 health-check failover can switch within about a minute.
tldr: A very short RTO needs a warm standby that is already running, with Route 53 health-check failover.

wrong_reasons.A: stopped instances take longer than 60 seconds to start, and IP-based routing is not a failover mechanism.
wrong_reasons.B: redeploying the infrastructure with CloudFormation takes far longer than 60 seconds.
wrong_reasons.C: recreating instances from snapshots and changing DNS by hand is far too slow.

question: A solutions architect wants to design a data warehouse by using an Amazon Redshift cluster in the eu-west-1 Region. The data warehouse will initially ingest data from Amazon DynamoDB tables in eu-west-1. The VPC that the Redshift cluster will be deployed in must not connect to the internet. Which solution will securely load data MOST cost-effectively?
hint: DynamoDB has a free endpoint type that works through route tables.
keywords: must not connect to the internet

options.A: Create a DynamoDB gateway VPC endpoint within the VPC. Add a route from the VPC subnets to the DynamoDB prefix list by using the gateway endpoint. Add a resource policy to the endpoint to allow the Redshift cluster to access the specific workload tables.
options.B: Create a DynamoDB interface VPC endpoint within the VPC. Add a route from the VPC subnets to the DynamoDB prefix list by using the interface endpoint. Configure the security group of the interface endpoint to allow connections from the Redshift cluster VPC.
options.C: Deploy a DynamoDB interface VPC endpoint within the VPC. Enable private DNS resolution for the endpoint. Enable the interface endpoint in all data warehouse Availability Zones.
options.D: Deploy a VPC peering connection to the DynamoDB VPC. Add a route from the VPC subnets to the DynamoDB CIDR range by using the peering connection. Add a return route from the DynamoDB VPC to the Redshift cluster VPC.

explanation: A is correct: a gateway endpoint gives private access to DynamoDB through a route table at no charge, and its policy limits access to the needed tables.
B is wrong: interface endpoints do not use route table entries, and they cost more than a gateway endpoint.
C is wrong: an interface endpoint works privately but has hourly and per-GB charges.
D is wrong: DynamoDB is not in a VPC you can peer with.
tldr: A DynamoDB gateway endpoint gives private, no-cost access from a VPC without internet access.

wrong_reasons.B: interface endpoints do not use route table entries, and they cost more than a gateway endpoint.
wrong_reasons.C: an interface endpoint works privately but has hourly and per-GB charges.
wrong_reasons.D: DynamoDB is not in a VPC you can peer with.

question: A company has a legacy .NET Framework application that runs on Windows Server 2012. The company wants to migrate the application to AWS. The company cannot rewrite code or update to the most recent version of the .NET Framework. The company needs to use AWS managed services to minimize operational responsibilities. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
hint: Old .NET Framework apps need Windows. Which option runs the app unchanged?

options.A: Use AWS Migration Hub Orchestrator to containerize the .NET application. Use Amazon ECS to deploy the application.
options.B: Use AWS Lambda functions to run the application by using .NET libraries.
options.C: Use an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to deploy Amazon EC2 instances that run the most recent version of Windows Server. Run the application on the EC2 instances.
options.D: Use AWS Application Migration Service to convert the application to the most recent version of the .NET Framework. Use Amazon ECS to deploy the application.

explanation: A is wrong: containerizing the application is a significant change the company wants to avoid.
B is wrong: Lambda does not run .NET Framework applications.
C is correct: EC2 instances with a current Windows Server AMI run the existing .NET Framework application without rewriting it.
D is wrong: Application Migration Service rehosts servers; it does not upgrade .NET code.
tldr: Legacy .NET Framework apps that cannot be rewritten run as-is on Windows EC2 instances.

wrong_reasons.A: containerizing the application is a significant change the company wants to avoid.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda does not run .NET Framework applications.
wrong_reasons.D: Application Migration Service rehosts servers; it does not upgrade .NET code.

question: A solutions architect is creating an AWS Lambda function that needs network access to private resources in a VPC. Which solution will provide this access with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Lambda can be attached to your own VPC subnets directly.
keywords: network access to private resources in a VPC

options.A: Attach the Lambda function to the VPC through private subnets. Create a security group that allows network access to the private resources. Associate the security group with the Lambda function.
options.B: Configure the Lambda function to route traffic through a VPN connection. Create a security group that allows network access to the private resources. Associate the security group with the Lambda function.
options.C: Configure a VPC endpoint connection for the Lambda function. Set up the VPC endpoint to route traffic through a NAT gateway.
options.D: Configure an AWS PrivateLink endpoint for the private resources. Configure the Lambda function to reference the PrivateLink endpoint.

explanation: A is correct: attaching the function to private subnets with a suitable security group gives it direct access to private resources.
B is wrong: Lambda cannot use a VPN connection by itself.
C is wrong: VPC endpoints give access to AWS services, not to a function's route into a VPC.
D is wrong: exposing each private resource through PrivateLink is extra work that VPC access removes.
tldr: Attach Lambda to private subnets with a security group to reach private VPC resources.

wrong_reasons.B: Lambda cannot use a VPN connection by itself.
wrong_reasons.C: VPC endpoints give access to AWS services, not to a function's route into a VPC.
wrong_reasons.D: exposing each private resource through PrivateLink is extra work that VPC access removes.

question: A company uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to run its applications in the us-east-1 Region. The company also uses machine learning (ML) models to forecast annual revenue based on near real-time reports. The reports are generated by using the same RDS for PostgreSQL database. The database performance slows during business hours. The company needs to improve database performance. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Move the report reads off the primary, as cheaply as possible and without leaving the Region.
keywords: database performance slows during business hours

options.A: Create a cross-Region read replica. Configure the reports to be generated from the read replica.
options.B: Activate Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for RDS for PostgreSQL. Configure the reports to be generated from the standby database.
options.C: Use AWS DMS to logically replicate data to a new database. Configure the reports to be generated from the new database.
options.D: Create a read replica in us-east-1. Configure the reports to be generated from the read replica.

explanation: A is wrong: a cross-Region replica adds data transfer cost and latency for no benefit.
B is wrong: a Multi-AZ instance standby cannot serve reads.
C is wrong: DMS replication to a new database adds cost and a pipeline to manage.
D is correct: a read replica in the same Region takes the report queries off the primary at the lowest cost.
tldr: Offload reporting to a same-Region read replica: cheaper than cross-Region and keeps the primary fast.

wrong_reasons.A: a cross-Region replica adds data transfer cost and latency for no benefit.
wrong_reasons.B: a Multi-AZ instance standby cannot serve reads.
wrong_reasons.C: DMS replication to a new database adds cost and a pipeline to manage.

question: A large company requires a data backup strategy. The solution must replicate long-term backups from a source AWS account to a dedicated backup AWS account. All backups must be encrypted. The encryption keys must be available for both encryption and decryption operations in the source account and the backup account. Only specific AWS accounts, resource, and users must have access permissions for the encryption keys. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Cross-account backup copies need keys whose policies you control in both accounts, and a managed service to copy the backups.
keywords: available for both encryption and decryption operations in the source account and the backup account
Only specific AWS accounts, resource, and users

options.A: Deploy a third-party encryption solution from the AWS Marketplace in the source account to manage the encryption keys. Create an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by a custom event to replicate backups to the backup account.
options.B: Use AWS-managed AWS KMS keys that have default policies for encryption. Create an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by AWS Backup events that have a status of COMPLETED in Amazon EventBridge. Configure the function to replicate backups to the backup account.
options.C: Deploy an AWS CloudHSM cluster in the source account to manage the encryption keys. Create an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by AWS Backup events that have a status of COMPLETED in Amazon EventBridge. Configure the function to replicate backups to the backup account.
options.D: Use customer-managed AWS KMS keys that have appropriate policies attached in both the source account and the backup account. Configure AWS Backup to automate the backup and replication process.

explanation: A is wrong: third-party key management and custom Lambda replication add cost and complexity.
B is wrong: AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts, and custom replication is unnecessary.
C is wrong: CloudHSM and a custom Lambda are far more work than managed options.
D is correct: customer managed keys with key policies in both accounts control exactly who can use them, and AWS Backup copies backups to the backup account automatically.
tldr: Cross-account encrypted backups: customer managed KMS keys with tailored key policies plus AWS Backup cross-account copy.

wrong_reasons.A: third-party key management and custom Lambda replication add cost and complexity.
wrong_reasons.B: AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts, and custom replication is unnecessary.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudHSM and a custom Lambda are far more work than managed options.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application needs to access an Amazon RDS database. The company wants to grant the EC2 instances access permissions to the RDS database while following the principle of least privilege. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: EC2 gets permissions from a role through an instance profile, never from stored keys.
keywords: access permissions to the RDS database

options.A: Create an IAM user that has a policy that grants administrative permissions. Use the IAM user's access keys on the EC2 instances to access the RDS database.
options.B: Create an IAM user that has a policy that grants the minimum required permissions to access the RDS database. Embed the IAM user's access keys on the EC2 instances to access the RDS database.
options.C: Create an IAM role that has a policy that grants the minimum required permissions to access the RDS database. Attach the IAM role access key and the IAM role secret key to the EC2 instance profile.
options.D: Create an IAM role that has a policy that grants the minimum required permissions to access the RDS database. Attach the IAM role to an EC2 instance profile. Associate the instance profile with the instances.

explanation: A is wrong: administrative permissions and stored access keys break least privilege and security practice.
B is wrong: embedding user access keys on instances risks leaking long-term credentials.
C is wrong: roles have no long-term access key and secret key to attach.
D is correct: an IAM role with only the needed RDS permissions, attached through an instance profile, gives the instances temporary credentials.
tldr: Give EC2 least-privilege permissions with an IAM role attached through an instance profile.

wrong_reasons.A: administrative permissions and stored access keys break least privilege and security practice.
wrong_reasons.B: embedding user access keys on instances risks leaking long-term credentials.
wrong_reasons.C: roles have no long-term access key and secret key to attach.

question: A solutions architect is storing sensitive data generated by an application in Amazon S3. The solutions architect wants to encrypt the data at rest. A company policy requires an audit trail of when the AWS KMS key was used and by whom. Which encryption option will meet these requirements?
hint: Only one of these options uses KMS, where every key use is logged in CloudTrail.
keywords: audit trail of when the AWS KMS key was used and by whom

options.A: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
options.B: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed keys (SSE-KMS)
options.C: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
options.D: Server-side encryption with self-managed keys.

explanation: A is wrong: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 and their use is not logged per request in CloudTrail.
B is correct: SSE-KMS records every use of the key in CloudTrail, showing when and by whom.
C is wrong: SSE-C uses keys you supply with each request; KMS is not involved.
D is wrong: self-managed keys are outside KMS, so there is no KMS audit trail.
tldr: SSE-KMS logs every use of the key in CloudTrail, giving an audit trail of who used it and when.

wrong_reasons.A: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 and their use is not logged per request in CloudTrail.
wrong_reasons.C: SSE-C uses keys you supply with each request; KMS is not involved.
wrong_reasons.D: self-managed keys are outside KMS, so there is no KMS audit trail.

question: A company uses Amazon Neptune and an AWS Lambda function as part of a fraud detection solution. The company has additional Neptune database clusters that are not part of the fraud detection solution. The fraud detection Lambda function must follow the principle of least privilege to access the fraud detection data in the Neptune database. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Neptune IAM authentication uses its own action name, scoped to one cluster ARN.

options.A: Add a custom IAM policy to the Lambda function's execution role. Configure the policy to allow the neptune-db:connect action. Specify the Neptune cluster's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the resource.
options.B: Attach the AmazonNeptuneFullAccess managed policy to the Lambda function's execution role.
options.C: Create a custom inline IAM policy. Configure the policy to include "Action": "*" and "Resource": "arn:aws:neptune:*". Add the policy to the Lambda function's execution role.
options.D: Add a custom IAM policy to the Lambda function's execution role. Configure the policy to allow the rds-db:connect action. Specify the Neptune cluster's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the resource.

explanation: A is correct: allowing neptune-db:connect on only the fraud detection cluster's ARN gives the function exactly the access it needs.
B is wrong: the full-access managed policy grants far more than the function needs, across all clusters.
C is wrong: wildcard actions and resources break least privilege.
D is wrong: rds-db:connect is for RDS IAM authentication, not Neptune.
tldr: Grant Neptune access with neptune-db:connect scoped to the specific cluster ARN.

wrong_reasons.B: the full-access managed policy grants far more than the function needs, across all clusters.
wrong_reasons.C: wildcard actions and resources break least privilege.
wrong_reasons.D: rds-db:connect is for RDS IAM authentication, not Neptune.

question: A company has developed a new content-sharing application that runs on Amazon ECS. The application runs on Amazon Linux Docker tasks that use the Amazon EC2 launch type. The application requires a storage solution that has the following characteristics: accessibility for multiple ECS tasks through bind mounts, resiliency across Availability Zones, burstable throughput of up to 3 Gbps, and the ability to be scaled up over time. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
hint: Shared by many Linux tasks, resilient across AZs, bursting throughput, and grows by itself.
keywords: Burstable throughput of up to 3 Gbps

options.A: Launch an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ instance. Configure the ECS task definitions to mount the Amazon FSx instance volume at launch.
options.B: Launch an Amazon EFS instance. Configure the ECS task definitions to mount the EFS instance volume at launch.
options.C: Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volume with Multi-Attach set to enabled. Attach the EBS volume to the ECS EC2 instance. Configure ECS task definitions to mount the EBS instance volume at launch.
options.D: Launch an EC2 instance with several Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volumes attached in a RAID 0 configuration. Configure the EC2 instance as an NFS storage server. Configure ECS task definitions to mount the volumes at launch.

explanation: A is wrong: FSx for Windows is SMB storage, not a natural fit for Linux containers.
B is correct: EFS is shared NFS storage that ECS tasks can mount, stores data across Availability Zones, bursts throughput, and grows automatically.
C is wrong: EBS Multi-Attach is limited to one Availability Zone and needs a cluster-aware file system.
D is wrong: a self-managed NFS server on one instance is a single point of failure and a lot of work.
tldr: Shared Linux storage for ECS tasks across AZs with burstable throughput: Amazon EFS.

wrong_reasons.A: FSx for Windows is SMB storage, not a natural fit for Linux containers.
wrong_reasons.C: EBS Multi-Attach is limited to one Availability Zone and needs a cluster-aware file system.
wrong_reasons.D: a self-managed NFS server on one instance is a single point of failure and a lot of work.

question: A healthcare company is designing a system to store and manage logs in the AWS Cloud. The system ingests and stores logs that are in JSON format. The logs contain sensitive patient information. The company must identify any sensitive data. The company must be able to search the log data by using SQL queries. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Store in S3, find sensitive data with the managed discovery service, and query with serverless SQL.

options.A: Store the logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data. Use Amazon Athena to query the logs.
options.B: Store the logs in an Amazon EBS volume. Create an application that uses Amazon SageMaker AI to detect sensitive data. Use Amazon RDS to query the logs.
options.C: Store the logs in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS KMS to discover sensitive data. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the logs.
options.D: Store the logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Inspector to discover sensitive data. Use Amazon Athena to query the logs.

explanation: A is correct: S3 stores the logs, Macie discovers sensitive data in them, and Athena runs SQL directly on the JSON files.
B is wrong: EBS is block storage for one instance, and a custom ML application is unnecessary.
C is wrong: KMS encrypts data; it does not discover sensitive data.
D is wrong: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities, not data in S3.
tldr: Logs in S3: Macie finds sensitive data, and Athena queries the JSON with SQL.

wrong_reasons.B: EBS is block storage for one instance, and a custom ML application is unnecessary.
wrong_reasons.C: KMS encrypts data; it does not discover sensitive data.
wrong_reasons.D: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities, not data in S3.

question: A company runs its infrastructure on AWS and has a registered base of 700,000 users for its document management application. The company intends to create a product that converts large pdf files to jpg image files. The pdf files average 5 MB in size. The company needs to store the original files and the converted files. A solutions architect must design a scalable solution to accommodate demand that will grow rapidly over time. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Store files cheaply and convert them only when they arrive.

options.A: Save the .pdf files to Amazon S3. Configure an S3 PUT event to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in Amazon S3.
options.B: Save the .pdf files to Amazon DynamoDB. Use the DynamoDB Streams feature to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in DynamoDB.
options.C: Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon EBS storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the files to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.
options.D: Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon EFS storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the files to .jpg format. Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EFS store.

explanation: A is correct: S3 stores both file types cheaply at any scale, and an S3 event invokes Lambda to convert each file only when it arrives.
B is wrong: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, and storing files there is expensive.
C is wrong: always-on EC2 instances with EBS cost more, and EBS is tied to individual instances.
D is wrong: always-on EC2 instances and EFS storage cost more than S3 and Lambda.
tldr: Event-driven processing: S3 upload triggers Lambda, which writes the result back to S3.

wrong_reasons.B: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, and storing files there is expensive.
wrong_reasons.C: always-on EC2 instances with EBS cost more, and EBS is tied to individual instances.
wrong_reasons.D: always-on EC2 instances and EFS storage cost more than S3 and Lambda.

question: An insurance company wants to migrate an application that calculates insurance premiums to AWS. The company needs to run calculations immediately when a customer submits information through the application. The application usually takes 10 seconds to process a calculation. A solutions architect needs to develop an architecture on AWS to handle the application. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: A short, synchronous calculation behind an API.

options.A: Set up an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to receive the data. Use an AWS Lambda function to process the data immediately.
options.B: Upload the customer data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Start an Amazon EC2 Spot Instance to process every data upload.
options.C: Set up AWS Transfer Family to receive the customer data. Configure an Amazon EKS job to process the customer data on a schedule.
options.D: Upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Invoke an AWS Batch job to process every customer data upload.

explanation: A is correct: API Gateway receives each submission and Lambda runs the 10-second calculation immediately.
B is wrong: starting a Spot Instance per upload is slow and can be interrupted.
C is wrong: processing on a schedule is not immediate.
D is wrong: Batch jobs queue and start slowly, not immediately.
tldr: Short request-response work behind an API: API Gateway invoking Lambda.

wrong_reasons.B: starting a Spot Instance per upload is slow and can be interrupted.
wrong_reasons.C: processing on a schedule is not immediate.
wrong_reasons.D: Batch jobs queue and start slowly, not immediately.

question: A company is creating a web application that will store a large number of images in Amazon S3. The images will be accessed by users over variable periods of time. The company wants to retain all the images, incur no cost for retrieval, have minimal management overhead, and have the images available with no impact on retrieval time. Which solution meets these requirements?
hint: Unknown access patterns, no retrieval fees and no management.

options.A: Implement S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.B: Implement S3 storage class analysis.
options.C: Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to move data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
options.D: Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to move data to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).

explanation: A is correct: Intelligent-Tiering moves images between tiers automatically with no retrieval fees and no change in retrieval time.
B is wrong: storage class analysis only recommends; it changes nothing.
C is wrong: Standard-IA charges for retrievals.
D is wrong: One Zone-IA charges for retrievals and stores data in only one Availability Zone.
tldr: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes cost for unpredictable access with no retrieval fees or lifecycle management.

wrong_reasons.B: storage class analysis only recommends; it changes nothing.
wrong_reasons.C: Standard-IA charges for retrievals.
wrong_reasons.D: One Zone-IA charges for retrievals and stores data in only one Availability Zone.

question: A company is migrating an on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud. The company is using Amazon FSx for Windows File Server to perform test deployments into a single Availability Zone. After testing, the company determines that it needs to improve availability and fault tolerance for its shared Windows file system. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: The deployment type of an FSx file system cannot be changed after creation. How do you move the data?

options.A: Set up a new FSx for Windows File Server file system in a second Availability Zone. Use AWS Transfer Family to replicate data from the original file system. Use the new file system as a failover option.
options.B: Shut down the existing FSx for Windows File Server file system. Change the deployment configuration to a Multi-AZ deployment type. Restart the file system.
options.C: Set up a new FSx for Windows File Server file system that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS DataSync to transfer data from the original file system to the new file system.
options.D: Set up a new FSx for Windows File Server file system that has a Multi-AZ deployment type. Use AWS DMS to transfer data from the original file system to the new file system.

explanation: A is wrong: Transfer Family is for SFTP/FTP file transfers, not replicating file systems, and a manual failover option is weaker than Multi-AZ.
B is wrong: the deployment type cannot be changed on an existing file system.
C is correct: a new Multi-AZ file system gives automatic failover, and DataSync copies the data from the old file system.
D is wrong: DMS migrates databases, not file systems.
tldr: You cannot convert FSx for Windows from Single-AZ to Multi-AZ; create a Multi-AZ file system and move the data with DataSync.

wrong_reasons.A: Transfer Family is for SFTP/FTP file transfers, not replicating file systems, and a manual failover option is weaker than Multi-AZ.
wrong_reasons.B: the deployment type cannot be changed on an existing file system.
wrong_reasons.D: DMS migrates databases, not file systems.

question: A company wants to protect resources that the company hosts on AWS, including Application Load Balancers and Amazon CloudFront distributions. The company wants an AWS service that can provide near real-time visibility into attacks on the company's resources. The service must also have a dedicated AWS team to assist with (DDoS) attacks. Which AWS service will meet these requirements?
hint: Which tier of DDoS protection includes the Shield Response Team?

options.A: AWS WAF.
options.B: AWS Shield Standard.
options.C: Amazon Macie.
options.D: AWS Shield Advanced.

explanation: A is wrong: WAF filters web requests but includes no dedicated response team.
B is wrong: Shield Standard is automatic basic protection with no attack visibility or response team.
C is wrong: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.
D is correct: Shield Advanced gives near real-time attack visibility and access to the Shield Response Team.
tldr: Shield Advanced adds attack visibility, cost protection and the Shield Response Team (SRT) for DDoS events.

wrong_reasons.A: WAF filters web requests but includes no dedicated response team.
wrong_reasons.B: Shield Standard is automatic basic protection with no attack visibility or response team.
wrong_reasons.C: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.

question: A company uses AWS to run its workloads. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The company needs to identify which departments are responsible for specific costs. New accounts are constantly created in the Organizations account structure. The Organizations continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) framework already adds the populated department tag to the AWS resources. The company wants to use an AWS Cost Explorer report to identify the service costs by department from all AWS accounts. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency? (Select TWO.)
hint: The pipeline already tags every resource. What is the minimum needed to make that tag usable in Cost Explorer across all accounts?
keywords: identify the service costs by department from all AWS accounts

options.A: Activate the aws:createdBy cost allocation tag and the department cost allocation tag in the management account.
options.B: Create a new cost and usage report in Cost Explorer. Group by the department cost allocation tag. Apply a filter to see all linked accounts and services.
options.C: Activate only the department cost allocation tag in the management account.
options.D: Create a new cost and usage report in Cost Explorer. Group by the department cost allocation tag without any other filters.
options.E: Activate only the aws:createdBy cost allocation tag in the management account.

explanation: A is wrong: the department tag is needed, but aws:createdBy is irrelevant here because the CI/CD pipeline already tags every resource with its department.
B is wrong: the management account's Cost Explorer already includes all linked accounts and services, so adding a filter for them is an unnecessary step.
C is correct: activating only the department cost allocation tag in the management account makes it usable in Cost Explorer for every account, and nothing else is required.
D is correct: grouping by the department tag in the management account shows costs by department across all linked accounts and services, with no extra filters.
E is wrong: aws:createdBy shows who created resources, not which department owns them.
tldr: Activate the user-defined tag as a cost allocation tag in the management account, then group Cost Explorer by it; the management account already sees all linked accounts and services.

wrong_reasons.A: the department tag is needed, but aws:createdBy is irrelevant here because the CI/CD pipeline already tags every resource with its department.
wrong_reasons.B: the management account's Cost Explorer already includes all linked accounts and services, so adding a filter for them is an unnecessary step.
wrong_reasons.E: aws:createdBy shows who created resources, not which department owns them.

question: A company wants to host a scalable web application on AWS. Users from around the world will access the application. Application users must have the ability to download and upload objects up to 5 GB in size. The company wants a cost-effective solution to minimize upload and download latency and maximize performance. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Speed up long-distance transfers of large objects to and from S3.

options.A: Use Amazon S3 with Transfer Acceleration to host the application.
options.B: Use Amazon S3 with Cache-Control headers to host the application.
options.C: Host the application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution to use the EC2 instances as the origin.
options.D: Host the application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster, and integrate the cluster with the EC2 instances.

explanation: A is correct: S3 stores the large objects, and Transfer Acceleration routes uploads and downloads through the nearest edge location over the AWS network.
B is wrong: Cache-Control headers do not speed up uploads.
C is wrong: EC2 and CloudFront add servers to manage and do not speed up uploads into storage as simply.
D is wrong: a Redis cache cannot hold 5 GB objects for users worldwide.
tldr: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads and downloads through edge locations.

wrong_reasons.B: Cache-Control headers do not speed up uploads.
wrong_reasons.C: EC2 and CloudFront add servers to manage and do not speed up uploads into storage as simply.
wrong_reasons.D: a Redis cache cannot hold 5 GB objects for users worldwide.

question: A company hosts an internal web application on a single Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet. The company is running NAT software on an EC2 instance for outbound internet access to the application. To improve fault tolerance and help ensure high availability, the company needs a more resilient architecture for both the application and its outbound connectivity. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Remove both single points of failure: the application instance and the NAT instance.
keywords: NAT software on an EC2 instance

options.A: Launch a standby NAT instance in a different Availability Zone. Update the route tables if the primary instance becomes unavailable.
options.B: Attach a Network Load Balancer in front of the web application. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to attempt to recover the instance.
options.C: Deploy EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Place the EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.D: Replace the NAT instance with a single NAT gateway in one Availability Zone. Associate the NAT gateway with all private subnets across the VPC.
options.E: Provision a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone. Update the private subnet route tables to use the local NAT gateway.

explanation: A is wrong: a standby NAT instance with manual route changes is slow and error-prone.
B is wrong: an NLB in front of one instance still has a single point of failure.
C is correct: an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones behind an ALB makes the application highly available.
D is wrong: a single NAT gateway fails if its Availability Zone fails.
E is correct: a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, used by that zone's subnets, removes the NAT single point of failure.
tldr: Resilience: an Auto Scaling group across AZs behind an ALB, plus a NAT gateway in each AZ.

wrong_reasons.A: a standby NAT instance with manual route changes is slow and error-prone.
wrong_reasons.B: an NLB in front of one instance still has a single point of failure.
wrong_reasons.D: a single NAT gateway fails if its Availability Zone fails.

question: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled to manage its AWS accounts. The company created an organizational unit (OU) in Organizations that contains accounts for developers. The company established a daily spending threshold for each developer account. The company wants to use an Amazon SNS topic to receive notification when an account reaches the daily spending threshold. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which service compares spending with a threshold and sends alerts?

options.A: Use AWS Cost Explorer to track spending for each account. Set up a dashboard to track each account's daily spending. Configure Amazon SNS to send an SNS alert when an account's spending reaches the daily spending threshold.
options.B: Use AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to detect anomalies in spending. Configure Amazon SNS to send an SNS alert when AWS Cost Anomaly Detection detects an anomaly.
options.C: Use AWS Budgets to set up a threshold for each account. Set up budget actions to send an SNS alert when an account's spending reaches the threshold.
options.D: Set up a composite Amazon CloudWatch alarm to send an SNS alert when the sum of all cost metrics exceeds the account's daily spending threshold.

explanation: A is wrong: Cost Explorer dashboards do not send SNS alerts on thresholds.
B is wrong: anomaly detection flags unusual patterns, not a fixed threshold.
C is correct: a daily budget per account alerts the SNS topic as soon as spending reaches the threshold.
D is wrong: CloudWatch billing metrics are account-wide estimates and cannot express a daily threshold for each account this simply.
tldr: AWS Budgets tracks spending per account against a threshold (daily budgets are supported) and alerts SNS.

wrong_reasons.A: Cost Explorer dashboards do not send SNS alerts on thresholds.
wrong_reasons.B: anomaly detection flags unusual patterns, not a fixed threshold.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudWatch billing metrics are account-wide estimates and cannot express a daily threshold for each account this simply.

question: A software company recently modernized its video processing application to run on containers. Depending on the video length and quality, the video processing jobs could take 1 hour or more to finish. The video processing jobs are expected to serve thousands of requests each second. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Jobs longer than 15 minutes rule out Lambda. Which option runs containers without servers?

options.A: Install Kubernetes on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. Deploy the application.
options.B: Run the application by using AWS Lambda functions that use a container image.
options.C: Deploy the application on Amazon ECS containers that run on AWS Fargate.
options.D: Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances that run on an AWS Outposts rack.

explanation: A is wrong: self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 is the most operational work.
B is wrong: Lambda times out after 15 minutes, and jobs run for an hour or more.
C is correct: Fargate runs long container jobs and scales without servers to manage.
D is wrong: Outposts puts AWS hardware on premises, which does not reduce overhead.
tldr: Long-running containerized jobs at scale: ECS on Fargate; Lambda stops at 15 minutes.

wrong_reasons.A: self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 is the most operational work.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda times out after 15 minutes, and jobs run for an hour or more.
wrong_reasons.D: Outposts puts AWS hardware on premises, which does not reduce overhead.

question: A company runs code compilation tasks that span many virtual machines (VMs) in its on-premises data center. These tasks require low latency and high bandwidth between servers. The company wants to migrate this workload to run on Amazon EC2 instances in the AWS Cloud. After the migration, the workload must maintain low latency and high bandwidth between EC2 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which placement group packs instances close together on the network?

options.A: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a cluster placement group. Enable enhanced networking on the EC2 instances.
options.B: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances in a partition placement group. Enable enhanced networking on the EC2 instances.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon EKS cluster that uses a managed node group of Amazon EC2 instances. Configure the cluster to use a container network interface (CNI) for enhanced networking.
options.D: Configure an AWS Batch fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. Enable enhanced networking on the EC2 instances. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate compilation tasks.

explanation: A is correct: a cluster placement group puts instances close together in one Availability Zone, and enhanced networking raises bandwidth and lowers latency.
B is wrong: partition placement groups spread instances for fault isolation, not low latency.
C is wrong: EKS adds container orchestration that the compilation tasks do not need.
D is wrong: Batch and Step Functions add orchestration without placing instances close together.
tldr: Cluster placement groups with enhanced networking give the lowest latency and highest bandwidth between instances.

wrong_reasons.B: partition placement groups spread instances for fault isolation, not low latency.
wrong_reasons.C: EKS adds container orchestration that the compilation tasks do not need.
wrong_reasons.D: Batch and Step Functions add orchestration without placing instances close together.

question: A financial services company needs to store and manage trading documentation. The documentation includes real-time trade confirmation data, financial statements, and settlement documents that frequently exceed 1 MB in size. The company's current provisioned database solution stores and manages this documentation. This current solution experiences high-volume trading activity during market hours but very low activity during off-hours. The company currently uses a provisioned database solution that is sized to handle the load for peak trading hours. This solution results in significant unused capacity during off-hours. The company needs a solution that will maintain performance during peak hours. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Check the size limit per item or document in each database, then find one that scales capacity automatically.

options.A: Deploy Amazon RDS for MySQL on Reserved Instances with read replicas for scaling.
options.B: Deploy Amazon DocumentDB serverless with automatic capacity scaling.
options.C: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB with auto scaling.
options.D: Deploy a MongoDB cluster on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.

explanation: A is wrong: Reserved Instances pay for peak capacity all the time, which is the waste the company wants to remove.
B is correct: DocumentDB serverless stores documents up to 16 MB and scales capacity automatically, so the company pays little during quiet hours.
C is wrong: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, but these documents often exceed 1 MB.
D is wrong: self-managed MongoDB on EC2 is a lot of operational work.
tldr: Large JSON-style documents with spiky demand: DocumentDB serverless (16 MB documents, automatic scaling); DynamoDB items max out at 400 KB.

wrong_reasons.A: Reserved Instances pay for peak capacity all the time, which is the waste the company wants to remove.
wrong_reasons.C: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, but these documents often exceed 1 MB.
wrong_reasons.D: self-managed MongoDB on EC2 is a lot of operational work.

question: A company has built a public API by using an Amazon API Gateway REST API and an AWS Lambda function in one AWS Region. The API must maintain high availability. The company's compliance policy requires that the application be deployed across multiple Regions. Users must be routed automatically to an available API endpoint without requiring any changes on the users' side. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Deploy a second Regional API, then let DNS route users to a healthy one.
keywords: routed automatically to an available API endpoint

options.A: Deploy the API as an edge-optimized REST API with the Lambda function to achieve Regional failover.
options.B: Deploy the API as a Regional REST API with the Lambda function in an additional Region.
options.C: Use Amazon Route 53. Configure Route 53 with a simple routing policy that splits traffic between all API Gateway REST API endpoints.
options.D: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the API endpoints. Use origin failover to switch between Regions.
options.E: Use Amazon Route 53. Configure Route 53 with latency-based routing and health checks to route traffic to healthy API endpoints.

explanation: A is wrong: an edge-optimized API still runs in one Region, so it gives no Regional failover.
B is correct: a Regional REST API and function in a second Region gives another place to serve from.
C is wrong: simple routing has no health checks and cannot avoid a failed Region.
D is wrong: CloudFront origin failover only retries certain errors and is not the standard design for multi-Region APIs.
E is correct: latency-based routing with health checks sends users to the nearest healthy API endpoint automatically.
tldr: Multi-Region API: Regional endpoints in each Region plus Route 53 latency routing with health checks.

wrong_reasons.A: an edge-optimized API still runs in one Region, so it gives no Regional failover.
wrong_reasons.C: simple routing has no health checks and cannot avoid a failed Region.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudFront origin failover only retries certain errors and is not the standard design for multi-Region APIs.

question: A company that recently started using AWS establishes a Site-to-Site VPN between its on-premises data center and AWS. The company's security mandate states that traffic originating from on premises should stay within the company's private IP space when communicating with an Amazon ECS cluster that is hosting a sample web application. Which solution meets this requirement?
hint: Expose the service privately with a load balancer and an interface endpoint in the same VPC.
keywords: stay within the company's private IP space

options.A: Configure a gateway endpoint for Amazon ECS. Modify the route table to include an entry pointing to the ECS cluster.
options.B: Create a Network Load Balancer and AWS PrivateLink endpoint for Amazon ECS in the same VPC that is hosting the ECS cluster.
options.C: Create a Network Load Balancer in one VPC and an AWS PrivateLink endpoint for Amazon ECS in another VPC. Connect the two VPCs by using VPC peering.
options.D: Configure an Amazon Route 53 record with Amazon ECS as the target. Apply a server certificate to Route 53 from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for SSL offloading.

explanation: A is wrong: there is no gateway endpoint for ECS workloads; gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
B is correct: an NLB in front of the ECS service with a PrivateLink endpoint gives on-premises clients a private IP to reach over the VPN.
C is wrong: splitting across two peered VPCs adds complexity for no benefit.
D is wrong: Route 53 cannot hold certificates or target ECS directly.
tldr: Reach a service privately over VPN with a Network Load Balancer and PrivateLink, keeping traffic on private IPs.

wrong_reasons.A: there is no gateway endpoint for ECS workloads; gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
wrong_reasons.C: splitting across two peered VPCs adds complexity for no benefit.
wrong_reasons.D: Route 53 cannot hold certificates or target ECS directly.

question: A company is developing an AWS Lambda function that publishes notifications to an encrypted Amazon SNS topic. The notifications contain personal health information (PHI). The SNS topic uses AWS KMS customer managed keys for encryption. The company must ensure that the application has the necessary permissions to publish messages securely to the SNS topic. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
hint: Publishing to an encrypted topic needs permission on the topic, on the KMS key, and in the function's own role.

options.A: Create a resource policy for the SNS topic that allows the Lambda function to publish messages to the SNS topic.
options.B: Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) for the SNS topic to encrypt the PHI.
options.C: Create a resource policy for the encryption key that the SNS topic uses that has the necessary AWS KMS permissions.
options.D: Specify the Lambda function's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SNS topic's resource policy.
options.E: Integrate an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with the SNS topic to control access to the topic by using API Gateway resource policies.
options.F: Configure a Lambda execution role that has the necessary IAM permissions to use a customer managed key in AWS KMS.

explanation: A is correct: the topic's resource policy must allow the function (through its role) to publish.
B is wrong: SNS does not use SSE-S3; its encryption uses KMS keys.
C is correct: the key policy must allow the publisher to use the customer managed key.
D is wrong: topic policies identify the caller by its IAM role, not by the function ARN.
E is wrong: API Gateway is not needed to control who can publish to SNS.
F is correct: the execution role needs KMS permissions such as kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt for the key.
tldr: Publishing to a KMS-encrypted SNS topic needs a topic policy, a key policy, and KMS permissions on the publisher's role.

wrong_reasons.B: SNS does not use SSE-S3; its encryption uses KMS keys.
wrong_reasons.D: topic policies identify the caller by its IAM role, not by the function ARN.
wrong_reasons.E: API Gateway is not needed to control who can publish to SNS.

question: A company is deploying a critical application by using Amazon RDS for MySQL. The application must be highly available and must recover automatically. The company needs to support interactive users (transactional queries) and batch reporting (analytical queries) with no more than a 4-hour lag. The analytical queries must not affect the performance of the transactional queries. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which RDS Multi-AZ option has standbys that also serve reads through a reader endpoint?
keywords: analytical queries must not affect the performance of the transactional queries

options.A: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with one standby instance. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to a secondary DB instance that runs in a different Availability Zone.
options.B: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two standby instances. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to the reader endpoint.
options.C: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL to use multiple read replicas across multiple Availability Zones. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to one of the replicas in a different Availability Zone.
options.D: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL as the primary database for the transactional queries with automated backups enabled. Configure automated backups. Each night, create a read-only database from the most recent snapshot to support the analytical queries. Terminate the previously created database.

explanation: A is wrong: the standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment cannot serve reads.
B is correct: a Multi-AZ DB cluster fails over automatically, and its reader endpoint sends analytical queries to the readable standbys.
C is wrong: read replicas do not fail over automatically.
D is wrong: nightly restores are a lot of work and give no automatic recovery.
tldr: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys: automatic failover plus a reader endpoint for analytics.

wrong_reasons.A: the standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment cannot serve reads.
wrong_reasons.C: read replicas do not fail over automatically.
wrong_reasons.D: nightly restores are a lot of work and give no automatic recovery.

question: An e-commerce company wants to use machine learning (ML) algorithms to build and train models. The company will use the models to visualize complex scenarios and to detect trends in customer data. The architecture team wants to integrate its ML models with a reporting platform to analyze the augmented data and to use the data directly in its business intelligence dashboards. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: A managed ML platform plus a managed BI service.

options.A: Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
options.B: Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
options.C: Use an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
options.D: Use Amazon QuickSight to build and train models and to visualize the data.

explanation: A is wrong: Glue ML transforms are for tasks such as deduplication, not general model training, and OpenSearch is not a BI tool.
B is correct: SageMaker builds and trains models, and QuickSight dashboards visualize the augmented data.
C is wrong: self-managed AMIs add operational work.
D is wrong: QuickSight does not build and train custom ML models.
tldr: Managed ML and BI: SageMaker to build and train models, QuickSight to visualize the results.

wrong_reasons.A: Glue ML transforms are for tasks such as deduplication, not general model training, and OpenSearch is not a BI tool.
wrong_reasons.C: self-managed AMIs add operational work.
wrong_reasons.D: QuickSight does not build and train custom ML models.

question: A company is building a serverless application to process orders from an e-commerce site. The application needs to handle bursts of traffic during peak usage hours and to maintain high availability. The orders must be processed asynchronously in the order the application receives them. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Ordered, buffered and serverless.
keywords: in the order the application receives them

options.A: Use an Amazon SNS topic to receive orders. Use an AWS Lambda function to process the orders.
options.B: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue to receive orders. Use an AWS Lambda function to process the orders.
options.C: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue to receive orders. Use AWS Batch jobs to process the orders.
options.D: Use an Amazon SNS topic to receive orders. Use AWS Batch jobs to process the orders.

explanation: A is wrong: SNS standard topics do not preserve order.
B is correct: a FIFO queue buffers bursts and keeps orders in sequence, and Lambda processes them asynchronously.
C is wrong: standard queues do not guarantee order, and Batch is not serverless.
D is wrong: SNS does not preserve order, and Batch is not serverless.
tldr: SQS FIFO queues keep order and buffer bursts; Lambda processes the messages serverlessly.

wrong_reasons.A: SNS standard topics do not preserve order.
wrong_reasons.C: standard queues do not guarantee order, and Batch is not serverless.
wrong_reasons.D: SNS does not preserve order, and Batch is not serverless.

question: A solutions architect needs to design a disaster recovery (DR) plan for an application on AWS. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. The recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) are 15 minutes each. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)
hint: Data must be only minutes behind, and compute must be ready to scale, but not at full size.
keywords: recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) are 15 minutes each

options.A: Configure Aurora backups to be exported to the DR Region.
options.B: Configure the Aurora cluster to replicate data to the DR Region by using the Aurora global database option.
options.C: Configure the DR Region with an ALB and an Auto Scaling group. Use the same configuration as in the primary Region.
options.D: Configure the DR Region with an ALB and an Auto Scaling group. Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity, maximum capacity, and desired capacity to 1.
options.E: Manually launch a new ALB and a new Auto Scaling group by using AWS CloudFormation during a failover activity.

explanation: A is wrong: exported backups are too old and too slow to restore for a 15-minute RPO and RTO.
B is correct: Aurora Global Database replicates to the DR Region with about a second of lag and can be promoted in minutes.
C is wrong: full production capacity in the DR Region costs more than needed.
D is correct: a minimal ALB and Auto Scaling group is ready to scale out quickly at low cost.
E is wrong: building everything during failover risks missing the 15-minute RTO.
tldr: Pilot light/warm standby for 15-minute RTO/RPO: Aurora Global Database plus a minimal Auto Scaling group in the DR Region.

wrong_reasons.A: exported backups are too old and too slow to restore for a 15-minute RPO and RTO.
wrong_reasons.C: full production capacity in the DR Region costs more than needed.
wrong_reasons.E: building everything during failover risks missing the 15-minute RTO.

question: A company develops a multi-tenant application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an AWS account. The company performs a security audit. The security audit identifies that the company must separate tenants into dedicated AWS accounts to reduce the potential impact of exploited vulnerabilities across customers. The company recently purchased a Savings Plan for the account where the application runs. The company wants to use the discounts in all the accounts where the application will run. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements while following AWS Well-Architected design patterns? (Select TWO.)
hint: Savings Plan discounts are shared through consolidated billing in an organization, controlled from the management account.
keywords: separate tenants into dedicated AWS accounts

options.A: From the management account in the AWS Management Console, turn on discount sharing from the billing preferences section.
options.B: From the AWS Management Console of the account that purchased the existing Savings Plan, turn on discount sharing from the billing preferences section. Include all accounts.
options.C: From the AWS Organizations management account, use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the Savings Plan with other accounts.
options.D: Create a new AWS account and enable AWS Organizations. Invite the existing AWS account to join the organization. Create new AWS accounts from the management account.
options.E: Create a new AWS account and enable AWS Organizations. Invite the existing AWS account to join the organization. Create the required new AWS accounts from the Organizations management console.

explanation: A is correct: discount sharing is turned on in the management account's billing preferences.
B is wrong: member accounts cannot control discount sharing; the management account does.
C is wrong: Savings Plans cannot be shared with AWS RAM.
D is wrong: this creates the organization, but the new accounts should be created through the Organizations console so they join it directly.
E is correct: creating an organization, inviting the existing account and creating the tenant accounts from the Organizations console puts all accounts under consolidated billing.
tldr: Share Savings Plan discounts by putting accounts in one organization and enabling discount sharing in the management account.

wrong_reasons.B: member accounts cannot control discount sharing; the management account does.
wrong_reasons.C: Savings Plans cannot be shared with AWS RAM.
wrong_reasons.D: this creates the organization, but the new accounts should be created through the Organizations console so they join it directly.

question: A company's e-commerce platform experiences unpredictable surges in traffic related to periodic sale events. The platform's web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. EC2 worker instances in an Auto Scaling group process orders. The company needs a solution that accepts orders immediately, processes the orders asynchronously, and never loses orders if a worker instance experiences an application problem. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Buffer orders durably between the web tier and the workers.

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function. Configure the web tier EC2 instances to invoke the Lambda function synchronously for each order. Configure the Lambda function to write the processed results directly to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.B: Configure the web tier EC2 instances to publish order details to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe a shared worker email address to the topic for processing.
options.C: Configure the web tier EC2 instances to place order messages into an Amazon SQS standard queue. Configure the Auto Scaling group of worker EC2 instances to poll the queue and write the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.D: Configure the web tier EC2 instances to insert orders into an Amazon RDS for MySQL table. Configure an AWS Lambda function to query unprocessed rows once each minute and update the row status.

explanation: A is wrong: synchronous Lambda calls make the web tier wait and are not asynchronous.
B is wrong: emailing orders to a shared inbox is manual and loses orders easily.
C is correct: SQS stores each order until a worker processes it, and a message returns to the queue if the worker fails.
D is wrong: polling a database table every minute is custom work and adds delay.
tldr: SQS decouples the web tier from workers; messages stay in the queue until processed, so orders are not lost.

wrong_reasons.A: synchronous Lambda calls make the web tier wait and are not asynchronous.
wrong_reasons.B: emailing orders to a shared inbox is manual and loses orders easily.
wrong_reasons.D: polling a database table every minute is custom work and adds delay.

question: An e-commerce company has an application that collects order-related information from customers. The company uses one Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. Customers can check out without creating an account. The application copies the customer information to a second DynamoDB table if a customer does create an account. The company requires a solution to delete personally identifiable information (PII) for customers who did not create an account within 28 days. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: DynamoDB can expire items by itself based on a timestamp attribute.

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function to delete items from the first DynamoDB table that have a delivery date more than 28 days in the past. Use a scheduled Amazon EventBridge rule to run the Lambda function every day.
options.B: Update the application to store PII in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire the objects after 28 days. Move the data to DynamoDB when a user creates an account.
options.C: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure a daily cron job to run on the instance. Configure the cron job to use AWS CLI commands to delete items from DynamoDB.
options.D: Use a createdAt timestamp to set TTL for data in the first DynamoDB table to 28 days.

explanation: A is wrong: a scheduled Lambda function is code to write and maintain.
B is wrong: moving PII storage to S3 means redesigning the application.
C is wrong: a cron job on EC2 is infrastructure and scripts to maintain.
D is correct: TTL based on a createdAt timestamp deletes the guest records automatically after 28 days with no code.
tldr: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items automatically at no cost; set it from a creation timestamp.

wrong_reasons.A: a scheduled Lambda function is code to write and maintain.
wrong_reasons.B: moving PII storage to S3 means redesigning the application.
wrong_reasons.C: a cron job on EC2 is infrastructure and scripts to maintain.

question: A company is creating a prototype of an e-commerce website on AWS. The website consists of an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances for web servers, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that runs with the Single-AZ configuration. The website is slow to respond during searches of the product catalog. The product catalog is a group of tables in the MySQL database that the company does not update frequently. A solutions architect has determined that the CPU utilization on the DB instance is high when product catalog searches occur. What should the solutions architect recommend to improve the performance of the website during searches of the product catalog?
hint: Rarely changing data read over and over: serve it from memory.
keywords: CPU utilization on the DB instance is high

options.A: Migrate the product catalog to an Amazon Redshift database. Use the COPY command to load the product catalog tables.
options.B: Implement an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster to cache the product catalog. Use lazy loading to populate the cache.
options.C: Add an additional scaling policy to the Auto Scaling group to launch additional EC2 instances when database response is slow.
options.D: Turn on the Multi-AZ configuration for the DB instance. Configure the EC2 instances to throttle the product catalog queries that are sent to the database.

explanation: A is wrong: Redshift is for analytics, not low-latency catalog lookups for a website.
B is correct: caching the catalog in Redis with lazy loading serves repeated searches from memory and cuts database CPU.
C is wrong: more web servers send even more queries to the database.
D is wrong: the Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, and throttling hurts users.
tldr: Cache rarely changing, frequently read data in ElastiCache with lazy loading to take load off the database.

wrong_reasons.A: Redshift is for analytics, not low-latency catalog lookups for a website.
wrong_reasons.C: more web servers send even more queries to the database.
wrong_reasons.D: the Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, and throttling hurts users.

question: A company runs a non-production Oracle database on an Amazon EC2 instance. The database contains 1 TB of data. The EC2 instance runs in a private subnet of a VPC. A backup of the EC2 instance is taken every day and uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. The current backup process uses a NAT gateway to access the S3 bucket. The company does not want the backup process to use public IP addresses. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Private, free access to S3 from a private subnet.
keywords: uses a NAT gateway to access the S3 bucket
does not want the backup process to use public IP addresses

options.A: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. Update the route tables.
options.B: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket. Compress the backup files and use multipart uploads.
options.C: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution, and set the S3 bucket as the origin. Upload the backup files to the CloudFront distribution.
options.D: Use a third-party tool to mount the S3 bucket as a file share on the EC2 instance operating system. Use the file share as the backup target.

explanation: A is correct: a gateway endpoint gives private access to S3 through the route table at no charge.
B is wrong: Transfer Acceleration uses public endpoints and adds cost.
C is wrong: CloudFront is for delivery to viewers and uses public endpoints.
D is wrong: mounting S3 with a third-party tool still goes through the NAT gateway.
tldr: An S3 gateway endpoint keeps S3 traffic private and removes NAT gateway charges.

wrong_reasons.B: Transfer Acceleration uses public endpoints and adds cost.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudFront is for delivery to viewers and uses public endpoints.
wrong_reasons.D: mounting S3 with a third-party tool still goes through the NAT gateway.

question: A company hosts an application on an Amazon EC2 instance in a single AWS Region. The application requires support for non-HTTP TCP traffic and HTTP traffic. The company wants to deliver content with low latency by using the AWS network. The company also wants to implement an Auto Scaling group with an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer. How should a solutions architect meet these requirements?
hint: Non-HTTP TCP rules out ALB and CloudFront. Which accelerator works with any TCP?
keywords: non-HTTP TCP traffic and HTTP traffic
low latency by using the AWS network

options.A: Create an Auto Scaling group with an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the ALB as the origin.
options.B: Create an Auto Scaling group with an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Add an accelerator with AWS Global Accelerator with the ALB as an endpoint.
options.C: Create an Auto Scaling group with a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the NLB as the origin.
options.D: Create an Auto Scaling group with a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Add an accelerator with AWS Global Accelerator with the NLB as an endpoint.

explanation: A is wrong: an ALB handles only HTTP/HTTPS, and CloudFront cannot carry arbitrary TCP.
B is wrong: an ALB cannot handle non-HTTP TCP traffic.
C is wrong: CloudFront cannot deliver non-HTTP TCP traffic.
D is correct: an NLB handles any TCP traffic including HTTP, and Global Accelerator carries it over the AWS network for low latency.
tldr: Non-HTTP TCP plus HTTP over the AWS network: an NLB behind Global Accelerator.

wrong_reasons.A: an ALB handles only HTTP/HTTPS, and CloudFront cannot carry arbitrary TCP.
wrong_reasons.B: an ALB cannot handle non-HTTP TCP traffic.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudFront cannot deliver non-HTTP TCP traffic.

question: An e-commerce company is migrating its on-premises workload to the AWS Cloud. The workload currently consists of a web application and a backend Microsoft SQL database for storage. The company expects a high volume of customers during a promotional event. The new infrastructure in the AWS Cloud must be highly available and scalable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?
hint: Scale the web tier automatically, and make the managed database highly available.

options.A: Migrate the web application to two Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server with read replicas in both Availability Zones.
options.B: Migrate the web application to an Amazon EC2 instance that runs in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to two EC2 instances across separate AWS Regions with database replication.
options.C: Migrate the web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ deployment.
options.D: Migrate the web application to three Amazon EC2 instances across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Migrate the database to three EC2 instances across three Availability Zones.

explanation: A is wrong: two fixed instances do not scale, and RDS read replicas are not the high-availability mechanism.
B is wrong: a self-managed database on EC2 across Regions is a lot of work.
C is correct: an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones scales the web tier, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps the database available with automatic failover.
D is wrong: fixed instances do not scale, and a self-managed database on EC2 is a lot of work.
tldr: Auto Scaling across AZs behind an ALB for the web tier, RDS Multi-AZ for the database.

wrong_reasons.A: two fixed instances do not scale, and RDS read replicas are not the high-availability mechanism.
wrong_reasons.B: a self-managed database on EC2 across Regions is a lot of work.
wrong_reasons.D: fixed instances do not scale, and a self-managed database on EC2 is a lot of work.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that have instance store volumes attached. The application uses Amazon EFS to store files that are shared across a cluster of Linux servers. The shared files are at least 1 GB in size. The company accesses the files often for the first 7 days after creation. The files must remain readily available after the first 7 days. The company wants to optimize costs for the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Keep the files in EFS but move older ones to a cheaper storage class automatically.
keywords: accesses the files often for the first 7 days

options.A: Configure an AWS Storage Gateway Amazon S3 File Gateway to cache frequently accessed files locally. Store older files in Amazon S3.
options.B: Move the files from Amazon EFS, and store the the files locally on each EC2 instance.
options.C: Configure a lifecycle policy to move the files to the EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage class after 7 days.
options.D: Deploy AWS DataSync to automatically move files older than 7 days to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation: A is wrong: File Gateway is for on-premises access, and changing to S3 alters the application.
B is wrong: instance store is temporary and not shared between servers.
