C is correct: a lifecycle policy moves files to EFS Infrequent Access after 7 days, lowering cost while keeping them available at the same path.
D is wrong: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, so the files would not be readily available.
tldr: EFS lifecycle management moves files not accessed for a set period to EFS Infrequent Access, which is cheaper and still readily available.

wrong_reasons.A: File Gateway is for on-premises access, and changing to S3 alters the application.
wrong_reasons.B: instance store is temporary and not shared between servers.
wrong_reasons.D: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, so the files would not be readily available.

question: A company is migrating some workloads to AWS. However, many workloads will remain on premises. The on-premises workloads require secure and reliable connectivity to AWS with consistent, low-latency performance. The company has deployed the AWS workloads across multiple AWS accounts and multiple VPCs. The company plans to scale to hundreds of VPCs within the next year. The company must establish connectivity between each of the VPCs and from the on-premises environment to each VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Consistent latency means Direct Connect. Hundreds of VPCs means a hub.
keywords: between each of the VPCs and from the on-premises environment

options.A: Use an AWS Direct Connect connection to connect the on-premises environment to AWS. Configure VPC peering to establish connectivity between VPCs.
options.B: Use multiple AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections to connect the on-premises environment to AWS. Create a transit gateway to establish connectivity between VPCs.
options.C: Use an AWS Direct Connect connection with a Direct Connect gateway to connect the on-premises environment to AWS. Create a transit gateway to establish connectivity between VPCs. Associate the transit gateway with the Direct Connect gateway.
options.D: Use an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to connect the on-premises environment to AWS. Configure VPC peering to establish connectivity between VPCs.

explanation: A is wrong: VPC peering does not scale to hundreds of VPCs.
B is wrong: VPN runs over the internet, so its latency is not consistent.
C is correct: Direct Connect gives consistent low latency, and a transit gateway associated with a Direct Connect gateway connects every VPC to each other and to on premises.
D is wrong: VPN latency is not consistent, and peering does not scale.
tldr: Direct Connect + Direct Connect gateway + transit gateway connects on premises and hundreds of VPCs with consistent performance.

wrong_reasons.A: VPC peering does not scale to hundreds of VPCs.
wrong_reasons.B: VPN runs over the internet, so its latency is not consistent.
wrong_reasons.D: VPN latency is not consistent, and peering does not scale.

question: A company wants to improve its ability to clone large amounts of production data into a test environment in the same AWS Region. The data is stored in Amazon EC2 instances on Amazon EBS volumes. Modifications to the cloned data must not affect the production environment. The software that accesses this data requires consistently high I/O performance. A solutions architect needs to minimize the time that is required to clone the production data into the test environment. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Volumes restored from snapshots load lazily unless the snapshot is pre-warmed.
keywords: clone large amounts of production data

options.A: Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Restore the snapshots onto EC2 instance store volumes in the test environment.
options.B: Configure the production EBS volumes to use the EBS Multi-Attach feature. Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Attach the production EBS volumes to the EC2 instances in the test environment.
options.C: Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Create and initialize new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment before restoring the volumes from the production EBS snapshots.
options.D: Take EBS snapshots of the production EBS volumes. Turn on the EBS fast snapshot restore feature on the EBS snapshots. Restore the snapshots into new EBS volumes. Attach the new EBS volumes to EC2 instances in the test environment.

explanation: A is wrong: snapshots cannot be restored onto instance store volumes.
B is wrong: attaching production volumes to test instances lets tests change production data.
C is wrong: volumes are not restored after being attached, and initializing them takes a long time.
D is correct: fast snapshot restore creates fully initialized volumes, so the test copies deliver full performance right away without touching production.
tldr: EBS fast snapshot restore gives volumes full performance immediately after they are created from a snapshot.

wrong_reasons.A: snapshots cannot be restored onto instance store volumes.
wrong_reasons.B: attaching production volumes to test instances lets tests change production data.
wrong_reasons.C: volumes are not restored after being attached, and initializing them takes a long time.

question: A company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run a script to poll for and process messages in an Amazon SQS queue. The company wants to reduce operational overhead while maintaining its ability to process an increasing number of messages that are added to the queue. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which compute service reads from SQS for you and scales with the queue?
keywords: poll for and process messages in an Amazon SQS queue

options.A: Increase the size of the EC2 instance to process messages in the SQS queue faster.
options.B: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to turn off the EC2 instance when the SQS queue is empty.
options.C: Migrate the script on the EC2 instance to an AWS Lambda function with an event source of the SQS queue.
options.D: Configure an AWS Systems Manager Run Command to run the script on demand.

explanation: A is wrong: a bigger instance still needs managing and has a fixed limit.
B is wrong: turning the instance off when idle does not help it handle more messages.
C is correct: Lambda with an SQS event source polls and scales with the number of messages, with no servers to manage.
D is wrong: running the script on demand with Run Command does not scale automatically.
tldr: Replace an EC2 polling script with Lambda using SQS as an event source; it scales with queue depth.

wrong_reasons.A: a bigger instance still needs managing and has a fixed limit.
wrong_reasons.B: turning the instance off when idle does not help it handle more messages.
wrong_reasons.D: running the script on demand with Run Command does not scale automatically.

question: A company has a website that handles dynamic traffic loads. The website architecture is based on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that is configured to use scheduled scaling. Each EC2 instance runs code from an Amazon EFS volume and stores shared data back to the same volume. The company wants to optimize costs for the website. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Traffic is dynamic, but capacity follows a fixed schedule.

options.A: Reconfigure the Auto Scaling group to set a desired number of instances. Turn off scheduled scaling.
options.B: Create a new launch template version for the Auto Scaling group that uses larger EC2 instances.
options.C: Reconfigure the Auto Scaling group to use a target tracking scaling policy.
options.D: Replace the EFS volume with instance store volumes.

explanation: A is wrong: a fixed desired count cannot follow changing traffic.
B is wrong: larger instances cost more.
C is correct: target tracking adds and removes instances based on actual load, so the company pays only for what it needs.
D is wrong: instance store is not shared between instances and is lost when they stop.
tldr: For unpredictable traffic, target tracking scales with actual load instead of a fixed schedule.

wrong_reasons.A: a fixed desired count cannot follow changing traffic.
wrong_reasons.B: larger instances cost more.
wrong_reasons.D: instance store is not shared between instances and is lost when they stop.

question: An insurance company is creating an application to record personal user data. The data includes name, age, and health data about users. The company wants to run the application in a private subnet on AWS. Because of data security requirements, the company must have access to the operating system of the compute resource that run the application tier. The company must use a low-latency NoSQL database to store the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: OS access rules out Lambda and Fargate. Low-latency NoSQL is DynamoDB, reached privately.

options.A: Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application tier. Use an Amazon DynamoDB table for the database tier. Create a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB. Assign the instances an instance profile that has permission to access DynamoDB.
options.B: Use AWS Lambda functions for the application tier. Use an Amazon DynamoDB table for the database tier. Assign a Lambda function an appropriate IAM role to access the table.
options.C: Use AWS Fargate for the application tier. Create an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL instance inside in a private subnet for the database tier.
options.D: Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application tier. Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store the data in JSON format. Configure the application to use Amazon Athena to read and write the data to and from the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct: EC2 gives OS access, DynamoDB is a low-latency NoSQL database, and a VPC endpoint plus an instance profile keep access private and keyless.
B is wrong: Lambda gives no access to the operating system.
C is wrong: Fargate gives no OS access, and Aurora PostgreSQL is relational, not NoSQL.
D is wrong: S3 with Athena is not a low-latency database.
tldr: OS access needs EC2; reach DynamoDB privately with a VPC endpoint and an instance profile.

wrong_reasons.B: Lambda gives no access to the operating system.
wrong_reasons.C: Fargate gives no OS access, and Aurora PostgreSQL is relational, not NoSQL.
wrong_reasons.D: S3 with Athena is not a low-latency database.

question: A company is building a RESTful serverless web application on AWS by using Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The users of this web application will be geographically distributed, and the company wants to reduce the latency of API requests to these users. Which type of endpoint should a solutions architect use to meet these requirements?
hint: Which API Gateway endpoint type routes requests through CloudFront edge locations?
keywords: reduce the latency of API requests

options.A: Private endpoint.
options.B: Regional endpoint.
options.C: Interface VPC endpoint.
options.D: Edge-optimized endpoint.

explanation: A is wrong: private endpoints are reachable only from inside a VPC.
B is wrong: Regional endpoints suit clients in the same Region.
C is wrong: interface VPC endpoints are for private access, not for public users.
D is correct: edge-optimized endpoints bring requests into the nearest CloudFront edge location, reducing latency for users worldwide.
tldr: Edge-optimized API Gateway endpoints route requests through CloudFront edge locations for distributed clients.

wrong_reasons.A: private endpoints are reachable only from inside a VPC.
wrong_reasons.B: Regional endpoints suit clients in the same Region.
wrong_reasons.C: interface VPC endpoints are for private access, not for public users.

question: A company's compliance archive holds 120 TB of objects in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Standard access tier. The company accesses the objects frequently during the first 30 days after creation. After the initial 30 days, the company rarely reads the objects. However, the objects must be retrievable in under 1 minute when the company needs the objects. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
hint: Rarely read, but must come back in under a minute: which Glacier class gives millisecond access?

options.A: Store objects in S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) for the full retention period.
options.B: Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days.
options.C: Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days.
options.D: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to store objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive automatically after 30 days.

explanation: A is wrong: Standard-IA for the whole period is more expensive than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely read data, and the first 30 days are accessed often.
B is correct: Glacier Instant Retrieval is the cheapest class that still returns objects in milliseconds.
C is wrong: Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, so it cannot guarantee under 1 minute.
D is wrong: Deep Archive takes hours to restore.
tldr: Rarely read data that still needs millisecond access belongs in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

wrong_reasons.A: Standard-IA for the whole period is more expensive than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely read data, and the first 30 days are accessed often.
wrong_reasons.C: Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, so it cannot guarantee under 1 minute.
wrong_reasons.D: Deep Archive takes hours to restore.

question: A company runs a MySQL database on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The company needs to improve availability of the database to prepare for power outages. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Protect the database against losing a whole data center.

options.A: Add an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the EC2 instance.
options.B: Configure EC2 automatic instance recovery to move the instance to another Availability Zone.
options.C: Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS and enable Multi-AZ deployment.
options.D: Enable termination protection for the EC2 instance.

explanation: A is wrong: a load balancer in front of one instance adds no redundancy.
B is wrong: automatic recovery restarts the instance in the same Availability Zone, not another one.
C is correct: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically if power fails.
D is wrong: termination protection prevents accidental deletion, not outages.
tldr: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically.

wrong_reasons.A: a load balancer in front of one instance adds no redundancy.
wrong_reasons.B: automatic recovery restarts the instance in the same Availability Zone, not another one.
wrong_reasons.D: termination protection prevents accidental deletion, not outages.

question: A company operates a data lake in Amazon S3 that stores large datasets in multiple formats. The company has an application that retrieves and processes subsets of data from multiple objects in the data lake based on filtering criteria. For each data query, the application currently downloads the entire S3 object and performs transformations. The current process requires a large amount of transformation time. The company wants a solution that will give the application the ability to query and filter directly on S3 objects without downloading the objects. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Serverless SQL over data in S3.
keywords: query and filter directly on S3 objects without downloading the objects

options.A: Use Amazon Athena to query and filter the objects in Amazon S3.
options.B: Use Amazon EMR to process and filter the objects.
options.C: Use Amazon API Gateway to create an API to retrieve filtered results from Amazon S3.
options.D: Use Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey) to cache the objects.

explanation: A is correct: Athena runs SQL on the objects in S3 and returns only the matching data.
B is wrong: EMR clusters are heavier to run and still read the data.
C is wrong: API Gateway cannot filter inside S3 objects.
D is wrong: caching whole objects does not filter data inside them.
tldr: Athena queries and filters data in place in S3 with SQL.

wrong_reasons.B: EMR clusters are heavier to run and still read the data.
wrong_reasons.C: API Gateway cannot filter inside S3 objects.
wrong_reasons.D: caching whole objects does not filter data inside them.

question: A solutions architect needs to design a website for a critical application. The website needs to serve only static webpages. The solutions architect must maximize fault tolerance and high availability in the solution. Which combination of configurations will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Put the pages in S3 in two Regions, and let CloudFront fail over between them.
keywords: maximize fault tolerance and high availability

options.A: Put the static webpages on an Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume. Share the volume between two Amazon EC2 instances.
options.B: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store the static webpages. Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to an S3 bucket in another AWS Region.
options.C: Configure an Application Load Balancer in front of the Amazon EC2 instances that share the gp2 volume.
options.D: Set up an origin group for the replicated Amazon S3 buckets in Amazon CloudFront. Use the CloudFront endpoint to serve the static webpages.
options.E: Configure two Amazon EC2 instances with two elastic network interfaces to provide redundant connectivity to two subnets.

explanation: A is wrong: a gp2 volume cannot be shared between instances, and EC2 adds points of failure.
B is correct: S3 with Cross-Region Replication keeps a copy of the site in a second Region.
C is wrong: the instances would share a volume that cannot be shared, and EC2 is less available than S3.
D is correct: a CloudFront origin group fails over to the replicated bucket if the primary is unavailable.
E is wrong: extra network interfaces on two instances do not make a static site highly available.
tldr: Maximum availability for a static site: S3 with Cross-Region Replication and a CloudFront origin group for failover.

wrong_reasons.A: a gp2 volume cannot be shared between instances, and EC2 adds points of failure.
wrong_reasons.C: the instances would share a volume that cannot be shared, and EC2 is less available than S3.
wrong_reasons.E: extra network interfaces on two instances do not make a static site highly available.

question: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances spread across two Availability Zones to provide large and small maps to customers. The large maps do not change. The company updates the small maps by adding small metadata files each day. Customers download the large maps once but download the smaller maps frequently. Several Amazon EBS volumes of replicated data are spread between the Availability Zones. Which solutions will store the map data MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)
hint: Replace the replicated EBS volumes with shared storage that moves old files to a cheaper class.

options.A: Deploy an Amazon EFS file system. Mount the file system to the EC2 instances. Move the map and metadata files to the file system. Apply a storage lifecycle policy to move files older than 30 days into the EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage class.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to read data files from the S3 bucket. Apply an S3 Lifecycle configuration to move files older than 30 days into the S3 Infrequent Access (IA) storage class.
options.C: Create an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system. Move the map and metadata files to the file system. Configure the file system to use the Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
options.D: Create a shared EBS volume. Connect the EC2 instances to the shared volume. Move the map and metadata files into the new volume. Detach and delete the original EBS volumes from the EC2 instances.
options.E: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses the SCRATCH_2 deployment type. Move the map and metadata files to the file system.

explanation: A is correct: EFS is shared across Availability Zones, and a lifecycle policy moves the unchanging large maps to cheaper Infrequent Access storage.
B is correct: S3 is the cheapest shared store, and a lifecycle rule moves older maps to Infrequent Access.
C is wrong: FSx for OpenZFS has no Intelligent-Tiering storage class and costs more.
D is wrong: EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones.
E is wrong: FSx for Lustre scratch storage is temporary high-performance storage, not durable, cheap storage.
tldr: Shared storage with lifecycle tiering (EFS IA or S3 IA) is cheaper than replicated EBS volumes.

wrong_reasons.C: FSx for OpenZFS has no Intelligent-Tiering storage class and costs more.
wrong_reasons.D: EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones.
wrong_reasons.E: FSx for Lustre scratch storage is temporary high-performance storage, not durable, cheap storage.

question: A company is planning to migrate to AWS. The network layout will include more than 1,000 VPCs in a single AWS Region. The resources in the VPCs need to communicate with each other. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
hint: Which hub connects thousands of VPCs?

options.A: Create VPN tunnels from all the VPCs to each other. Enable route propagation.
options.B: Create an AWS Direct Connect gateway, and attach a public virtual interface (VIF) to each VPC. Enable route propagation.
options.C: Peer all the VPCs together by creating and accepting peering requests. Update route tables with the new routes.
options.D: Create a transit gateway, and place attachments in subnets of all the VPCs. Configure a transit gateway route table with the new routes.

explanation: A is wrong: a full mesh of VPN tunnels is impossible to manage at this scale.
B is wrong: public VIFs reach public AWS endpoints; they do not connect VPCs to each other.
C is wrong: peering over 1,000 VPCs exceeds limits and is unmanageable.
D is correct: a transit gateway attaches to every VPC and routes between them from central route tables.
tldr: Transit Gateway connects thousands of VPCs through one hub with central route tables.

wrong_reasons.A: a full mesh of VPN tunnels is impossible to manage at this scale.
wrong_reasons.B: public VIFs reach public AWS endpoints; they do not connect VPCs to each other.
wrong_reasons.C: peering over 1,000 VPCs exceeds limits and is unmanageable.

question: A company has a three-tier web application that processes orders from customers. The web tier consists of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The processing tier consists of EC2 instances. The company decoupled the web tier and processing tier by using Amazon SQS. The storage layer uses Amazon DynamoDB. At peak times, some users report order processing delays and halts. The company has noticed that during these delays, the EC2 instances are running at 100% CPU usage, and the SQS queue fills up. The peak times are variable and unpredictable. The company needs to improve the performance of the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Scale the workers on the queue's backlog, not on a schedule.

options.A: Use scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out the processing tier instances for the duration of peak usage times. Use the CPUUtilization metric to determine when to scale.
options.B: Use Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) in front of the DynamoDB backend tier. Use target utilization as a metric to determine when to scale.
options.C: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache the responses for the web tier. Use HTTP latency as a metric to determine when to scale.
options.D: Use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy to scale out the processing tier instances. Use the ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute to determine when to scale.

explanation: A is wrong: the peaks are unpredictable, so a schedule cannot follow them.
B is wrong: the bottleneck is the processing tier, not DynamoDB reads.
C is wrong: caching web responses does not speed up order processing.
D is correct: target tracking on the number of messages in the queue adds workers as the backlog grows.
tldr: Scale queue workers with target tracking on queue depth (for example ApproximateNumberOfMessages, or backlog per instance).

wrong_reasons.A: the peaks are unpredictable, so a schedule cannot follow them.
wrong_reasons.B: the bottleneck is the processing tier, not DynamoDB reads.
wrong_reasons.C: caching web responses does not speed up order processing.

question: A solutions architect is migrating an on-premises application to AWS. The application currently runs on containers. The components of the application are loosely coupled. The application consumes messages from a message queue. The solutions architect needs to design a new architecture for the application on AWS. The solutions architect wants to use fully managed AWS services for the new architecture. The new architecture must provide unlimited scalability for the message queue's throughput. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which queue has nearly unlimited throughput, and which container option has no servers?
keywords: unlimited scalability for the message queue's throughput

options.A: Use Amazon SQS to create a new message queue. Subscribe the SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances that run Kubernetes containers to consume messages from the message queue.
options.B: Use Amazon MQ to create a new message queue. Subscribe the Amazon MQ queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon EKS containers on AWS Fargate to consume messages from the message queue.
options.C: Use Amazon MQ to create a new message queue. Subscribe the Amazon MQ queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use AWS Lambda functions to poll messages from the Amazon MQ queue by using Lambda event source mappings.
options.D: Use Amazon SQS to create a new message queue. Subscribe the SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon ECS containers on AWS Fargate to consume messages from the message queue.

explanation: A is wrong: Kubernetes on EC2 Reserved Instances is not fully managed.
B is wrong: Amazon MQ runs on brokers with fixed capacity, so its throughput is not unlimited.
C is wrong: Amazon MQ brokers limit throughput.
D is correct: SQS scales throughput almost without limit, and ECS on Fargate runs the containers with no servers to manage.
tldr: SQS standard queues have nearly unlimited throughput; ECS on Fargate consumes them without servers.

wrong_reasons.A: Kubernetes on EC2 Reserved Instances is not fully managed.
wrong_reasons.B: Amazon MQ runs on brokers with fixed capacity, so its throughput is not unlimited.
wrong_reasons.C: Amazon MQ brokers limit throughput.

question: A company is building a data processing application that uses AWS Lambda functions. The application's Lambda functions need to communicate with an Amazon RDS DB instance that is deployed within a VPC in the same AWS account. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST secure way?
hint: Keep everything private, and let the database accept traffic only from the function's security group.
keywords: RDS DB instance that is deployed within a VPC

options.A: Configure the DB instance to allow public access. Update the DB instance security group to allow access from the Lambda public address space for the AWS Region.
options.B: Deploy the Lambda functions inside the VPC. Attach a network ACL to the Lambda subnet. Provide outbound rule access to the VPC CIDR range only. Update the DB instance security group to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0.
options.C: Deploy the Lambda functions inside the VPC. Attach a security group to the Lambda functions. Provide outbound rule access to the VPC CIDR range only. Update the DB instance security group to allow traffic from the Lambda security group.
options.D: Peer the Lambda default VPC with the VPC that hosts the DB instance to allow direct network access without the need for security groups.

explanation: A is wrong: making the database public exposes it to the internet.
B is wrong: a database security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 is far too permissive.
C is correct: running the functions in the VPC and allowing only their security group into the database keeps access private and tightly scoped.
D is wrong: the Lambda service VPC cannot be peered, and security groups are always needed.
tldr: VPC-attached Lambda with its own security group; the database security group allows only that group.

wrong_reasons.A: making the database public exposes it to the internet.
wrong_reasons.B: a database security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 is far too permissive.
wrong_reasons.D: the Lambda service VPC cannot be peered, and security groups are always needed.

question: A company is migrating a document management application to AWS. The application runs on Linux servers. The company will migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The company stores 7 TiB of documents in a shared storage file system. An external relational database tracks the documents. Documents are stored once and can be retrieved multiple times for reference at any time. The company cannot modify the application during the migration. The storage solution must be highly available and must support scaling over time. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Shared file storage with no app change, available across AZs, cheaper for rarely read files.
keywords: highly available and must support scaling

options.A: Deploy an EC2 instance with enhanced networking as a shared NFS storage system. Export the NFS share. Mount the NFS share on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Mount the S3 bucket on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.
options.C: Deploy an SFTP server endpoint by using AWS Transfer for SFTP and an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group to connect to the SFTP server.
options.D: Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount points in multiple Availability Zones. Use the EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) storage class. Mount the NFS share on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.

explanation: A is wrong: a single NFS server is a single point of failure and must be managed.
B is wrong: S3 is not a native file system, so the application would need changes.
C is wrong: SFTP means changing how the application reads files.
D is correct: EFS with mount targets in several Availability Zones is highly available and elastic, and Standard-IA cuts cost for documents read only occasionally.
tldr: EFS across AZs with the Infrequent Access class gives cheap, shared, highly available NFS storage.

wrong_reasons.A: a single NFS server is a single point of failure and must be managed.
wrong_reasons.B: S3 is not a native file system, so the application would need changes.
wrong_reasons.C: SFTP means changing how the application reads files.

question: A company is developing software that uses a PostgreSQL database schema. The company needs to configure development environments and test environments for its developers. Each developer at the company uses their own development environment, which includes a PostgreSQL database. On average, each development environment is used for an 8-hour workday. The test environments will be used for load testing that can take up to 2 hours each day. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Each database is busy only part of the day. Which option scales down when idle?

options.A: Configure development environments and test environments with their own Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 PostgreSQL database.
options.B: For each development environment, configure an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instance. For the test environment, configure a single Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance.
options.C: Configure development environments and test environments with their own Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
options.D: Configure an Amazon Aurora global database. Allow developers to connect to the database with their own credentials.

explanation: A is correct: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity down when environments are idle, so the company pays mainly for the hours they are used.
B is wrong: provisioned instances bill around the clock even when unused.
C is wrong: provisioned Aurora clusters bill for capacity around the clock.
D is wrong: a global database is for multi-Region needs and costs more.
tldr: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with use, so part-time dev and test databases cost less.

wrong_reasons.B: provisioned instances bill around the clock even when unused.
wrong_reasons.C: provisioned Aurora clusters bill for capacity around the clock.
wrong_reasons.D: a global database is for multi-Region needs and costs more.

question: A company operates an online photo-sharing service and stores data in AWS Account A in a centralized Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to grant a second AWS account named Account B access to the centralized S3 bucket. The company owns Account B. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Cross-account access to a bucket is granted by a resource policy on the bucket.
keywords: second AWS account named Account B

options.A: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to provide Account B access to the centralized S3 bucket in Account A.
options.B: Enable cross-Region replication between Account A and Account B to share the S3 bucket data.
options.C: Use Amazon CloudFront to distribute the S3 bucket contents. Grant Account B access the bucket contents through a signed URL.
options.D: Create a bucket policy that grants Account B permission to access the centralized S3 bucket in Account A.

explanation: A is wrong: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers; it does not grant access.
B is wrong: replication copies data; it does not share the original bucket.
C is wrong: signed URLs are for viewers of content, not account-level access.
D is correct: a bucket policy that grants Account B the needed actions gives it access, delegated to its own users and roles.
tldr: Grant another account access to a bucket with a bucket policy that names that account.

wrong_reasons.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers; it does not grant access.
wrong_reasons.B: replication copies data; it does not share the original bucket.
wrong_reasons.C: signed URLs are for viewers of content, not account-level access.

question: A company hosts an industrial control application that receives sensor input through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The application needs to support new sensors for real-time anomaly detection in monitored equipment. The company wants to integrate new sensors in a loosely-coupled, fully managed, and serverless way. The company cannot modify the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Process the existing stream in real time with a serverless service, and hand results back through another stream.

options.A: Forward the existing stream in Kinesis Data Streams to Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink for anomaly detection. Use a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send the Flink output to the application.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Firehose to stream data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to perform anomaly detection on the S3 data. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function that sends analyzed data to the application through a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams.
options.C: Configure Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to consume data from the data stream and to perform anomaly detection. Create a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send data from the EC2 instances to the application.
options.D: Configure an Amazon ECS task that uses Amazon EC2 instances to consume data from the data stream and to perform anomaly detection. Create a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send data from the containers to the application.

explanation: A is correct: Flink reads the existing stream and detects anomalies in real time without servers, and a second stream returns the results to the unchanged application.
B is wrong: Firehose to S3 with Redshift Spectrum is batch analysis, not real time.
C is wrong: EC2 instances are not serverless.
D is wrong: ECS on EC2 instances is not serverless.
tldr: Real-time stream analytics without servers: Managed Service for Apache Flink reads from and writes to Kinesis streams.

wrong_reasons.B: Firehose to S3 with Redshift Spectrum is batch analysis, not real time.
wrong_reasons.C: EC2 instances are not serverless.
wrong_reasons.D: ECS on EC2 instances is not serverless.

question: A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application uses hardcoded credentials to access an Amazon RDS database. To comply with new regulations, the company needs to automatically rotate the database password for the application service account every 90 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which service stores database credentials and rotates them on a schedule?

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function to generate new randomized passwords. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the Lambda function every 90 days. Configure the Lambda function to upload a JSON file that contains the new password to the existing EC2 instances by using SSH.
options.B: Create a secret for the database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Schedule an AWS Lambda function in Secrets Manager to rotate the secret every 90 days. Modify the application to read the database credentials from Secrets Manager.
options.C: Create a new Amazon ECS task to generate new randomized passwords. Configure the task to launch every 90 days. Configure the task to upload a JSON file that contains the new password to the existing EC2 instances by using SSH.
options.D: Create a new EC2 instance that runs a cron job every 90 days. Use the cron job to generate new randomized passwords. Configure the new EC2 instance to upload a JSON file that contains the new password to the existing EC2 instances by using SSH.

explanation: A is wrong: pushing password files over SSH is custom, insecure and error-prone.
B is correct: Secrets Manager stores the credentials and rotates them every 90 days, and the application reads the current value.
C is wrong: an ECS task that pushes files over SSH is custom and insecure.
D is wrong: a cron server that pushes files over SSH is custom and insecure.
tldr: Store database credentials in Secrets Manager with scheduled rotation and have the app read them at runtime.

wrong_reasons.A: pushing password files over SSH is custom, insecure and error-prone.
wrong_reasons.C: an ECS task that pushes files over SSH is custom and insecure.
wrong_reasons.D: a cron server that pushes files over SSH is custom and insecure.

question: A company recently migrated a data warehouse to AWS. The company has an AWS Direct Connect connection to AWS. Company users query the data warehouse by using a visualization tool. The average size of the queries that the data warehouse returns is 50 MB. The average visualization that the visualization tool produces is 500 KB in size. The result sets that the data warehouse returns are not cached. The company wants to optimize costs for data transfers between the data warehouse and the company. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Keep the large results inside AWS; send only the small visualizations out, over the cheaper path.

options.A: Host the visualization tool on premises. Connect to the data warehouse directly through the internet.
options.B: Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse. Access the visualization tool through the internet.
options.C: Host the visualization tool on premises. Connect to the data warehouse through the Direct Connect connection.
options.D: Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse. Access the visualization tool through the Direct Connect connection.

explanation: A is wrong: sending 50 MB results over the internet has the highest data transfer out cost.
B is wrong: internet transfer out costs more per GB than Direct Connect.
C is wrong: the 50 MB query results would still leave AWS for every query.
D is correct: with the tool next to the warehouse, only 500 KB visualizations leave AWS, over Direct Connect's lower transfer rates.
tldr: Keep heavy query results inside the Region and send only small results out over Direct Connect, which has lower transfer-out rates.

wrong_reasons.A: sending 50 MB results over the internet has the highest data transfer out cost.
wrong_reasons.B: internet transfer out costs more per GB than Direct Connect.
wrong_reasons.C: the 50 MB query results would still leave AWS for every query.

question: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website serves static content. Website traffic is increasing. The company wants to minimize the website hosting costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Static content needs no servers.

options.A: Move the website to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket.
options.B: Move the website to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon ElastiCache cluster for the S3 bucket.
options.C: Move the website to AWS Amplify. Configure an ALB to resolve to the Amplify website.
options.D: Move the website to AWS Amplify. Configure EC2 instances to cache the website.

explanation: A is correct: S3 hosts static content with no servers, and CloudFront caches it at the edge.
B is wrong: ElastiCache cannot front an S3 bucket for a website.
C is wrong: an ALB cannot resolve to an Amplify website, and it adds cost.
D is wrong: EC2 caching servers add cost.
tldr: Static sites are cheapest on S3 behind CloudFront, with no servers to run.

wrong_reasons.B: ElastiCache cannot front an S3 bucket for a website.
wrong_reasons.C: an ALB cannot resolve to an Amplify website, and it adds cost.
wrong_reasons.D: EC2 caching servers add cost.

question: A company is running a two-tier web-based application in an on-premises data center. The application layer consists of a single server running a stateful application. The application connects to a PostgreSQL database running on a separate server. The application's user base is expected to grow significantly, so the company is migrating the application and database to AWS. The solution will use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, and Elastic Load Balancing. Which solution will provide a consistent user experience that will allow the application and database tiers to scale?
hint: Aurora scales reads with replicas (writers do not auto scale). A stateful web app needs sticky sessions on a layer 7 load balancer.

options.A: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.B: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora writers. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.C: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.D: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora writers. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.

explanation: A is wrong: NLBs do not have a least outstanding requests algorithm.
B is wrong: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas, not writers.
C is correct: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas for reads, and an ALB with sticky sessions keeps each user on the same stateful instance.
D is wrong: Aurora does not auto scale writers, and NLBs lack that routing algorithm.
tldr: Scale Aurora reads with replica auto scaling, and keep stateful users on one instance with ALB sticky sessions.

wrong_reasons.A: NLBs do not have a least outstanding requests algorithm.
wrong_reasons.B: Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas, not writers.
wrong_reasons.D: Aurora does not auto scale writers, and NLBs lack that routing algorithm.

question: A research laboratory needs to process a multi-terabyte dataset multiple times each day. The laboratory requires sub-millisecond latency while processing the data. Hundreds of Amazon EC2 Linux instances will process the data from the source and store the data in a different location. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Parallel, sub-millisecond file access for hundreds of Linux instances, linked to S3.
keywords: Hundreds of Amazon EC2 Linux instances

options.A: Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. Set each volume's tiering policy to All. Import the raw data into the file system. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent SSD storage. Configure the FSx for Lustre file system to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent HDD storage. Configure the FSx for Lustre file system to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Access the file system by using a Gateway Load Balancer.
options.D: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with HDD storage. Enable shadow copies. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances by using SMB protocol.

explanation: A is wrong: a tiering policy of All puts data in the capacity pool, which has higher latency.
B is correct: FSx for Lustre on persistent SSD gives sub-millisecond parallel access and imports and exports data to S3.
C is wrong: HDD storage does not give sub-millisecond latency, and clients do not connect through a Gateway Load Balancer.
D is wrong: FSx for Windows on HDD over SMB is not built for Linux HPC and is slower.
tldr: FSx for Lustre on SSD, linked to S3 for import and export, gives sub-millisecond parallel access for HPC.

wrong_reasons.A: a tiering policy of All puts data in the capacity pool, which has higher latency.
wrong_reasons.C: HDD storage does not give sub-millisecond latency, and clients do not connect through a Gateway Load Balancer.
wrong_reasons.D: FSx for Windows on HDD over SMB is not built for Linux HPC and is slower.

question: A company manages an application that stores data on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. High traffic on the application is causing increased latency for many read queries. A solutions architect must improve the performance of the application. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Add capacity for reads specifically.
keywords: increased latency for many read queries

options.A: Enable Amazon RDS Performance Insights. Configure storage capacity to scale automatically.
options.B: Configure the DB instance to use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options.C: Create a read replica of the DB instance. Serve read traffic from the read replica.
options.D: Use Amazon Data Firehose between the application and Amazon RDS to increase the concurrency of database requests.

explanation: A is wrong: Performance Insights diagnoses problems, and storage scaling does not help reads.
B is wrong: DAX works only with DynamoDB.
C is correct: a read replica serves read traffic and takes the load off the primary.
D is wrong: Firehose delivers streaming data; it does not sit between an application and a database.
tldr: Serve read-heavy traffic from RDS read replicas; the Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads.

wrong_reasons.A: Performance Insights diagnoses problems, and storage scaling does not help reads.
wrong_reasons.B: DAX works only with DynamoDB.
wrong_reasons.D: Firehose delivers streaming data; it does not sit between an application and a database.

question: A company is designing the network for an online multi-player game. The game uses the UDP networking protocol and will be deployed in eight AWS Regions. The network architecture needs to minimize latency and packet loss to give end users a high-quality gaming experience. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which edge service supports UDP and routes players over the AWS backbone to the nearest Region?

options.A: Set up a transit gateway in each Region. Create inter-Region peering attachments between each transit gateway.
options.B: Set up AWS Global Accelerator with UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region.
options.C: Set up Amazon CloudFront with UDP turned on. Configure an origin in each Region.
options.D: Set up a VPC peering mesh between each Region. Turn on UDP for each VPC.

explanation: A is wrong: transit gateway peering connects VPCs; it does not bring players onto the AWS network.
B is correct: Global Accelerator has UDP listeners and routes each player through the nearest edge location to the closest Region, cutting latency and packet loss.
C is wrong: CloudFront does not support UDP.
D is wrong: VPC peering is for VPC-to-VPC traffic and has no UDP setting.
tldr: Global Accelerator supports UDP and routes users to the nearest healthy Region over the AWS network.

wrong_reasons.A: transit gateway peering connects VPCs; it does not bring players onto the AWS network.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudFront does not support UDP.
wrong_reasons.D: VPC peering is for VPC-to-VPC traffic and has no UDP setting.

question: An e-commerce company hosts a three-tier web application in a VPC. The web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The company stores a product catalog and customer sales information in Amazon DynamoDB. The company's finance team uses a reporting application to generate reports of daily product sales. When the finance team runs the daily reports, a sudden performance decrease affects website customers. The company wants to improve the performance of the system. Which solution will meet these requirements with MINIMAL changes to the current architecture?
hint: Take the heavy reads off DynamoDB without changing the database.

options.A: Migrate the application to larger EC2 Instances. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure a read replica of the database in a second Availability Zone.
options.B: Increase the compute capacity of the EC2 instances. Migrate the database to Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached).
options.C: Implement DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options.D: Configure DynamoDB streams.

explanation: A is wrong: migrating to RDS is a major change.
B is wrong: replacing the database with Memcached loses durability and is a major change.
C is correct: DAX caches DynamoDB reads in memory, so the report queries no longer slow the website, with only a client change.
D is wrong: Streams capture changes; they do not speed up reads.
tldr: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that absorbs heavy reads with minimal code changes.

wrong_reasons.A: migrating to RDS is a major change.
wrong_reasons.B: replacing the database with Memcached loses durability and is a major change.
wrong_reasons.D: Streams capture changes; they do not speed up reads.

question: A company has deployed its infrastructure in a single VPC spanning three Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone contains private subnets for workloads that require outbound internet access to download updates and communicate with external APIs. Currently, a single NAT gateway is deployed in one Availability Zone. All private subnets in the VPC have route table entries that point to this NAT gateway for internet access. The company wants to increase the fault tolerance of the company's connectivity solution without permitting inbound traffic. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Remove the single NAT gateway as a point of failure.
keywords: single NAT gateway is deployed in one Availability Zone

options.A: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone. Update the route table of each private subnet to use the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone.
options.B: Create a public subnet in each Availability Zone. Move the workloads from private subnets to public subnets.
options.C: Move all instances to public subnets. Assign public IP addresses to the instances. Route traffic directly through the internet gateway that is associated with the VPC.
options.D: Use AWS Global Accelerator to route outbound traffic through AWS managed endpoints in other AWS Regions.

explanation: A is correct: a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, used by that zone's subnets, keeps outbound access working if one zone fails.
B is wrong: moving workloads to public subnets exposes them to inbound traffic.
C is wrong: public IP addresses allow inbound traffic.
D is wrong: Global Accelerator is for inbound traffic from users, not outbound internet access.
tldr: Put a NAT gateway in each AZ and route each AZ's private subnets to their local one.

wrong_reasons.B: moving workloads to public subnets exposes them to inbound traffic.
wrong_reasons.C: public IP addresses allow inbound traffic.
wrong_reasons.D: Global Accelerator is for inbound traffic from users, not outbound internet access.

question: A company needs to run its external website on Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtualized servers. The AWS environment has a 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection to the data center. The application has IP addresses that will not change. The on-premises and AWS servers are able to restart themselves while maintaining the same IP address if a failure occurs. Some website users have to add their vendors to an allow list, so the solution must have a fixed IP address. The company needs a solution with the lowest operational overhead to handle this split traffic. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
hint: Which load balancer gives static IP addresses and can target on-premises IPs over Direct Connect?

options.A: Deploy an Amazon Route 53 Resolver with rules pointing to the on-premises and AWS IP addresses.
options.B: Deploy a Network Load Balancer on AWS. Create target groups for the on-premises and AWS IP addresses.
options.C: Deploy an Application Load Balancer on AWS. Register the on-premises and AWS IP addresses with the target group.
options.D: Deploy Amazon API Gateway to direct traffic to the on-premises and AWS IP addresses based on the header of the request.

explanation: A is wrong: Route 53 Resolver rules forward DNS queries; they do not spread website traffic.
B is correct: an NLB provides fixed IP addresses for allow lists, and IP target groups can include both on-premises and AWS servers.
C is wrong: an ALB's IP addresses change, so it cannot be allow-listed by fixed IP.
D is wrong: API Gateway does not give fixed IP addresses or balance traffic to servers.
tldr: An NLB has static IPs per AZ and can target on-premises servers by IP address over Direct Connect.

wrong_reasons.A: Route 53 Resolver rules forward DNS queries; they do not spread website traffic.
wrong_reasons.C: an ALB's IP addresses change, so it cannot be allow-listed by fixed IP.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway does not give fixed IP addresses or balance traffic to servers.

question: A company needs a durable storage solution for telemetry data. The company wants to encrypt the data by using keys that the company manages. The storage solution must rotate the encryption keys every 90 days. The company will access the telemetry data infrequently for the first 30 days. The storage solution must expire the data after 360 days. Which solutions will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)
hint: One option is the storage with lifecycle rules; the other is a key the company controls that KMS can rotate on a 90-day schedule.
keywords: rotate the encryption keys every 90 days

options.A: Store telemetry data in an Amazon S3 bucket by using the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class after 30 days and expire objects after 360 days.
options.B: Create an AWS KMS customer managed key. Enable automatic key rotation with a rotation period of 90 days. Update the key policy to grant the chosen storage service permission to use the key.
options.C: Store the telemetry data in an Amazon S3 bucket in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to expire objects that are older than 360 days.
options.D: Use the Amazon EFS General Purpose performance mode to store telemetry data in a file system. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule an AWS Lambda function to scan the file system and delete files that are older than 360 days.
options.E: Set up a company-defined encryption key in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the key to rotate every 90 days. Grant Secrets Manager permissions to access the storage service.

explanation: A is correct: Standard-IA suits infrequent access in the first 30 days, Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheaper after that, and the lifecycle rule expires objects at 360 days.

B is correct: a customer managed KMS key is a key the company manages, automatic rotation can be set to every 90 days (KMS supports rotation periods from 90 to 2,560 days), and the key policy grants the storage service permission to use it.
C is wrong: Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object, and the access pattern is already known.
D is wrong: EFS costs more, and deleting files with a custom Lambda function is extra work.
E is wrong: Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords; it is not an encryption key service that storage services can use.
tldr: Infrequently read data with a fixed expiry: Standard-IA to Glacier with lifecycle expiration; encrypt with a customer managed KMS key set to rotate automatically every 90 days.

wrong_reasons.C: Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object, and the access pattern is already known.
wrong_reasons.D: EFS costs more, and deleting files with a custom Lambda function is extra work.
wrong_reasons.E: Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords; it is not an encryption key service that storage services can use.

question: A financial services company must keep log data for 1 year. The company stores log files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to prevent any user from deleting or overwriting the log files for 1 year. The data must be available for read-only requests. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: No one, including administrators, may delete or overwrite. Which Object Lock mode guarantees that?
keywords: prevent any user from deleting or overwriting the log files for 1 year

options.A: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket. Use Object Lock in compliance mode with a 1-year retention period.
options.B: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. Create an S3 Lifecycle Configuration rule to move objects to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year.
options.C: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket. Create an S3 Lifecycle Configuration rule to move objects to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 year.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function to programmatically check the timestamp of S3 data and to move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive if the data is older than 1 year.

explanation: A is correct: Object Lock in compliance mode with 1-year retention stops anyone from deleting or overwriting the logs, and reads still work.
B is wrong: Transfer Acceleration and lifecycle transitions do not prevent deletion.
C is wrong: versioning keeps old versions but users can still delete them.
D is wrong: moving data with a custom function does not stop deletion.
tldr: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode (with versioning) blocks deletes and overwrites by anyone for the retention period.

wrong_reasons.B: Transfer Acceleration and lifecycle transitions do not prevent deletion.
wrong_reasons.C: versioning keeps old versions but users can still delete them.
wrong_reasons.D: moving data with a custom function does not stop deletion.

question: A company needs to design a resilient web application to process customer orders. The web application must automatically handle increases in web traffic and application usage without affecting the customer experience or losing customer orders. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Load balancer, scaling workers, a durable queue for pending orders, and a highly available database.
keywords: automatically handle increases in web traffic

options.A: Use a NAT gateway to manage web traffic. Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups to receive, process, and store processed customer orders. Use an AWS Lambda function to capture and store unprocessed orders.
options.B: Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to manage web traffic. Use an Application Load Balancer to receive customer orders from the NLB. Use Amazon Redshift with a Multi-AZ deployment to store unprocessed and processed customer orders.
options.C: Use a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) to manage web traffic. Use Amazon ECS to receive and process customer orders. Use the GWLB to capture and store unprocessed orders. Use Amazon DynamoDB to store processed customer orders.
options.D: Use an Application Load Balancer to manage web traffic. Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups to receive and process customer orders. Use Amazon SQS to store unprocessed orders. Use Amazon RDS with a Multi-AZ deployment to store processed customer orders.

explanation: A is wrong: a NAT gateway does not manage incoming web traffic, and Lambda is not a place to store orders.
B is wrong: Redshift is a data warehouse, not an order store, and chaining NLB to ALB adds nothing.
C is wrong: a Gateway Load Balancer is for network appliances and cannot store orders.
D is correct: the ALB spreads traffic, Auto Scaling handles load, SQS holds unprocessed orders so none are lost, and RDS Multi-AZ stores processed orders.
tldr: ALB + Auto Scaling for the web tier, SQS to hold unprocessed orders, RDS Multi-AZ for processed ones.

wrong_reasons.A: a NAT gateway does not manage incoming web traffic, and Lambda is not a place to store orders.
wrong_reasons.B: Redshift is a data warehouse, not an order store, and chaining NLB to ALB adds nothing.
wrong_reasons.C: a Gateway Load Balancer is for network appliances and cannot store orders.

question: A company wants to receive an email notification when IAM users are added to or deleted from an AWS account. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: User creation and deletion are API calls, recorded by CloudTrail and matchable in EventBridge.
keywords: added to or deleted from an AWS account

options.A: Enable Amazon Inspector. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to Amazon Inspector findings. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company's email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.B: Enable Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to GuardDuty findings. Configure an event pattern of Impact IAMUser/Anomalous Behavior. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company's email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.C: Enable Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to Macie findings. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company's email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.D: Enable management events in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to AWS API calls through CloudTrail. Configure an event pattern for CreateUser and DeleteUser actions. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company's email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.

explanation: A is wrong: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities, not IAM changes.
B is wrong: GuardDuty flags suspicious behavior, not every user creation or deletion.
C is wrong: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.
D is correct: CloudTrail records the CreateUser and DeleteUser calls, and an EventBridge rule matching them sends an email through SNS.
tldr: Alert on specific API calls with an EventBridge rule on CloudTrail events, targeting SNS for email.

wrong_reasons.A: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities, not IAM changes.
wrong_reasons.B: GuardDuty flags suspicious behavior, not every user creation or deletion.
wrong_reasons.C: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

question: A company hosts a PostgreSQL database on an Amazon EC2 instance. Database usage has increased recently. Users are experiencing higher latency during queries on the database. The company needs to update the database to reduce latency for users. The new solution must achieve a recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO) of less than 5 minutes. The company also wants to deploy the database to multiple AWS Regions to meet new availability requirements. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Managed, faster PostgreSQL that spans Regions and fails over within minutes.
keywords: recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO) of less than 5 minutes

options.A: Use AWS Backup to automatically create backups of the EC2 instance. In the event of a database failure, use the backups to restore the EC2 instance to a second Region.
options.B: Use AWS DMS to migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. Configure the Aurora database as a global database. Set the Aurora parameter group RPO setting to 60 seconds. In the event of a database failure, promote a secondary database in a second Region automatically.
options.C: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery service to replicate the EC2 instance to a second Region. In the event of a database failure, use the Elastic Disaster Recovery dashboard to perform a failover.
options.D: Use AWS DMS to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Create cross-Region read replicas in the Regions where most users are located. In the event of a database failure, manually promote a read replica to become the primary database.

explanation: A is wrong: restoring from backups takes far longer than 5 minutes and loses recent data.
B is correct: Aurora improves performance, and a global database replicates across Regions with an RPO setting and fast promotion of a secondary Region.
C is wrong: Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers, but it does not improve query performance or spread the database across Regions.
D is wrong: manually promoting a read replica makes it hard to meet a 5-minute RTO.
tldr: Aurora PostgreSQL Global Database gives multi-Region reads, managed RPO control and fast cross-Region failover.

wrong_reasons.A: restoring from backups takes far longer than 5 minutes and loses recent data.
wrong_reasons.C: Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers, but it does not improve query performance or spread the database across Regions.
wrong_reasons.D: manually promoting a read replica makes it hard to meet a 5-minute RTO.

question: A home security company is expanding its business globally. The company needs to encrypt customer data. The company does not want to manage its own keys. The company needs the keys to be usable in multiple AWS Regions and needs to control access to the keys. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: AWS-managed key material that works interchangeably in several Regions.
keywords: does not want to manage its own keys

options.A: Use AWS KMS to create multi-Region keys. Apply tags to identify each key. Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) condition keys to control access to the keys.
options.B: Use AWS KMS to create multiple keys by importing key material. Apply tags to identify each key. Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) condition keys to control access to the keys.
options.C: Use AWS CloudHSM to create a CloudHSM cluster in the company's primary Region. Synchronize the CloudHSM cluster to additional Regions by using the CloudHSM Management Utility (CMU).
options.D: Use AWS CloudHSM to create users. Use the CloudHSM Management Utility (CMU) to share keys with the users. Use the shareKey command to share or unshare the key with additional users in each Region.

explanation: A is correct: multi-Region KMS keys work in every Region with AWS-managed key material, and tag-based conditions control access.
B is wrong: imported key material means managing the keys yourself.
C is wrong: CloudHSM clusters are keys the company must manage.
D is wrong: CloudHSM key sharing across Regions is manual and complex.
tldr: KMS multi-Region keys share key material across Regions; tags plus ABAC control access.

wrong_reasons.B: imported key material means managing the keys yourself.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudHSM clusters are keys the company must manage.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudHSM key sharing across Regions is manual and complex.

question: A company uses Amazon S3 to store customer data that contains personally identifiable information (PII) attributes. The company needs to make the customer information available to company resources through an AWS Glue Catalog. The company needs to have fine-grained access control for the data so that only specific IAM roles can access the PII data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
hint: Column-level control over catalog tables, enforced for every service.

options.A: Create one IAM policy that grants access to PII. Create a second IAM policy that grants access to non-PII data. Assign the PII policy to the specified IAM roles.
options.B: Create one IAM role that grants access to PII. Create a second IAM role that grants access to non-PII data. Assign the PII policy to the specified IAM roles.
options.C: Use AWS Lake Formation to provide the specified IAM roles access to the PII data.
options.D: Use AWS Glue to create one view for PII data. Create a second view for non-PII data. Provide the specified IAM roles access to the PII view.

explanation: A is wrong: IAM policies cannot restrict access to individual columns in a table.
B is wrong: IAM roles cannot restrict access to individual columns either.
C is correct: Lake Formation grants the chosen roles access to the PII columns and hides them from everyone else.
D is wrong: separate views must be built and kept in sync.
tldr: Lake Formation grants fine-grained (column/row) access to Glue Catalog tables for specific roles.

wrong_reasons.A: IAM policies cannot restrict access to individual columns in a table.
wrong_reasons.B: IAM roles cannot restrict access to individual columns either.
wrong_reasons.D: separate views must be built and kept in sync.

question: A company runs an application as a task in an Amazon ECS cluster. The application must have read and write access to a specific group of Amazon S3 buckets. The S3 buckets are in the same AWS Region and AWS account as the ECS cluster. The company needs to grant the application access to the S3 buckets according to the principle of least privilege. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: List exactly the buckets, and give the permissions to the task itself, not the host.
keywords: specific group of Amazon S3 buckets

options.A: Add a tag to each bucket. Create an IAM policy that includes a StringEquals condition that matches the tags and values of the buckets.
options.B: Create an IAM policy that lists the full Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for each S3 bucket.
options.C: Attach the IAM policy to the instance role of the ECS task.
options.D: Create an IAM policy that includes a wildcard Amazon Resource Name (ARN) that matches all combinations of the S3 bucket names.
options.E: Attach the IAM policy to the task role of the ECS task.

explanation: A is wrong: tag conditions work for some actions, but not all S3 actions support bucket tag conditions, so listing ARNs is clearer.
B is correct: listing the exact ARN of each bucket grants access only to those buckets.
C is wrong: the instance role is shared by every task on the instance.
D is wrong: a wildcard can match buckets that should not be included.
E is correct: the task role gives only this application's containers the permissions.
tldr: Least privilege for ECS tasks: a policy listing exact bucket ARNs, attached to the task role.

wrong_reasons.A: tag conditions work for some actions, but not all S3 actions support bucket tag conditions, so listing ARNs is clearer.
wrong_reasons.C: the instance role is shared by every task on the instance.
wrong_reasons.D: a wildcard can match buckets that should not be included.

question: A company has an online delivery system that runs on Amazon EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. The RDS for MySQL instance stores 10 GB of delivery and transaction data. The company wants to implement a database disaster recovery (DR) strategy that achieves a recovery time objective (RTO) of less than 3 hours. The company also wants the database DR strategy to achieve a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Worst-case data loss is set by how often transaction logs are copied. Restoring must fit in 3 hours.
keywords: recovery time objective (RTO) of less than 3 hours

options.A: Schedule a database backup to Amazon S3 Glacier every 15 minutes. Copy the transaction logs to an Amazon S3 bucket every 5 minutes.
options.B: Schedule a database backup to Amazon S3 every hour. Copy the transaction logs to an S3 bucket every 5 minutes.
options.C: Set up asynchronous replication in the database by using a Multi-AZ deployment configuration. Copy the transaction logs to an Amazon S3 bucket every 20 minutes.
options.D: Schedule a database backup to AWS Storage Gateway every hour. Copy the transaction logs to an Amazon S3 bucket every 20 minutes.

explanation: A is wrong: restoring from Glacier can be slow, and backups every 15 minutes are unnecessary with frequent logs.
B is correct: hourly backups in S3 plus transaction logs every 5 minutes keep data loss under 15 minutes, and a 10 GB restore finishes well within 3 hours.
C is wrong: Multi-AZ replication is synchronous, and logs every 20 minutes miss the 15-minute RPO.
D is wrong: logs every 20 minutes miss the 15-minute RPO.
tldr: RPO depends on log shipping frequency: hourly backups plus 5-minute logs give at most about 5 minutes of loss.

wrong_reasons.A: restoring from Glacier can be slow, and backups every 15 minutes are unnecessary with frequent logs.
wrong_reasons.C: Multi-AZ replication is synchronous, and logs every 20 minutes miss the 15-minute RPO.
wrong_reasons.D: logs every 20 minutes miss the 15-minute RPO.

question: A company wants to migrate an application that processes logs to AWS. Currently, the application runs on an on-premises storage area network (SAN). The application reads and processes large log files sequentially. The application requires throughput of up to 500 MBps. A solutions architect needs to migrate the application with minimal change to the application architecture. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
hint: Large sequential reads at 500 MB/s: which cheaper HDD type reaches that throughput?

options.A: Use a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume with 500 MBps provisioned throughput.
options.B: Use a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) Amazon EBS volume with provisioned storage based on the throughput requirement.
options.C: Use a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume with provisioned storage based on the throughput requirement.
options.D: Use a Provisioned IOPS (io1) Amazon EBS volume with 500 MBps Provisioned throughput.

explanation: A is wrong: gp3 can reach this throughput but costs more per GB than st1.
B is correct: st1 reaches up to 500 MiB/s on large sequential reads at a low price, with throughput set by volume size.
C is wrong: sc1 tops out at 250 MiB/s.
D is wrong: io1 is priced for IOPS the workload does not need.
tldr: st1 delivers up to 500 MiB/s for large sequential workloads at a much lower cost than SSD.

wrong_reasons.A: gp3 can reach this throughput but costs more per GB than st1.
wrong_reasons.C: sc1 tops out at 250 MiB/s.
wrong_reasons.D: io1 is priced for IOPS the workload does not need.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. For compliance reasons, the EC2 instances cannot be accessible from the internet. The EC2 instances must run within private subnets that use a shared route table. The VPC contains a single NAT gateway for internet connectivity. The company wants to improve the reliability of the connectivity to an AWS Systems Manager service. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
hint: Reach Systems Manager privately in every AZ without depending on the NAT gateway. Which endpoints does the SSM Agent need?
keywords: improve the reliability of the connectivity to an AWS Systems Manager service

options.A: Deploy an additional NAT gateway in each Availability Zone. Update the shared route table with the new NAT gateway addresses.
options.B: Take an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the existing EC2 instances. Relaunch the instances into public subnets. Enable VPC Block Public Access.
options.C: Create interface VPC endpoints for Systems Manager (ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages). Specify a subnet in each Availability Zone.
options.D: Create an AWS Transit Gateway and a centralized outbound VPC to access the Systems Manager service.

explanation: A is wrong: a shared route table can point to only one NAT gateway, so per-AZ gateways would need separate route tables.
B is wrong: instances in public subnets break the requirement that they not be reachable from the internet.
C is correct: interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages in each Availability Zone let the instances reach Systems Manager privately without depending on the single NAT gateway.
D is wrong: a transit gateway and central egress VPC is far more work.
tldr: Systems Manager needs interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages; placing them in each AZ removes the dependence on a single NAT gateway.

wrong_reasons.A: a shared route table can point to only one NAT gateway, so per-AZ gateways would need separate route tables.
wrong_reasons.B: instances in public subnets break the requirement that they not be reachable from the internet.
wrong_reasons.D: a transit gateway and central egress VPC is far more work.

question: A company allows users to upload and store photos through its website. The website has users from all around the world. All images that users upload are stored in a centralized Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to increase the speed in which its entire user base can upload photos through the website. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?
hint: Faster long-distance uploads straight into S3, and the special endpoint that uses it.
keywords: users from all around the world

options.A: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class to store files.
options.B: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the distribution settings and origin.
options.C: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket. Use the standard S3 endpoint to upload files.
options.D: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket. Use the S3 Accelerate endpoint to upload files.
