explanation: A is wrong: CloudFront mainly speeds downloads, and a storage class does not change upload speed.
B is wrong: CloudFront is mainly for downloads; Transfer Acceleration is designed for uploads into S3.
C is wrong: Transfer Acceleration works only through the accelerate endpoint, not the standard one.
D is correct: Transfer Acceleration sends uploads through the nearest edge location, and clients use the accelerate endpoint to get the benefit.
tldr: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads from distant users; clients must use the accelerate endpoint.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudFront mainly speeds downloads, and a storage class does not change upload speed.
wrong_reasons.B: CloudFront is mainly for downloads; Transfer Acceleration is designed for uploads into S3.
wrong_reasons.C: Transfer Acceleration works only through the accelerate endpoint, not the standard one.

question: A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics application is highly resilient and is designed to run in stateless mode. The company notices that the application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: A stateless app that tolerates interruption can scale on the cheapest capacity.
keywords: highly resilient and is designed to run in stateless mode

options.A: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
options.B: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization is more than 75%.
options.D: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group that includes the launch template. Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.

explanation: A is wrong: two fixed instances do not scale.
B is wrong: DNS weighting does not scale and does not react to instance health quickly.
C is wrong: resizing a single instance needs downtime and has limits.
D is correct: an Auto Scaling group using Spot capacity behind an ALB scales with demand at the lowest cost, and the stateless app tolerates interruptions.
tldr: Stateless, interruption-tolerant apps scale cheaply with an Auto Scaling group of Spot capacity behind an ALB.

wrong_reasons.A: two fixed instances do not scale.
wrong_reasons.B: DNS weighting does not scale and does not react to instance health quickly.
wrong_reasons.C: resizing a single instance needs downtime and has limits.

question: A company runs a critical data analysis job each week before the first day of the work week. The job requires at least 1 hour to complete the analysis. The job is stateful and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company needs a solution to run the job on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: More than 15 minutes rules out Lambda, and no interruptions rules out Spot.

options.A: Create a container for the job. Schedule the job to run as an AWS Fargate task on an Amazon ECS cluster by using Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
options.B: Configure the job to run in an AWS Lambda function. Create a scheduled rule in Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function.
options.C: Configure an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that run Amazon Linux. Configure a crontab entry on the instances to run the analysis.
options.D: Configure an AWS DataSync task to run the job. Configure a cron expression to run the task on a schedule.

explanation: A is correct: a Fargate task started on a schedule runs as long as needed with no servers and no Spot interruptions.
B is wrong: Lambda stops after 15 minutes.
C is wrong: Spot Instances can be interrupted.
D is wrong: DataSync transfers data; it does not run analysis jobs.
tldr: Scheduled long-running, uninterruptible jobs: a container on ECS Fargate started by EventBridge Scheduler.

wrong_reasons.B: Lambda stops after 15 minutes.
wrong_reasons.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted.
wrong_reasons.D: DataSync transfers data; it does not run analysis jobs.

question: A company runs a Python script on an employee's laptop to transform and update data that is stored in an Amazon RDS database. The company wants to migrate the transformation workload to the AWS Cloud. The solution must run the Python script every 30 minutes. Each run of the script takes approximately 20 seconds to update the data in the RDS database. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: A 20-second task every 30 minutes: pay only for those seconds.

options.A: Launch an Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance to run the Python script. Configure the EC2 instance to access the RDS database. Configure a cron job to invoke the Python script.
options.B: Launch an Amazon EC2 Spot Instance to run the Python script. Configure the EC2 instance to access the RDS database. Configure a cron job to invoke the Python script.
options.C: Configure an AWS Lambda function to access the RDS database. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the Lambda function.
options.D: Configure an AWS Lambda function to access the RDS database. Configure the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation: A is wrong: an always-on instance pays for about 29 idle minutes out of every 30.
B is wrong: a Spot Instance can be interrupted and still bills while idle.
C is correct: Lambda runs the 20-second script every 30 minutes and bills only for those seconds.
D is wrong: provisioned concurrency and API Gateway add cost for a scheduled task.
tldr: Short scheduled tasks are cheapest as Lambda functions invoked by EventBridge Scheduler.

wrong_reasons.A: an always-on instance pays for about 29 idle minutes out of every 30.
wrong_reasons.B: a Spot Instance can be interrupted and still bills while idle.
wrong_reasons.D: provisioned concurrency and API Gateway add cost for a scheduled task.

question: A company receives data transfers from a small number of external clients that use SFTP software on an Amazon EC2 instance. The clients use an SFTP client to upload data. The clients use SSH keys for authentication. Every hour, an automated script transfers new uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket for processing. The company wants to move the transfer process to an AWS managed service and to reduce the time required to start data processing. The company wants to retain the existing user management and SSH key generation process. The solution must not require clients to make significant changes to their existing processes. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: A managed SFTP server that writes straight to S3 and keeps SSH key users.

options.A: Reconfigure the script that runs on the EC2 instance to run every 15 minutes. Create an S3 Event Notifications rule for all new object creation events. Set an Amazon SNS topic as the destination.
options.B: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that uses the existing S3 bucket as a target. Use service-managed users to enable authentication.
options.C: Require clients to add the AWS DataSync agent into their local environments. Create an IAM user for each client that has permission to upload data to the target S3 bucket.
options.D: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP connector that has permission to access the target S3 bucket for each client. Store credentials in AWS Systems Manager. Create an IAM role to allow the SFTP connector to securely use the credentials.

explanation: A is wrong: the script still runs on a self-managed EC2 instance, and processing is still delayed.
B is correct: a Transfer Family SFTP server writes uploads directly to the S3 bucket, and service-managed users keep the existing SSH keys, so clients change nothing.
C is wrong: installing DataSync agents changes the clients' processes.
D is wrong: an SFTP connector sends files to remote servers; it does not receive uploads.
tldr: AWS Transfer Family SFTP writes uploads straight into S3, with service-managed users authenticated by SSH keys.

wrong_reasons.A: the script still runs on a self-managed EC2 instance, and processing is still delayed.
wrong_reasons.C: installing DataSync agents changes the clients' processes.
wrong_reasons.D: an SFTP connector sends files to remote servers; it does not receive uploads.

question: A company uses an organization in AWS Organizations to manage a multi-account landing zone. The company requires all users who access AWS accounts in the organization to use a centralized identity system that follows the principle of least privilege for operational tasks. The company currently uses an external identity provider (IdP). Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: One service centralizes access across the organization and connects to the external IdP; permission sets define least-privilege access.

options.A: Use IAM to create IAM users and IAM user groups in each AWS account.
options.B: Create permission sets in AWS IAM Identity Center. Assign the appropriate permission sets to the IAM users and IAM user groups in the accounts.
options.C: Assign each IAM user to an IAM role by using an inline IAM policy based on operational duties. Assign each role to the appropriate AWS account in the organization.
options.D: Configure a SAML identity provider in IAM in each AWS account to establish a trust relationship with the company's external IdP.
options.E: Enable AWS IAM Identity Center in the organization management account. Create user accounts and user groups.

explanation: A is wrong: IAM users in every account are not centralized.
B is correct: permission sets define least-privilege access for each job and are assigned to users and groups across accounts.
C is wrong: inline policies per user are not centralized and are hard to manage.
D is wrong: a SAML provider in every account is decentralized and repetitive.
E is correct: enabling IAM Identity Center in the management account centralizes identities and connects to the external IdP.
tldr: IAM Identity Center in the management account with permission sets gives central, least-privilege access across accounts.

wrong_reasons.A: IAM users in every account are not centralized.
wrong_reasons.C: inline policies per user are not centralized and are hard to manage.
wrong_reasons.D: a SAML provider in every account is decentralized and repetitive.

question: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances that run Amazon Linux. The instances are behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and are part of an Auto Scaling group. Each instance uses Amazon EBS volumes to store product manuals. New instances often have outdated data. The new instances occasionally take up to 30 minutes to receive updates from an external source. The company must ensure that all instances have up-to-date product manuals. The company needs a solution that can adapt quickly to increased demand. The solution must not require modifications for the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Put the manuals on shared storage every instance mounts.
keywords: New instances often have outdated data
must not require modifications for the application code

options.A: Store the product manuals on instance store volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance.
options.B: Store the product manuals in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the EC2 instances to download updates from the S3 bucket.
options.C: Store the product manuals in an Amazon EFS volume. Mount the EFS volume on the EC2 instances.
options.D: Store the product manuals in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Configure the EC2 instances to download updates from the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: instance store is local and temporary, so each instance still needs its own copy.
B is wrong: downloading from S3 needs code or scripts and still leaves copies out of date.
C is correct: EFS is mounted by every instance, so new instances see the current manuals immediately without code changes.
D is wrong: downloading copies still leaves them out of date, and Standard-IA adds retrieval fees.
tldr: Shared EFS storage gives every instance, including new ones, the same current files without code changes.

wrong_reasons.A: instance store is local and temporary, so each instance still needs its own copy.
wrong_reasons.B: downloading from S3 needs code or scripts and still leaves copies out of date.
wrong_reasons.D: downloading copies still leaves them out of date, and Standard-IA adds retrieval fees.

question: A company is designing a new web application that will run on Amazon EC2 Instances. The application will use Amazon DynamoDB for backend data storage. The application traffic will be unpredictable. The company expects that the application read and write throughput to the database will be moderate to high. The company needs to scale in response to application traffic. Which DynamoDB table configuration will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Unpredictable traffic points to one capacity mode. Is the data read rarely, or often?

options.A: Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
options.B: Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard table class.
options.C: Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
options.D: Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.

explanation: A is wrong: auto scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes and can throttle.
B is correct: on-demand mode scales instantly with unpredictable traffic, and the Standard class suits frequently accessed data.
C is wrong: Standard-IA raises the cost of reads and writes for busy tables.
D is wrong: Standard-IA suits rarely accessed data, not moderate-to-high throughput.
tldr: Unpredictable, active traffic: DynamoDB on-demand with the Standard table class.

wrong_reasons.A: auto scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes and can throttle.
wrong_reasons.C: Standard-IA raises the cost of reads and writes for busy tables.
wrong_reasons.D: Standard-IA suits rarely accessed data, not moderate-to-high throughput.

question: A marketing company provides services to customers through a web application. The web application uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL database to store customer data. The company has an existing analytics application in Amazon Redshift. The company wants to build a process that loads the customer data into the existing analytics application. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
hint: Is there a built-in integration that replicates Aurora data into Redshift with no pipeline?

options.A: Configure AWS DMS tasks to load the data.
options.B: Use a Redshift zero-ETL integration to load the data.
options.C: Use an AWS Glue Studio job to load the data.
options.D: Use Amazon EMR to configure Apache Spark jobs to load the data.

explanation: A is wrong: DMS tasks must be configured and monitored.
B is correct: zero-ETL integration replicates Aurora data into Redshift automatically, with no pipeline to build.
C is wrong: a Glue job is ETL you must build and schedule.
D is wrong: EMR Spark jobs are the most work.
tldr: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Redshift replicates data in near real time with no pipelines to build.

wrong_reasons.A: DMS tasks must be configured and monitored.
wrong_reasons.C: a Glue job is ETL you must build and schedule.
wrong_reasons.D: EMR Spark jobs are the most work.

question: A company is migrating its order processing system to the AWS Cloud. The order processing system must use exact message ordering, a highly available architecture, and loosely coupled components. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Ordered, managed queue plus serverless processing.

options.A: Ingest the orders in an Amazon SQS standard queue. Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the orders.
options.B: Push the orders to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the SNS topic to process the orders.
options.C: Push the orders to a stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the orders.
options.D: Ingest the orders in an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the orders.

explanation: A is wrong: standard queues do not guarantee order, and Spot Instances can be interrupted.
B is wrong: SNS standard topics do not guarantee order.
C is wrong: Kinesis orders records only per shard, and Spot Instances can be interrupted.
D is correct: a FIFO queue keeps orders in exact sequence, and Lambda processes them on managed, highly available compute.
tldr: SQS FIFO keeps exact order; Lambda processes messages with high availability and no servers.

wrong_reasons.A: standard queues do not guarantee order, and Spot Instances can be interrupted.
wrong_reasons.B: SNS standard topics do not guarantee order.
wrong_reasons.C: Kinesis orders records only per shard, and Spot Instances can be interrupted.

question: A company runs several applications on Amazon EC2 instances. The company stores configuration files in an Amazon S3 bucket. A solutions architect must provide the company's applications with access to the configuration files. The solutions architect must follow AWS best practices for security. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Applications on EC2 should use temporary credentials from a role.
keywords: configuration files in an Amazon S3 bucket

options.A: Use the AWS account root user access keys.
options.B: Use the AWS access key ID and the EC2 secret access key.
options.C: Use an IAM role to grant the necessary permissions to the applications.
options.D: Activate multi-factor authentication (MFA) and versioning on the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: root user access keys should never be used by applications.
B is wrong: stored access keys are long-term credentials that can leak.
C is correct: an IAM role gives the applications temporary credentials with only the permissions they need.
D is wrong: MFA delete and versioning protect objects; they do not grant access.
tldr: Applications on EC2 access AWS with an IAM role (instance profile), never stored keys.

wrong_reasons.A: root user access keys should never be used by applications.
wrong_reasons.B: stored access keys are long-term credentials that can leak.
wrong_reasons.D: MFA delete and versioning protect objects; they do not grant access.

question: A company creates a VPC that has one public subnet and one private subnet. The company attaches an internet gateway to the VPC. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the public subnet communicates with Amazon EC2 instances in the private subnet. The EC2 instances in the private subnet must be able to download operating system (OS) and application updates from the internet. The instances must not be accessible from the internet. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
hint: A NAT gateway lives in the public subnet, needs an Elastic IP, and the private subnet routes to it.
keywords: download operating system (OS) and application updates from the internet
must not be accessible from the internet

options.A: Associate an Elastic IP address with the NAT gateway.
options.B: Add a route of 0.0.0.0/0 to the private subnet route table. Set the NAT gateway as a target.
options.C: Deploy a NAT gateway in the public subnet.
options.D: Deploy a NAT gateway in the private subnet.
options.E: Add a route of 0.0.0.0/0 to the public subnet route table. Set the NAT gateway as a target.
options.F: Associate an Elastic IP address with the internet gateway.

explanation: A is correct: a public NAT gateway needs an Elastic IP address.
B is correct: the private subnet's default route must point to the NAT gateway.
C is correct: the NAT gateway must be in the public subnet, which routes to the internet gateway.
D is wrong: a NAT gateway in the private subnet cannot reach the internet gateway.
E is wrong: the public subnet's default route should point to the internet gateway, not the NAT gateway.
F is wrong: internet gateways do not take Elastic IP addresses.
tldr: Outbound-only internet: a NAT gateway with an Elastic IP in the public subnet, and a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it from the private subnet.

wrong_reasons.D: a NAT gateway in the private subnet cannot reach the internet gateway.
wrong_reasons.E: the public subnet's default route should point to the internet gateway, not the NAT gateway.
wrong_reasons.F: internet gateways do not take Elastic IP addresses.

question: A company runs an application that consists of multiple microservices. The company mandates that the microservices use messages to communicate with each other. The application must archive the microservices' messages for 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of development effort?
hint: Which bus routes and filters messages and has a built-in archive?
keywords: archive the microservices' messages for 30 days

options.A: Use an Amazon EventBridge event bus to route messages between the microservices. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Create an archive in Amazon EventBridge to store the messages for 30 days.
options.B: Use a single Amazon SNS topic to distribute the messages. Subscribe each microservice to the topic. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Use an Amazon SQS queue to store the messages for 30 days.
options.C: Use a single Amazon SNS topic to distribute the messages. Subscribe each microservice to the topic. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Store messages in an Amazon S3 bucket for 30 days.
options.D: Create a private Amazon API Gateway HTTP API for the microservices to send messages. Use an AWS Lambda function to forward the messages to the appropriate microservices based on query parameters. Archive messages in Amazon S3 for 30 days.

explanation: A is correct: EventBridge routes and filters messages between services, and a 30-day archive keeps them with no code.
B is wrong: an SQS queue is not an archive; messages are deleted when consumed.
C is wrong: writing messages to S3 needs extra code.
D is wrong: a custom API and Lambda router is a lot of development.
tldr: EventBridge routes and filters events and archives them for replay with no code.

wrong_reasons.B: an SQS queue is not an archive; messages are deleted when consumed.
wrong_reasons.C: writing messages to S3 needs extra code.
wrong_reasons.D: a custom API and Lambda router is a lot of development.

question: A company runs a critical Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone. The company must improve the availability of the DB instance. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Which RDS setting adds a standby in another Availability Zone?

options.A: Configure the DB instance to use a multi-Region DB instance deployment.
options.B: Create an Amazon SQS queue in the AWS Region where the company hosts the DB instance to manage writes to the DB instance.
options.C: Configure the DB instance to use a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.
options.D: Create an Amazon SQS queue in a different AWS Region than the Region where the company hosts the DB instance to manage writes to the DB instance.

explanation: A is wrong: RDS for MySQL has no multi-Region DB instance deployment.
B is wrong: a queue does not make the database available.
C is correct: a Multi-AZ deployment keeps a standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically.
D is wrong: a queue in another Region does not help database availability.
tldr: RDS Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby and automatic failover.

wrong_reasons.A: RDS for MySQL has no multi-Region DB instance deployment.
wrong_reasons.B: a queue does not make the database available.
wrong_reasons.D: a queue in another Region does not help database availability.

question: An e-commerce company hosts an API that handles sales requests. The company hosts the API frontend on Amazon EC2 instances that run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company hosts the API backend on EC2 instances that perform the transactions. The backend tiers are loosely coupled by an Amazon SQS queue. The company anticipates a significant increase in request volume during a new product launch event. The company wants to ensure that the API can handle increased loads successfully. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Scale each tier on its own signal: web traffic for the frontend, queue backlog for the backend.
keywords: loosely coupled by an Amazon SQS queue

options.A: Double the number of frontend and backend EC2 instances to handle the increased traffic during the product launch event. Create a dead-letter queue to retain unprocessed sales requests when the demand exceeds the system capacity.
options.B: Place the frontend EC2 instances into an Auto Scaling group. Create an Auto Scaling policy to launch new instances to handle the incoming network traffic.
options.C: Place the frontend EC2 instances into an Auto Scaling group. Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the ALB to reduce the amount of traffic the API needs to handle.
options.D: Place the frontend and backend EC2 instances into separate Auto Scaling groups. Create a policy for the frontend Auto Scaling group to launch instances based on incoming network traffic. Create a policy for the backend Auto Scaling group to launch instances based on the SQS queue backlog.

explanation: A is wrong: doubling capacity is a guess, and a dead-letter queue holds failed messages, not overflow.
B is wrong: scaling only the frontend leaves the backend as the bottleneck.
C is wrong: ElastiCache cannot sit in front of an ALB.
D is correct: separate Auto Scaling groups scale the frontend on traffic and the backend on the SQS backlog, so both tiers keep up.
tldr: Scale the frontend on traffic and SQS consumers on queue backlog, each in its own Auto Scaling group.

wrong_reasons.A: doubling capacity is a guess, and a dead-letter queue holds failed messages, not overflow.
wrong_reasons.B: scaling only the frontend leaves the backend as the bottleneck.
wrong_reasons.C: ElastiCache cannot sit in front of an ALB.

question: A company hosts an application on an Amazon EC2 instance. The application needs to access a MySQL database that the company hosts on a second EC2 instance. The EC2 instances are in separate VPCs within the same AWS account. The traffic between the application and MySQL database needs to be secure and private. What combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Connect the VPCs privately, then encrypt the database traffic.
keywords: separate VPCs within the same AWS account

options.A: Configure a VPC peering connection and routing between the VPCs.
options.B: Configure the application to use Amazon RDS Proxy to access the MySQL database.
options.C: Configure the MySQL instance to use an SSL certificate.
options.D: Ensure the public IP address of the application EC2 instance is allowed in the ACL of the VPC that contains the MySQL instance.
options.E: Ensure the security group ID of the application EC2 instance is allowed in the ACL of the VPC that contains the MySQL instance.

explanation: A is correct: VPC peering with routes lets the instances talk over private IP addresses.
B is wrong: RDS Proxy works only with RDS and Aurora, not a database on EC2.
C is correct: an SSL/TLS certificate on MySQL encrypts the traffic in transit.
D is wrong: public IP addresses mean traffic is not private.
E is wrong: network ACLs use CIDR ranges, not security group IDs.
tldr: Private cross-VPC database traffic: VPC peering for connectivity, TLS for encryption.

wrong_reasons.B: RDS Proxy works only with RDS and Aurora, not a database on EC2.
wrong_reasons.D: public IP addresses mean traffic is not private.
wrong_reasons.E: network ACLs use CIDR ranges, not security group IDs.

question: A solutions architect needs to optimize a large data analytics job that runs on an Amazon EMR cluster. The job takes 13 hours to finish. The cluster has multiple core nodes and worker nodes that are deployed on large, compute-optimized instances. After reviewing EMR logs, the solutions architect discovers that several nodes are idle for more than 5 hours while the job is running. The solutions architect needs to optimize cluster performance. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Nodes sit idle for hours. Let the cluster size follow the work.

options.A: Increase the number of core nodes to ensure there is enough processing power to handle the analytics job without any idle time.
options.B: Use the EMR managed scaling feature to automatically resize the cluster based on workload.
options.C: Migrate the analytics job to a set of AWS Lambda functions. Configure reserved concurrency for the functions.
options.D: Migrate the analytics job core nodes to a memory-optimized instance type to reduce the total job runtime.

explanation: A is wrong: more core nodes means even more idle capacity.
B is correct: managed scaling adds and removes nodes based on the workload, so the company stops paying for idle nodes.
C is wrong: a 13-hour analytics job does not fit Lambda's 15-minute limit.
D is wrong: different instance types do not fix nodes sitting idle.
tldr: EMR managed scaling resizes the cluster to the workload, removing idle nodes automatically.

wrong_reasons.A: more core nodes means even more idle capacity.
wrong_reasons.C: a 13-hour analytics job does not fit Lambda's 15-minute limit.
wrong_reasons.D: different instance types do not fix nodes sitting idle.

question: A company hosts a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group that scales in response to user demand. The company wants to optimize costs for the application but does not want to make any long-term commitments. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: No commitments rules out Reserved Instances. What is cheaper than On-Demand without a commitment?
keywords: scales in response to user demand
does not want to make any long-term commitments

options.A: Purchase Dedicated Instances only.
options.B: Purchase Reserved Instances with a partial upfront payment.
options.C: Purchase a mix of On-Demand Instances and Spot Instances.
options.D: Purchase a mix of On-Demand Instances and Reserved Instances.

explanation: A is wrong: Dedicated Instances cost more.
B is wrong: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment.
C is correct: On-Demand covers the baseline and Spot adds cheap extra capacity, with no commitment.
D is wrong: Reserved Instances are a long-term commitment.
tldr: Without commitments, mix On-Demand for the baseline with Spot for extra capacity.

wrong_reasons.A: Dedicated Instances cost more.
wrong_reasons.B: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment.
wrong_reasons.D: Reserved Instances are a long-term commitment.

question: A company runs a website on Amazon EC2 instances. Clients use the HTTP protocol to connect to the application. The company does not want the EC2 instances to have internet access. However, the application should remain available through the internet. The application must scale in response to traffic demands. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Public load balancer for HTTP, private instances with no internet route.
keywords: does not want the EC2 instances to have internet access
scale in response to traffic demands

options.A: Host the application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an internet-facing Network Load Balancer (NLB). Launch the EC2 instances in public subnets that use an internet gateway.
options.B: Host the application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an internet-facing Network Load Balancer (NLB). Launch the EC2 instances in private subnets that do not have internet access.
options.C: Host the application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB). Launch the EC2 instances in private subnets that do not have internet access.
options.D: Host the application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB). Launch the EC2 instances in public subnets that use an internet gateway.

explanation: A is wrong: instances in public subnets with an internet gateway have internet access.
B is wrong: this works, but an ALB is the load balancer designed for HTTP traffic.
C is correct: an internet-facing ALB serves HTTP clients, while the instances stay in private subnets without internet access and scale with Auto Scaling.
D is wrong: public subnets give the instances internet access.
tldr: Internet-facing ALB in public subnets, instances in private subnets with no internet route, scaled by Auto Scaling.

wrong_reasons.A: instances in public subnets with an internet gateway have internet access.
wrong_reasons.B: this works, but an ALB is the load balancer designed for HTTP traffic.
wrong_reasons.D: public subnets give the instances internet access.

question: A gaming company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to make files available for download for users around the world. The CloudFront distribution has a custom origin. The company wants to customize the files that are served to users from the cache and origin based on the country where each user is located. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: For the cache to hold a different file per country, the country header must be part of the cache key. Which policy sets the cache key?
keywords: from the cache and origin based on the country

options.A: Create an origin request policy. Attach the origin request policy to a cache behavior configuration.
options.B: Create a response header policy. Attach the response header policy to a cache behavior configuration.
options.C: Create a cache policy. Attach the cache policy to a cache behavior configuration.
options.D: Add a custom CloudFront-Viewer-Country header to the CloudFront origin.

explanation: A is wrong: an origin request policy forwards the header to the origin but does not add it to the cache key, so every country would get whichever version was cached first.
B is wrong: response headers policies add headers to responses; they do not change which file is served.

C is correct: a cache policy that includes CloudFront-Viewer-Country caches a separate version for each country and passes the header to the origin, so both cache and origin responses are country-specific.
D is wrong: CloudFront generates the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header itself; adding a custom origin header does not use the viewer's location.
tldr: To vary cached content by viewer country, add CloudFront-Viewer-Country to the cache policy (cache key); that also forwards it to the origin.

wrong_reasons.A: an origin request policy forwards the header to the origin but does not add it to the cache key, so every country would get whichever version was cached first.
wrong_reasons.B: response headers policies add headers to responses; they do not change which file is served.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudFront generates the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header itself; adding a custom origin header does not use the viewer's location.

question: A company is designing a new application that uploads files to an Amazon S3 bucket. The uploaded files are processed to extract metadata. Processing must take less than 5 seconds. The volume and frequency of the uploads vary from a few files each hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Short, event-driven processing that scales from nothing to hundreds at once.
keywords: few files each hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads

options.A: Configure AWS CloudTrail trails to log Amazon S3 API calls. Use AWS AppSync to process the files.
options.B: Configure a new object created S3 event notification within the bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the files.
options.C: Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to deliver the files to the S3 bucket. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the files.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance. Create a script that lists all files in the S3 bucket and processes new files. Use a cron job that runs every minute to run the script.

explanation: A is wrong: CloudTrail logging is not a trigger for processing, and AppSync is a GraphQL API service.
B is correct: an S3 event invokes Lambda for each new object, which scales with concurrent uploads and costs nothing when idle.
C is wrong: Kinesis Data Streams does not deliver files to S3, and a stream adds cost.
D is wrong: an always-on instance polling every minute costs more and adds delay.
tldr: S3 event notifications invoking Lambda process each upload on arrival, scaling automatically and costing nothing when idle.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudTrail logging is not a trigger for processing, and AppSync is a GraphQL API service.
wrong_reasons.C: Kinesis Data Streams does not deliver files to S3, and a stream adds cost.
wrong_reasons.D: an always-on instance polling every minute costs more and adds delay.

question: An application is experiencing performance issues based on increased demand. This increased demand is on read-only historical records pulled from an Amazon RDS-hosted database with custom views and queries. A solutions architect must improve performance without changing the database structure. Which approach will improve performance and MINIMIZE management overhead?
hint: Managed in-memory cache in front of RDS.

options.A: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB, move all the data, and point to DynamoDB.
options.B: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) and cache the data for the application.
options.C: Deploy Memcached on Amazon EC2 and cache the data for the application.
options.D: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) on Amazon RDS to improve cache performance.

explanation: A is wrong: moving to DynamoDB changes the database structure.
B is correct: ElastiCache for Redis is a managed cache that serves the repeated reads from memory without changing the database.
C is wrong: self-managed Memcached on EC2 adds operational work.
D is wrong: DAX works only with DynamoDB.
tldr: Managed ElastiCache (Redis) caches repeated reads in front of RDS with little operational work.

wrong_reasons.A: moving to DynamoDB changes the database structure.
wrong_reasons.C: self-managed Memcached on EC2 adds operational work.
wrong_reasons.D: DAX works only with DynamoDB.

question: A company has multiple petabytes (PB) of media files that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region. The company wants to move all the data to an S3 bucket in the us-west-2 Region as soon as possible. The company needs a data migration solution. The data needs to be verified after it is copied. The company also needs to have visibility into the data movement process. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Managed S3-to-S3 transfer with verification and reporting, in the mode built for very large datasets.
keywords: visibility into the data movement process

options.A: Use the AWS CLI to increase the max_concurrent_requests parameter value to 20 in the AWS CLI configuration. Use the AWS CLI to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.B: Use AWS DataSync with Basic mode to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.C: Use AWS DataSync with Enhanced mode to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.D: Use AWS DataSync with an agent that is deployed on an Amazon EC2 instance in eu-west-1 to move the data from the source bucket to the destination bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: the CLI gives no managed verification or progress visibility at petabyte scale.
B is wrong: Basic mode has lower performance and object-count limits for datasets this large.
C is correct: DataSync Enhanced mode copies very large S3 datasets quickly, verifies the data and reports detailed progress, with no agent.
D is wrong: no agent is needed for S3 to S3 transfers, and running one adds overhead.
tldr: DataSync Enhanced mode moves very large S3 datasets between Regions with verification, detailed metrics and higher performance.

wrong_reasons.A: the CLI gives no managed verification or progress visibility at petabyte scale.
wrong_reasons.B: Basic mode has lower performance and object-count limits for datasets this large.
wrong_reasons.D: no agent is needed for S3 to S3 transfers, and running one adds overhead.

question: A company wants to run transient workloads in an Amazon EMR cluster that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to use On-Demand Instances for core nodes and Spot Instances for task nodes. The company wants to use memory optimized EC2 instances to launch EMR clusters in the AWS Region where the company operates. The company has configured multiple subnets in multiple Availability Zones. The company must ensure that the EMR clusters are launched only in Availability Zones where specified instance types and purchasing options are available. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
hint: Which EMR configuration picks the best Availability Zone from several subnets based on capacity?
keywords: On-Demand Instances for core nodes and Spot Instances for task nodes
only in Availability Zones where specified instance types and purchasing options are available

options.A: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.B: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.
options.C: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.D: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.

explanation: A is wrong: instance groups use a single subnet and cannot choose between Availability Zones.
B is wrong: instance groups do not evaluate Availability Zone capacity.
C is correct: instance fleets across several subnets let EMR launch in an Availability Zone that has the requested instance types and purchasing options.
D is wrong: a single subnet leaves no choice of Availability Zone.
tldr: EMR instance fleets with multiple subnets let EMR choose an AZ that has the requested instance types and purchase options.

wrong_reasons.A: instance groups use a single subnet and cannot choose between Availability Zones.
wrong_reasons.B: instance groups do not evaluate Availability Zone capacity.
wrong_reasons.D: a single subnet leaves no choice of Availability Zone.

question: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances. The website processes classified data. The company stores the processed data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Because of security concerns, the company must ensure that traffic between the EC2 instances and the S3 bucket does not use public IP addresses. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Private path from EC2 to S3.
keywords: does not use public IP addresses

options.A: Create a gateway endpoint for the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 bucket policy to allow access from the endpoint.
options.B: Create an EC2 instance profile. Create an IAM policy to grant access from the EC2 instance IP addresses to the S3 bucket. Attach the IAM policy to the instance profile.
options.C: Create a NAT gateway. Update the VPC route table to route the prefixes defined by the AWS-managed S3 prefix list to the NAT gateway.
options.D: Create an IAM user that has an access key ID and a secret access key. Configure the EC2 instances to use the IAM user credentials to access the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct: a gateway endpoint keeps the traffic on private routes, and the bucket policy can limit access to that endpoint.
B is wrong: an IAM policy controls permissions, not the network path.
C is wrong: a NAT gateway still uses public IP addresses to reach S3.
D is wrong: IAM user keys do not change the network path and are insecure.
tldr: A gateway endpoint keeps EC2 to S3 traffic private; a bucket policy can limit access to that endpoint.

wrong_reasons.B: an IAM policy controls permissions, not the network path.
wrong_reasons.C: a NAT gateway still uses public IP addresses to reach S3.
wrong_reasons.D: IAM user keys do not change the network path and are insecure.

question: A company is building a new application that processes sensitive customer data. All data must comply with a data retention policy. The data must be immutable for 5 years. The data must be deleted after 10 years. The company decides to use Amazon S3 for storage and enables S3 Versioning. Which S3 configuration will meet these requirements?
hint: Truly immutable for 5 years, then deleted automatically at 10.

options.A: Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.
options.B: Configure S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a retention period of 5 years. Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.
options.C: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 10 years.
options.D: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 5 years. Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.

explanation: A is wrong: lifecycle deletion alone does not make data immutable.
B is wrong: governance mode can be bypassed, so data is not truly immutable.
C is wrong: a 10-year lock keeps data immutable longer than required and does not delete it.
D is correct: compliance mode makes the data immutable for 5 years, and a lifecycle rule deletes it after 10 years.
tldr: Object Lock compliance mode for the immutable period, plus a lifecycle rule to delete at the end of retention.

wrong_reasons.A: lifecycle deletion alone does not make data immutable.
wrong_reasons.B: governance mode can be bypassed, so data is not truly immutable.
wrong_reasons.C: a 10-year lock keeps data immutable longer than required and does not delete it.

question: A company stores petabytes of historical medical information on premises. The company has a process to manage encryption of the data to comply with regulations. The company needs a cloud-based solution for data backup, recovery, and archiving. The company must retain control over the encryption key material. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Keeping control of key material means importing your own into KMS, or supplying the key yourself with each request.
keywords: retain control over the encryption key material

options.A: Create an AWS KMS key without key material. Import the company's key material into the KMS key.
options.B: Create an AWS KMS encryption key that contains key material generated by AWS KMS.
options.C: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage. Use S3 Bucket Keys with AWS KMS keys.
options.D: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Glacier storage class. Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C).
options.E: Store the data in AWS Snowball devices. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).

explanation: A is correct: a KMS key with imported key material lets the company keep control of the material and delete it when needed.
B is wrong: key material generated by KMS is not controlled by the company.
C is wrong: Standard-IA is costlier than Glacier for archiving petabytes, and nothing here uses the company's own key material.

D is correct: S3 Glacier is the low-cost archive tier, and SSE-C means the company supplies its own key with every request; since April 2026 S3 blocks SSE-C by default on new buckets, so it must first be enabled on the bucket with PutBucketEncryption.
E is wrong: Snowball devices are for moving data, not ongoing backup and archive.
tldr: To keep control of key material: import your own material into KMS, or use SSE-C, where you supply the key with each request (SSE-C must now be enabled on the bucket first).

wrong_reasons.B: key material generated by KMS is not controlled by the company.
wrong_reasons.C: Standard-IA is costlier than Glacier for archiving petabytes, and nothing here uses the company's own key material.
wrong_reasons.E: Snowball devices are for moving data, not ongoing backup and archive.

question: A company stores data in Amazon S3. According to regulations, the data must not contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company recently discovered that S3 buckets have some objects that contain PII. The company needs to automatically detect PII in S3 buckets and to notify the company's security team. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: One service detects PII in S3; findings flow through EventBridge to a notification service.
keywords: automatically detect PII in S3 buckets

options.A: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon SNS notification to the security team.
options.B: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon SNS notification to the security team.
options.C: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData: S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon SQS notification to the security team.
options.D: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon SQS notification to the security team.

explanation: A is correct: Macie detects PII in S3, and an EventBridge rule on its sensitive-data findings sends an SNS notification to the security team.
B is wrong: GuardDuty detects threats, not PII in objects.
C is wrong: Macie is right, but SQS queues messages for programs; it does not notify people.
D is wrong: GuardDuty does not detect PII, and SQS does not notify people.
tldr: Macie detects PII in S3; route its SensitiveData findings through EventBridge to SNS to alert the team.

wrong_reasons.B: GuardDuty detects threats, not PII in objects.
wrong_reasons.C: Macie is right, but SQS queues messages for programs; it does not notify people.
wrong_reasons.D: GuardDuty does not detect PII, and SQS does not notify people.

question: A company is launching a new product and needs to collect data about the product's usage frequency. The company will review the data in an existing Amazon QuickSight dashboard. The data is in multiple formats, including Parquet, JSON, and CSV. The company wants to unify the data format and review the data by using ready-made SQL queries without using external tools. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Collect usage data into S3, convert it to one format, then query it with SQL that QuickSight can use.

options.A: Collect product data by using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Send the data to Amazon Data Firehose for processing. Set up a partition schema. Save the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.B: Set up an AWS Glue transformation job to convert data into Parquet format. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Prepare Amazon Athena queries for data reporting. Authorize connection access from the QuickSight dashboard to Athena.
options.C: Create an Amazon Managed Grafana dashboard that has prebuilt queries. Use Amazon CloudWatch as the data source. Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to run an AWS Lambda function that loads data from Amazon S3 into CloudWatch custom metrics.
options.D: Collect product information by using an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Integrate an AWS Lambda function with the REST API. Configure the Lambda function to sort data into a partition schema and store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.E: Set up an AWS Step Functions workflow to convert data into Parquet format. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct: Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose collect the usage data and store it in S3, partitioned for querying.
B is correct: a Glue job converts everything to Parquet, Athena runs saved SQL queries, and QuickSight connects to Athena.
C is wrong: Grafana and CloudWatch metrics are for monitoring, not SQL reporting on product data.
D is wrong: a custom Lambda function behind API Gateway to partition data is more work than Firehose.
E is wrong: Step Functions orchestrates steps; it does not convert data formats itself.
tldr: Kinesis and Firehose land usage data in S3; Glue converts it to Parquet; Athena queries feed QuickSight.

wrong_reasons.C: Grafana and CloudWatch metrics are for monitoring, not SQL reporting on product data.
wrong_reasons.D: a custom Lambda function behind API Gateway to partition data is more work than Firehose.
wrong_reasons.E: Step Functions orchestrates steps; it does not convert data formats itself.
